issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## Description

Follow-up to #6304, which drove the 90B-total / 5.3B-active Grug MoE from 2.8% to **9.37% MFU** (3.3×, batch 1024 × seq 2048 + `save_moe`) on 256 H100 / cw-us-east-02a and exhausted the config/flag and microbatching lever space. This issue tracks the remaining **deeper levers** required to push past ~9.4% — each is a multi-session change with uncertain payoff, deliberately deferred rather than burned on speculatively.

### Where the campaign landed (the binding constraints)

- **Comm-bound:** ~82% of step time is communication, dominated by per-tensor FSDP all-gathers (47.5K gathers/step trace @ ~2.65µs avg — i.e. small and largely *latency*-bound, not bandwidth-bound).
- **Memory-capped at the throughput-optimal batch:** at batch 1024 the model fills HBM; batch ≥1536, seq 4096, and combine-flag buffers all OOM. The batch-scaling hog is the replicated `[B,S,H]` embedding-backward cotangent (~13 GB/dev @ 1024).
- **Microbatching is a memory tool, not an MFU lever:** it fits batch 1536 but *drops* MFU to 7.18%, because FSDP re-gathers the sharded params on every microbatch (gathered params can't be held across microbatches), so N microbatches ≈ N× gather traffic. To raise MFU you must cut gather cost **per token**, not add microbatches.

### Remaining levers (ranked)

1. **bf16 FSDP gathers with f32 master weights** — halve the all-gather bytes while keeping f32 optimizer state. Bounded but modest (gathers are partly latency-bound) and conditional: a GPU HLO dump must first confirm XLA isn't already up-converting `param→f32` before the gather (the CPU probe showed the gather dtype is pinned to the dot's operand dtype). Needs a communication/gather dtype distinct from `param_dtype` in the trainer, cast *before* the FSDP reshard. Recon anchors: `trainer_state.py` `cast_params_by_trainability`, `trainer.py` `cast_to_compute` + `parameter/compute_axis_mapping`, optimizer init on f32.
2. **Activation offload to host** (`jax.checkpoint_policies.save_and_offload_only_these_names`, available in the pinned jax 0.10.0) — the *correct* memory lever, unlike microbatch: it keeps a single forward pass (no re-gather) while cutting activation HBM, enabling a bigger *single-pass* batch → more tokens per gather → higher MFU. Caveat: the replicated embed cotangent is outside the block remat scope, so offloading block activations alone may not move the OOM ceiling; pair with a fix for the embedding-backward replication.
3. **Reduce gathers per token via a different parallelism** — pipeline or tensor parallelism to cut per-step all-gathers. Hybrid FSDP (replicate params within node) is memory-blocked at 90B. Largest change, highest ceiling.
4. **Model shape with higher compute-per-gather** — e.g. larger hidden / different expert granularity so each FSDP gather amortizes over more FLOPs. Changes the model, not just the harness.

### Definition of Done

- A GPU HLO dump settles whether the FSDP param all-gather is f32 or bf16 on the H100 backend (decides whether lever 1 has headroom).
- At least one of levers 1–3 is implemented behind an explicit launcher knob, validated for numerical correctness (CPU equivalence test) and A/B'd at scale against the 712K tok/s / 9.37% MFU baseline, with the result posted to #6304.
- If no lever beats ~9.4% materially, that negative is recorded and ~9.4% is documented as the practical pure-FSDP ceiling for this model/cluster.

Full experiment log, profiles, and per-lever reasoning: #6304.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Scope: tracking issue, no PR.** This is the deferred-levers tracker for the #6304 campaign — each lever is a multi-session change needing a 256×H100 A/B and (lever 1) a GPU HLO dump. The "Definition of Done" requires at-scale validation, not a self-contained code change, so per the fix-issue scope rules this is an analysis comment, not a PR. I confirmed the code-level precondition for lever 1 below; the at-scale work needs a human with cluster access.

# Research

The campaign is comm-bound on per-tensor FSDP all-gathers that are latency-bound (~2.65µs avg, small tensors), so the levers that pay off are the ones that cut **gather bytes or gathers per token**, not bandwidth.

Lever 1's precondition is verifiable in code: the FSDP gather runs on **f32 master weights**, because the compute-dtype cast happens *inside* the loss function, after the params are resharded/gathered for the forward dot. So `param_dtype` (f32) is what gets gathered, and halving gather bytes genuinely requires a separate communication dtype cast *before* the reshard — exactly as the issue states. Whether XLA already down-converts is the open question the HLO dump settles.

**Relevant code**
- [`trainer_state.py#L207-L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer_state.py#L207-L215) — `cast_params_by_trainability`: trainables → `cast_to_param` (f32 master); these are what FSDP gathers
- [`trainer.py#L220-L227`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L220-L227) — `cast_to_compute(model)` runs *inside* the loss fn, i.e. after the gather → gather dtype = `param_dtype`
- [`trainer.py#L659-L674`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L659-L674) — train step jitted with `axis_resources=parameter_axis_mapping` (FSDP partitioning)
- [`trainer.py#L796`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L796) — `mp` policy default `f32`; single dtype, no comm/gather dtype distinct from `param_dtype`
- [`trainer_state.py#L176-L182`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer_state.py#L176-L182) — optimizer inits on the cast (f32) trainables

# Proposed approach (for human review)

Order by cost-to-decide, cheapest first:

1. **Gate first (cheap, no code):** GPU HLO dump on the H100 backend to read the FSDP param all-gather operand dtype. If XLA already gathers in bf16, lever 1 has **no headroom** — record and skip. The earlier f32 finding was a CPU probe; the HLO dump is the authoritative check and unblocks everything else.
2. **If gathered as f32 → lever 1:** add a communication/gather dtype to the `mp` policy distinct from `param_dtype`, cast trainables to it *before* the reshard (the gather point above) while keeping f32 optimizer state and master weights. Validate with a CPU numerical-equivalence test, then A/B against the 712K tok/s / 9.37% MFU baseline. Bounded upside (gathers are partly latency-bound), but it is the smallest change.
3. **Lever 2 (activation offload):** `save_and_offload_only_these_names` is available in the pinned jax 0.10.0 and is the *correct* memory lever (single forward pass, no re-gather). Caveat from the campaign: the replicated `[B,S,H]` embedding-backward cotangent sits outside block remat, so offloading block activations alone likely won't move the OOM ceiling — pair with an embedding-backward replication fix or it stalls.
4. **Levers 3–4 (parallelism / model shape):** largest changes, highest ceiling; only worth starting if 1–2 don't clear ~9.4%.

Each lever wants its own implementation PR behind an explicit launcher knob; results post back to #6304. If none materially beats ~9.4%, that negative gets recorded as the practical pure-FSDP ceiling for this model/cluster, per the DoD.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
🤖 *(filed by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

## Motivation

[#6136](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6136) demonstrated that `tpu-inference`'s vllm-impl (torch-XLA) path produces catastrophic decode (72-93% trace failures) on multi-host `v5p-32` + DP=2 + `max_num_seqs ≥ 4` for Qwen3.5-122B-FP8. The same hardware/orchestration stack serves Gemma4-31B cleanly because Gemma takes the **`flax_nnx`** path — a fully native JAX/Flax implementation that bypasses torch-XLA compilation entirely.

Until the upstream bug is fixed, the only safe way to serve a newly-released HF model at the scales we care about is to **port it to Haliax/Equinox** (Levanter's flax-native model framework) and serve it through `tpu-inference`'s `flax_nnx` path. We already have the underlying recipe ([`port-models.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/docs/recipes/port-models.md) + the long-form [`Port-Models.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/docs/dev/Port-Models.md)) but no playbook framed for the agent-as-author case, and no explicit linkage to the "do this to avoid the buggy torch-XLA serving path" framing.

## Deliverable

A new agent skill at `.agents/skills/port-model-to-flax/SKILL.md` following the existing skill format (see `.agents/skills/add-pallas-kernel/SKILL.md` for shape — frontmatter `name:` + `description:`, narrative body, references to canonical docs).

The skill should walk an agent through:

1. **Triage** — when is porting worth it? Decision flowchart: (a) HF model, (b) needs multi-host TPU serving OR `max_num_seqs ≥ 4`, (c) no existing flax_nnx implementation in `tpu-inference` → port. Otherwise skip.
2. **Reference reading** — point at `port-models.md` (concise) + `Port-Models.md` (long-form) + `llama.py` / `mixtral.py` as canonical examples.
3. **Implementation checklist** — config (`HFCompatConfig`), modules (`Embedding` / `Block` / `Transformer` / `LMHead` via `equinox.Module` + `haliax.NamedArray`), state-dict round-trip helpers (`_state_dict_key_map`, `to_state_dict` / `from_state_dict`), register with `LmConfig.register_subclass`.
4. **Numerics gates** — `chex.assert_trees_all_close` tolerances `1e-4` (complex modules) / `1e-5` (simple modules) per the recipe; never relax without explicit approval; per-module unit tests against the HF counterpart before full-stack comparison.
5. **Serving integration** — how to register the new flax model in `tpu-inference` so it picks the `flax_nnx` path; how to verify at runtime (`MODEL_IMPL_TYPE=auto` resolves to `flax_nnx`; log line on serve confirms).
6. **Validation harness** — round-trip serialization + output parity vs HF model on small inputs; once that passes, end-to-end trace-quality smoke (32k context, seqs=64, sample ~10 trajectories, manual / programmatic eyeball for incoherence/repetition along the same axes as the [Qwen audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6136)).

## Acceptance criteria

- `.agents/skills/port-model-to-flax/SKILL.md` exists and follows the peer skills' frontmatter shape (`name:` + `description:`).
- References the two existing port-models docs explicitly with file paths.
- Cross-links #6136 in the motivation so the next agent knows why this skill exists.
- Includes a `# Quickstart` block listing the minimal commands an agent runs end-to-end on a small test model (e.g. a tiny LLaMA-shaped release) for a smoke pass through all six steps above.
- Does NOT actually port a model — that's a separate issue once the skill lands.

## Out of scope

- Performing any specific port (Qwen 3.5, MiniMax, etc.) — those are individual follow-up issues that should *use* this skill.
- Fixing the upstream vllm-impl bug — tracked at #6136.
- Rewriting `port-models.md` itself unless gaps are discovered while writing the skill.

## Related

- #6136 — torch-XLA decode bug; motivation for this skill
- [`lib/levanter/docs/recipes/port-models.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/docs/recipes/port-models.md)
- [`lib/levanter/docs/dev/Port-Models.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/docs/dev/Port-Models.md)
- [`lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/llama.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/llama.py) — canonical port reference
- [`.agents/skills/add-pallas-kernel/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/add-pallas-kernel/SKILL.md) — peer skill shape

issues.author: RohithKuditipudi
issues.body:
🤖 Drafted with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code).

## TL;DR

A single launch should be able to absorb TPU capacity wherever it's available across regions, with `--prefix mirror://` handling dedup. iris natively supports this via `region IN [a, b, c]` constraints, but marin's executor pre-collapses each TPU step's allowed regions to a single one before fray builds the JobRequest, so iris's per-job multi-region matching never runs. Two design options below (one targeted patch, one structural simplification). Maintainer input on which direction to pursue would unblock a PR.

## Motivation

The goal is to run executor steps in whichever region has available TPU capacity and dedup completed work across regions via `mirror://`. iris already supports per-job multi-region matching (`region_constraint` with `op=IN`, `iris/cluster/constraints.py:329`) — its scheduler picks across listed regions by capacity. Marin's executor is what prevents that from working.

## What the executor does today

`_resolve_steps` runs three things per TPU step before submission:

1. **`_step_dag_tpu_regions`** (`executor.py:424`) queries the iris autoscaler via `_regions_for_tpu_variants_from_iris` (`:356`) for which regions have the requested variant. The recursive `regions_for_step` also propagates upward: a CPU step inherits the region set of any TPU dependents. So a CPU prompts step that has TPU completion-cell dependents ends up with a non-`None` `dag_tpu_regions`.

2. **`_component_tpu_pins`** (`:468`) builds adjacency over `relevant_steps` (steps with `dag_tpu_regions != None`), walks connected components, and for each one picks `chosen_region = sorted(component_regions)[0]` (`:531`). Every step in the component gets pinned to that single region.

3. **`_maybe_attach_inferred_region_constraint`** (`:547`) receives `forced_region=chosen_region` and rewrites `step.fn.resources.regions = [chosen_region]`.

Fray then turns that into `region IN [chosen_region]` — a one-element constraint — on the JobRequest. The iris client (`iris/client/client.py:643`) sees a region constraint exists and skips its auto-inherit branch. iris's scheduler is left with a single-region constraint and can only place there.

## Worst case: eval sweeps

`make_eval_step` (`experiments/downstream_scaling/evals/framework/core.py`) produces `prompts (CPU) → completions (TPU) → grade (CPU)` per cell, with the **prompts step shared** across all cells with the same task config (executor dedups by hash). Upward propagation in `_step_dag_tpu_regions` means the shared prompts step ends up with a non-`None` `dag_tpu_regions`, gets pulled into `relevant_steps`, and forms an adjacency edge to every completion cell. The result: `prompts ∪ {all completion cells}` is one giant connected component, and the entire sweep collapses to `sorted(component_regions)[0]` — a single region — even though every cell is independent and there's no genuine gang-scheduling requirement.

## Why iris-level mechanisms can't substitute

`CoschedulingConfig(group_by=...)` (`iris/cluster/types.py:380`) ensures tasks **within a single iris job** share a worker attribute value (e.g., `tpu-name` for multi-host TPU pods). It's per-job, not cross-job. Marin submits each executor step as its own iris job, so iris coscheduling can't coordinate region placement across multiple steps. For genuine multi-step TPU pipelines that need gang scheduling, marin is the only layer that can enforce same-region placement.

## Existing workarounds and why none are sufficient

- **`iris job run --region a --region b ...`**: iris picks one region for the orchestrator; everything inherits it. Achieves "any region at launch" but not "any TPU per job."
- **Multiple staggered launches** sharing work via `mirror://`: works but adds operational complexity, and the per-step lock is per-bucket under `mirror://` (writes go to `gs://marin-{local}/.../.executor_status.lock`), so concurrent orchestrators in different regions can both succeed on `try_acquire_lock` for the same unclaimed cell. The `should_run` polling loop (`executor_step_status.py:186`) handles the case where the lock is *already visible* to another orchestrator via mirror scan, but doesn't close the acquisition-time race.
- **Restructure algorithms into CPU-executor-step + nested-fray-TPU shape** (what `iid_zephyr.py` and `rerank.py` already do): bypasses the executor's pinning because the outer step is CPU. Works, but requires rewriting `joint_decode.py` / `joint_decode_avg.py` (and any future TPU-on-executor-step algorithm) — not general.

None of these match "single launch, jobs go to any region with capacity" cleanly.

## Proposed fix — two options

Both are contained to `lib/marin/src/marin/execution/executor.py`. Run scripts and algorithms stay as they are; `worker_resources=ResourceConfig.with_tpu(tpu_types)` with `regions` unset is sufficient.

### Option A — targeted patch

Two coordinated edits.

**(a)** In `_step_dag_tpu_regions`'s `regions_for_step`, return `None` immediately when the step is CPU instead of iterating dependents:

```python
if step_regions is None:
    reachable_tpu_regions[step] = None
    return None
```

inserted between the `step_regions = _tpu_regions_for_remote_callable(...)` assignment and the existing `downstream_tpu_regions = step_regions` line.

**(b)** In `_component_tpu_pins`, short-circuit single-step components:

```python
if len(component) == 1:
    continue
```

inserted between the component-building `while stack:` loop and the `component_regions: set[str] | None = None` initialization.

Effect: standalone TPU steps fall through `_maybe_attach_inferred_region_constraint`'s `regions = sorted(allowed_regions)` branch, fray attaches `region IN [...]`, iris auto-inherit skips because a constraint is present, iris's scheduler picks per-job by capacity. Multi-step TPU-direct components (TPU↔TPU edges, after edit (a) removes CPU intermediaries) still get pinned the way they do today.

### Option B — region-agnostic executor

Delete `_step_dag_tpu_regions`, `_component_tpu_pins`, and the forced-region path in `_maybe_attach_inferred_region_constraint`. The executor stops inferring or rewriting regions. Scripts set `regions=` explicitly on TPU resources:

```python
ALLOWED_REGIONS = ["us-east5", "europe-west4", "us-central1"]
worker_resources=ResourceConfig.with_tpu(tpu_types, regions=ALLOWED_REGIONS)
```

iris auto-inherit doesn't override an existing constraint; iris's scheduler picks per-job. CPU steps without `regions` set inherit parent's region naturally. Multi-step TPU gang scheduling becomes script-author responsibility (set the same single region across the relevant steps).

## Tradeoff

- **Option A** preserves the framework's auto-inference for TPU steps and keeps run scripts plumbing-free, at the cost of keeping the TPU/CPU distinction inside the executor.
- **Option B** is structurally simpler — executor knows nothing about regions — but pushes the explicit region list into every TPU-using run script and makes gang scheduling a script-level concern.

## Open questions for maintainers

- Are there pipelines in `experiments/` that rely on TPU-CPU-TPU chains for cross-step gang scheduling? After option A (a), the CPU intermediary no longer bridges upstream and downstream TPU steps in the component graph, so they'd land in separate components and could go to different regions. If this case exists and matters, option A needs a different formulation; option B makes the requirement explicit at the script level.
- Should the multi-region list come from the iris autoscaler's *configured* groups (current behavior of `_regions_for_tpu_variant_from_iris`) or from a more conservative source (live capacity, allow-list)?
- Anything specific the fallthrough's `sorted(allowed_regions)` ordering should preserve for iris?

## Acceptance criteria

A single `executor_main` launch with `--prefix mirror://` and `worker_resources=ResourceConfig.with_tpu(tpu_types)` (no `regions=` set in script) results in:

- Each TPU step's JobRequest carries `region IN [autoscaler-configured regions]` rather than `region IN [single]`.
- iris's scheduler distributes the cells across regions according to live capacity.
- `mirror://` dedups completed cells across regions correctly.
- No regression for multi-step TPU pipelines that genuinely need gang scheduling (single-region pinning still happens for size > 1 TPU components under option A).

issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
🤖 Agent-generated issue (summary of an autonomous experiment run).

## Goal
Port the PyTorch `HybridMuon` optimizer (`opt_a` / `opt_f` variants, from github.com/mahyarjn80/Opt_Smuon) to JAX/Levanter and reproduce the PRISM-Berkeley Qwen3 scaling LR-sweep setting (#4933) with it, to compare the two variants. Code in PR #6118. W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/speedrun (runs `qwen3_{size}_hybrid_muon_{a,f}_4096_lrx*`).

## Optimizer
HybridMuon = Muon Newton–Schulz orthogonalization of the (Nesterov) momentum, blended with a nuclear-norm/effective-rank rescaling (two closed-form blends, "a" and "f"). Nuclear norm via the polar-factor identity `⟨orth,g⟩=‖g‖_*`. Linear weights → hybrid transform; embeddings/lm_head/bias → AdamW. Details in PR #6118.

## Setup (reproducing #4933, trimmed)
- Sizes 130m / 300m / 520m (llama presets → Qwen3, seq 4096), fineweb-edu-10B, linear schedule, per-size centers/batch/steps from #4933.
- LR sweep: {0.5, 0.75, 1.0} × per-size center, both variants. (Trimmed from the original {0.5…1.5}×4-size grid — see "Infra" below.)
- Region-pinned single-region (no cross-region I/O), logged to marin-community/speedrun.

## Results

Final `train/loss` (lower = better):

| size | LR× | **opt_a** | **opt_f** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 130m | 0.5 / 0.75 / 1.0 | 3.390 / **3.328** / 3.417 | 3.842 / 3.896 / 3.895 |
| 300m | 0.5 / 0.75 / 1.0 | 3.054 / 3.040 / **3.022** | — / 3.149 / — |

**Findings**
1. **`opt_a` clearly outperforms `opt_f`** at every (size, LR): ~0.5 lower loss at 130m, ~0.13 lower at 300m (lrx0_75). `opt_a` has a clear LR optimum (~lrx0_75); `opt_f` is ~flat across LR.
2. **`opt_f` converges — no divergence**, despite ~8× larger raw update norms than `opt_a` at the same LR. It's simply a weaker optimizer here.
3. `opt_a` size-scaling: 130m best 3.328 → 300m best 3.022 (as expected).
4. 520m and the remaining `opt_f` LR points were still training when stopped, but the `opt_a > opt_f` verdict is already conclusive from 130m + 300m.

## Status
**Stopped.** Most of the sweep (130m + 300m fully; 520m partial) completed on preemptible v5p; the tail was grinding slowly under capacity contention and was wound down since the result was conclusive.

## Infra notes (debugging lessons; cost me real time, worth recording)
- **`--extra tpu` is required** for iris TPU launches. Without it the worker `uv sync`s the default jax-0.10 line with **no libtpu** → `libtpu.so: cannot open shared object file` → JAX falls back to CPU → `RuntimeError: No accelerator found`, which iris mislabels as a "bad node" and auto-retries forever. Read logs for `libtpu.so` before blaming hardware.
- **Coordinator/region co-location:** pinning only the child steps' `regions=[...]` isn't enough — the executor coordinator does constant `.executor_status.lock` bookkeeping on `MARIN_PREFIX`; if it runs in a different region, every lock op is cross-region egress (amplified by retries). Pin the coordinator too (`iris job run --region …`, which is mutually exclusive with `--reserve`).
- **Preemptible coordinator churn:** the preemptible CPU coordinator got preempted every ~15–30 min; each restart tore down children and reset progress. We trimmed scope (dropped 1_2b + high LRs) to make completion feasible and kept relaunching on stall.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Comparison vs the official `marin-community/speedrun` leaderboard (Paloma C4-EN BPB, lower = better).**

Pulled the Muon-family Qwen3-scaling baselines from `marin-community/speedrun` (`data/runs.json`, `eval_paloma_c4_en_bpb`) and compared against our HybridMuon-a runs' C4-EN BPB from W&B (our earlier numbers were `train/loss`; this is the leaderboard metric at matched model size / compute).

### Muon vs HybridMuon variant `a`

| size | Muon (`muon_qwen3_scaling`) | HybridMuon-a (best of our {0.5, 0.75, 1.0}× sweep) | Δ (HM_a − Muon) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 130m | **1.1663** | 1.1830 (lrx0_75) | **+0.0167 — Muon better** |
| 300m | **1.0582** | 1.0865 (lrx1) | **+0.0283 — Muon better** |

Per-LR HybridMuon-a BPB — 130m {0.5: 1.2017, 0.75: **1.1830**, 1.0: 1.2089}; 300m {0.5: 1.0976, 0.75: 1.0929, 1.0: **1.0865**}.

### Whole Muon family at these sizes (C4-EN BPB)

| family | 130m | 300m |
|---|---|---|
| MuonH | 1.1635 | 1.0560 |
| **Muon** | 1.1663 | 1.0582 |
| PRISM-Berkeley | 1.1703 | 1.0632 |
| MuonRemez | 1.1761 | 1.0654 |
| **HybridMuon-a (ours)** | **1.1830** | **1.0865** |

### Verdict
**Plain Muon beats HybridMuon variant `a`** on C4-EN BPB at both sizes (~0.017 at 130m, ~0.028 at 300m). HybridMuon-a is in fact the **worst of the Muon family** at these sizes — the nuclear-norm/effective-rank blend doesn't help here, landing slightly behind even MuonRemez (its closer cousin) and clearly behind Muon/MuonH. This is consistent with the intra-experiment finding (opt_a is a comparatively weak Muon variant; opt_f weaker still).

### Caveats
- HybridMuon-a used **PRISM-Berkeley's per-size hyperparameters** (momentum, β1=0.8, β2=0.98, wd=0.1, linear schedule, centers) — *not* independently tuned for HybridMuon, whereas each leaderboard family was tuned for itself. A fair head-to-head would re-tune.
- LR grid was **trimmed to 3 points** {0.5, 0.75, 1.0}×; the optimum could sit slightly outside (300m's best was at the edge, lrx1).
- 520m / 1_2b HybridMuon-a did not finish (preemptible-capacity tail), so this is 130m + 300m only.

issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment added correctness-first GrugMoE inference support across the Marin, vLLM, and tpu-inference handoff branches. The work mapped GrugMoE/Levanter semantics into vLLM with an unfused PyTorch `GrugMoeForCausalLM`, added tpu-inference auto-routing for that model type, and created a Marin parity harness that compares tiny seeded GrugMoE components and full hidden states against the Levanter/JAX reference. Local component and composed parity checks passed, then Iris validated the same strict-parity harness on a `v6e-4` TPU in `europe-west4` after resolving setup issues around SSH keys, TPU runtime extras, and TPU matmul precision. The current conclusion is that initial correctness support is validated; performance work, checkpoint export/loading, and real-model end-to-end smoke tests remain out of scope for this issue.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/grugmoe-vllm-tpu-support
- https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/tree/grugmoe-vllm-tpu-support
- https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/tree/grugmoe-vllm-tpu-support
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6106#issuecomment-4598509275
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Objective

Add initial correctness-first GrugMoE inference support to vLLM TPU, with Levanter as the correctness reference and tiny seeded random GrugMoE configs. Performance, Levanter checkpoint export, vLLM checkpoint loading, and real-model end-to-end smoke tests are out of scope.

## Gates

1. Repo map: identify GrugMoE in Marin/Levanter, vLLM/tpu-inference extension points, closest reusable model implementations, and the smallest useful dummy config.
2. Component parity: port/test GrugMoE components in isolation against Levanter with tiny seeded tensors.
3. Composed parity: assemble the minimal full GrugMoE forward path and compare against Levanter on the tiny random model.
4. TPU validation: run targeted correctness tests on one Dev TPU `v6e-4` slice in `europe-west4` via Iris, interactive priority.
5. Handoff: leave branch(es), tests/harnesses, issue notes, logbook/reference markdown, exact commands, blockers, and next steps.

## Initial status

Started from dev box on 2026-06-02. Marin source repo refreshed to `origin/main` before creating session worktree `/home/romain/dev/marin-wt/grugmoe-vllm-tpu-support`.

issues.title: Experiment: GrugMoE vLLM TPU support

issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
🤖 This issue documents the process of tuning the AMUSE (Schedule-Free style anytime averaging) optimizer combined with hyperball-normalized Muon (MuonH), against the canonical MuonH-combined baseline on the Grug MoE kitchen-sink combined architecture (d=512, K=5, 6302 steps, batch=32). Closing as **not planned** — the experiment is complete and the tuned recipe does not improve on the MuonH baseline.

## Background

- **AMUSE** (arXiv 2605.22432): Anytime Muon with Stable gradient evaluation. Y_t = (1−β_t)·Z_t + β_t·X_t, where Z is the base-optimizer sequence and X is an LR-weighted online average. Gradient is evaluated at Y; X is the deploy point.
- **MuonH**: Muon (NS5 orthogonalization) wrapped in hyperball normalization to preserve per-matrix Frobenius norm.
- **ScheduleFree+** (arXiv 2605.19095) recipe folded in: c-warmup (hold c_t=1 until step ``c_warmup_steps`` so X tracks Z), r-weighting (w_t = max_lr^p · t^r), constant LR after warmup, weight_decay=0.
- Selection metric: ``eval/ema/paloma/c4_en/loss`` (X-eval). Significance threshold: 2e-3.

## Setup

- Architecture: kitchen-sink combined arch (K=5 experts/token, shared_MLP=hidden/2) at d=512
- Steps: 6302 (matches baseline)
- Reference: MuonH-combined-reproduce baseline = **3.5931** (Y c4_en)
- Sweep methodology (user-defined): around an anchor, perturb one axis at a time in parallel; if a perturbed value beats anchor by ≥ 2e-3, that value becomes the new anchor and the per-axis sweep restarts. Repeat until no axis perturbation beats anchor.

## Variants

Defined by Z-hyperball × Y-normalization cross product:

| Variant | z_normalize | y_normalize | Idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | True | False | Standard MuonH inside AMUSE (Z-norm preserved) |
| B | False | True | Plain Muon inside AMUSE, with Y-norm applied after combine |
| C | True | True | Both Z- and Y-hyperball normalization |
| D | False | False | Pure plain Muon inside AMUSE (not tuned) |

## Tuning process

For each variant, ran R1 → R{converged} per-axis sweeps. Axes:

- **β** (constant β_t in AMUSE): 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99, (0.97, 0.995, 0.999 added on boundary extension)
- **c_warmup**: 400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2400, (600, 1000, 1400, 2000, 3200 added)
- **LR_mult**: 0.1–1.5× heuristic base LR
- **LR warmup fraction**: 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05
- **r-weighting**: 0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0

For each round, ~16–18 variants run in parallel for the full 6302 steps. Significance threshold for new anchor = **Δ ≤ −0.002** on X-eval c4_en final value (read from ``state=finished`` summary).

## Bugs encountered and fixed during tuning

1. **AMUSE-vs-MuonH divergence**: AMUSE controlled hard-coded ``nesterov=False`` and ``weight_decay=0.1``; MuonH default is ``nesterov=True``, ``weight_decay=0``. Exposed ``muon_nesterov`` and forced ``weight_decay=0`` in the launcher.
2. **Y-normalize invariant break (C v1)**: Rescaling only Y broke the ``Y = (1−β)Z + βX`` invariant — X c4_en *rose* during training (4 → 7+). Fix: apply the same per-matrix Frobenius scale factor to Y, Z, *and* X uniformly each step.
3. **Z=False sharding mismatch (B R1)**: When ``z_normalize=False``, plain Muon's NS5 output reshards to ``P(None, None)``; without hyperball to restore ``P(expert, data, model)``, AMUSE's ``z + base_update`` add throws ``ShardingTypeError`` on MoE 3-D params. Fix: add ``_match_named_update_sharding()`` to the optimizer chain in ``optimizer.py:935``.
4. **iris ``-e`` syntax**: ``-e KEY`` requires a paired value; ``-e A -e B`` was parsed as (KEY=A, VAL=-e), then leaked B as a positional command arg → all sweep jobs failed with ``exec: AMUSE_C_WARMUP: not found``. Fix: always pass ``-e KEY $VAL`` explicitly.
5. **Intermediate-vs-final read**: Reading wandb ``summary`` while step < final_eval under-reports the X improvement by 0.01–0.02. Wait for ``state=finished``.

## Results

### Variant A — CONVERGED (R4)

Anchor: **β=0.9, c_warm=1600, LR_mult=1.0, warmup=0.01, r=0**, weight_decay=0, muon_nesterov=True.

- R1 anchor (LR=1.0): 3.7022 → R2 anchor (LR=1.5): 3.6745 (Δ −0.028) → R3 anchor (cwarm=1600): 3.6182 (Δ −0.056) → R4 anchor (LR=1.0): **3.5998** (Δ −0.018, CONVERGED).
- Sweep closed an initial gap of +0.109 (R1) down to **+0.007 vs MuonH** (3.5931).

### Variant C — CONVERGED (R3)

Anchor: **β=0.9, c_warm=1200, LR_mult=0.5, warmup=0.01, r=0**.

- R1 (from A's anchor): 4.0546 → R1 winner C-lr-0.5x: 3.7217 (Δ −0.333 — y-norm needs lower LR) → R2 winner cwarm-1200: 3.7121 (Δ −0.010) → R3 CONVERGED at 3.7121.
- vs A: **+0.112 worse**. Y-normalization on top of Z-normalization hurts performance.

### Variant B — STOPPED at R3 boundary

Anchor (R3): **β=0.99, c_warm=1600, LR_mult=0.5, warmup=0.01, r=0**.

- R1 anchor (from A's anchor): 5.5023 → R1 winner beta-0.99: 3.9455 (Δ −1.557; near-perfect-monotonic β preference) → R2 winner lr-0.5x: 3.8477 (Δ −0.098) → R3 winner cwarm-2400: **3.8380** (Δ −0.010, at upper c_warm boundary).
- Sweep stopped at R3 verdict before extending c_warm grid past 2400.
- vs A: **+0.238 worse**. Removing Z-hyperball but keeping Y-norm hurts despite β=0.99 helping a lot.

### Summary

| Variant | z_norm | y_norm | Best X c4_en | Δ vs MuonH (3.5931) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | True | False | **3.5998** | **+0.007** | CONVERGED |
| C | True | True | 3.7121 | +0.119 | CONVERGED |
| B | False | True | 3.8380 | +0.245 | STOPPED at R3 (boundary open) |

## Verdict

The Schedule-Free + hyperball recipe was successfully tuned via systematic per-axis sweeps. **Variant A matches MuonH within noise** (0.007 c4_en), but does not exceed it on this architecture. Adding Y-normalization (variants B, C) systematically hurts performance. Closing as **not planned** — the recipe is fully tuned and the result is negative; no further iteration is warranted without changing the recipe itself (e.g., dropping the c-warmup, replacing the LR-weighted average with a different recency-weight schedule, or pairing with a different base optimizer).

Full per-round sweep history and per-axis curves: ``experiments/grug/moe/amuse_plan.md``.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Update — the growing-β schedule (never tested here) closes the gap.**

This ablation swept **constant β_t only** (0.5 / 0.7 / 0.9 / 0.95 / 0.99) and converged at Variant A = β0.9 / c_warm1600 / lr1.0 → X `c4_en` **3.5998** (+0.007 vs MuonH 3.5931), closing as "matches but does not improve." The verdict noted a *recipe change* (a different recency-weight schedule) might be needed — that is exactly what was missing.

Testing the AMUSE paper's **growing-β schedule** (`beta_schedule="amuse"`: β_t = β₁ until an absolute T₀, then →1 at ρ=0.8) with a **low initial β₁=0.6** — which the constant-β sweep could not express — closes it:

| recipe (X / ema `c4_en`) | c4_en | vs control |
|---|---|---|
| MuonH linear-decay control (`amuse-d512-...-amuse-as-muonh-control-wd0`) | 3.5920 | — |
| #6064 best (const β0.9, c1600, lr1.0) | 3.5998 | +0.0078 |
| **β₁=0.6 + growing-β (T₀=1400), lr0.8, c_warm1400, r0** | **3.5939** | **+0.0019 (match — well inside the ~0.007 "noise" band this issue already accepted for Variant A)** |

**Why it works:** with constant β≈0.9, Y≈X throughout, so β→1 just over-shifts (β₁=0.9-growing gave ~3.63). β₁=0.6 lets Y track **Z** early (fast base learning) then anneal to the **X**-average late — the decay analogue constant-β cannot represent.

**Robust, not knife-edge:** β₁∈{0.5,0.6,0.7} × T₀∈{1000,1400} all land **3.594–3.597**; β₁=0.4 is too low (3.602). Fully **budget-independent** (constant β₁, absolute T₀, no LR decay) and keeps **router z-loss smooth** (~25 vs constant-β's ~35; no blow-up).

Coordinate-descent dead-ends the constant-β-only sweep also did not surface: bias-in-AMUSE (neutral), r-weighting>0 (trades c4 for z-loss), Y-normalize (under-trains → 4.01), c_warmup>1800 (tail-average too sparse → 3.62), LR outside [0.8,1.1] (underfit/diverge).

Caveat: numbers are seed-0 (deterministic) + robust across the β₁/T₀ neighborhood; multi-seed variance runs are in flight to nail the match statistically and probe an outright beat. Full per-round history: `experiments/grug/moe/LOG.md`; wandb group `amuse-cd-c2`.

**Net: the "negative / not planned" verdict was an artifact of sweeping β as a constant — growing-β AMUSE (β₁=0.6) matches the MuonH baseline budget-independently.** Worth reopening if we want to chase a beat.

comments.body:
🤖 **β_t schedule plot** (the mechanism behind the growing-β win).

Y_t = (1−β_t)·Z_t + β_t·X_t. The constant-β sweep here pinned β_t flat (best 0.9). The growing-β recipe instead holds β_t=β₁ until an absolute T₀=1400, then anneals β_t→1 at ρ=0.8 — so **Y tracks the base sequence Z early (fast learning) and the X-average late (annealing)**, the decay analogue constant-β cannot express.

0.75 |                    ●●●●●●
0.70 |                ●●●●

0.60 |●●●●●●●●●●●●●●                                              <- β₁=0.6 growing (recipe)

| step | β₁=0.5 | β₁=0.6 (recipe) | β₁=0.7 | const 0.9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ≤1400 | 0.500 | 0.600 | 0.700 | 0.900 |
| 2000 | 0.624 | 0.699 | 0.775 | 0.900 |
| 3000 | 0.728 | 0.783 | 0.837 | 0.900 |

Constant β=0.9 over-weights X (≈the slow average) from step 1, which is why it tops out at 3.5998 while β₁=0.6-growing reaches 3.5939 ≈ control. comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 The β_t schedule figure (four curves: β₁∈{0.5,0.6,0.7} growing vs β=0.9 constant; T₀=1400, ρ=0.8, 6302 steps):

![AMUSE β_t schedule — growing-β vs constant](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/kaiyue/issue6064-beta-asset/experiments/grug/moe/beta_schedule.png)

The growing curves are held flat at β₁ until T₀=1400, then anneal toward ~1; the recipe (β₁=0.6) ends at ~0.88. The constant β=0.9 (this issue's best) is the flat dashed line at the top from step 0 — over-weighting the X-average throughout, which is the difference that costs it ~0.006 c4_en vs the growing-β recipe.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Decoupled weight decay (0.05) controls the router z-loss — and improves c4.**

A recurring problem with the schedule-free recipe was the router `z_loss` drifting up over training (a router-collapse risk, and the reason z-smoothness was a hard acceptance criterion). Adding **decoupled weight decay = 0.05 on the AdamW group** (embeddings / router / 1-D leaves; the MuonH/hyperball matrices are untouched) fixes it cleanly, with no loss cost — in fact a small loss *gain*:

| | no weight decay | **+ wd 0.05** |
|---|---|---|
| router z (6302-step, d512) | 28.9 | **9.6** |
| router z (hero, bs32 → ~40B tok so far) | **55+ and climbing** | **~5.7, flat** |
| c4_en X-eval (6302, same v6e hardware) | 3.5913 | **3.5875** |

So wd0.05 is strictly good here: it more than halves z at the compute-optimal budget, eliminates the z-drift entirely at hero scale (where no-wd marches toward router collapse), **and** lowers c4_en by ~0.004 (3.5875 also beats the linear-decay MuonH control 3.5920 by ~0.0045).

Before/after z-loss (left: 6302-step; right: long "hero" run, z vs tokens):

![z-loss before/after wd](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/research/moe-klsoaph-on-may-recipe/.agents/logbooks/zloss_wd_before_after.png)

Recipe (unchanged except adding wd): growing-β AMUSE (β₁0.6, T₀1400, ρ0.8) + power-law LR decay (exp 0.05) + c_warmup 1600 + **wd 0.05**, fully budget-independent. Ablations confirm the growing-β schedule (+0.019) and c-warmup (+0.069) are both load-bearing; wd0.05 and dropping the LR-warmup are the clean wins from a 10-idea program.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Schedule-free vs linear-decay baseline — comparison.**

**(1) Fixed compute-optimal budget (d512, 2.19e17 FLOP, 6302 steps, bs32) — head-to-head:**

| recipe | c4_en (X-eval) | router-z | LR schedule |
|---|---|---|---|
| linear-decay MuonH control (`amuse-as-muonh-control-wd0`) | 3.5920 | — | cosine/linear decay to 0, **tuned to the 6302-step horizon** |
| **schedule-free (pow0.05 + wd0.05)** | **3.5875** | 9.6 | **none keyed to T** (budget-independent) |

The schedule-free recipe **beats the tuned linear-decay control by 0.0045** at the same budget, with no horizon-specific LR schedule and a smoother router-z.

**(2) Across durations — one schedule-free run vs per-duration-tuned linear-decay (bs32 family):**

Each linear-decay baseline (`compopt`@1.4B, `R120`@2.5B, `R240`@5B) committed to its horizon and tuned its LR-decay for it. The schedule-free recipe is a **single run, no retuning** — yet its X-eval, read at any token count, tracks the lower envelope of those tuned baselines:

![sf vs linear-decay](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/research/moe-klsoaph-on-may-recipe/.agents/logbooks/sf_vs_lineardecay_curves.png)

So you get a budget-independent recipe that's competitive at *every* horizon without pre-committing one, and strictly better at the compute-optimal point. The long hero run is still extending toward 103.6B tokens (vs the `tpp5000` linear-decay reference at 3.0788); at ~39B it's at c4_en 3.162 and tracking. (Caveat: at intermediate token counts the schedule-free X-eval is mid-run / un-annealed, so the apples-to-apples comparison is endpoint-to-endpoint, where it's tie-to-better.)

issues.author: hulkund
issues.body:
The `gpu` extra installs Marin's patched PJRT wheel on any aarch64 GPU host. `lib/marin/pyproject.toml:185` keys the source on `platform_machine == 'aarch64'`, which is a CPU architecture test. Grace-Hopper (GH200, compute capability 9.0) and Grace-Blackwell (GB200, compute capability 10.0) are both aarch64, so a GH200 host installs a wheel built for a different GPU architecture.

The environment installs cleanly, and `jax.devices()`, matmuls, and NCCL collectives all work. The mismatch stays invisible until XLA loads a prebuilt cubin during a training step, at which point the process aborts with SIGABRT:

```
F0902 09:20:51 stream_executor_util.cc:504] Could not load RepeatBufferKernel:
INTERNAL: CUDA Runtime error: [0] Failed call to cudaGetFuncBySymbol:
cudaErrorNoKernelImageForDevice: no kernel image is available for execution on the device
```

Reproduce:
1. On a GH200 host, run `uv sync --all-packages --extra=gpu`.
2. Confirm `jax-cuda13-pjrt` resolved to `0.11.1+marin.<sha>` rather than `0.11.1`.
3. Run training that compiles a loss kernel, such as `python -m experiments.tutorials.train_tiny_model --device h100x1 --dataset wikitext --version dev --run`.

Expected: the resolver selects a PJRT build carrying kernel images for the host GPU.

Installing upstream `jax-cuda13-pjrt==0.11.1` over the patched wheel fixes it. Training then runs to completion and writes both Levanter and HuggingFace checkpoints. That workaround gives up the ragged all-to-all patch the Marin build carries, so it suits dense training and not MoE.

Found while bringing Marin up on JUPITER (JSC), which has four GH200 per node.
issues.title: [marin] Grace-Hopper hosts get a Blackwell PJRT wheel and abort in training

issues.author: hulkund
issues.body:
On GH200 the fused cross-entropy autotune cannot retain its result, so every call sweeps seven block-size candidates at roughly 25 seconds per sweep. A 100-step tutorial run spends most of its wall clock in the sweeps.

The kernel's preferred weight tile does not fit in Hopper's shared memory, and the miss surfaces as an unavailable jaxpr:

```
Fused CE autotune result will not be shared because the kernel jaxpr is unavailable:
Requested weight tile exceeds GPU shared-memory budget for this device:
requested=1048576 bytes, limit=101376 bytes, h_block_size=512, v_block_size=1024
Fused CE autotune miss for batched_xla. Sweeping 7 block-size candidates.
Fused CE autotune selected block sizes BlockSizes(b_block_size=1024, h_block_size=512, v_block_size=64) for batched_xla.
```

The sweep selects `v_block_size=64`, which fits the 101376-byte budget, but the result is not retained and the next call repeats the sweep.

Reproduce:
1. On a GH200 host, run `python -m experiments.tutorials.train_tiny_model --device h100x1 --dataset wikitext --version dev --run`.
2. Count `Fused CE autotune miss` lines in the log. Each one is followed by a fresh seven-candidate sweep.

Expected: the autotune result is cached after the first sweep on a device whose shared-memory budget rejects the default tile.

Relevant code: `lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/api.py:507` (`_autotune_block_sizes_on_miss`).
issues.title: [levanter] Fused CE autotune re-sweeps on every call on Hopper

issues.author: hulkund
issues.body:
Every size in the `v4-reserved` pool computes `max_slices` independently as
`2048 / size` (`lib/iris/config/marin.yaml:266`), while all sizes draw on one
shared 2048-TensorCore GCP reservation. One large slice can consume the entire
reservation and every other size still advertises headroom, so the autoscaler
keeps creating slices the reservation cannot back. Each attempt boots, fails,
and is retried once demand decays.

A `v4-2048` slice (1024 chips) created 2026-08-27T23:20Z has held the whole
reservation for 5 days. Since then `tpu_v4-reserved_128-us-central2-b` reports
`availability=available` with no quota block and cycles indefinitely: demand
appears, a slice is created, it never reaches ready, demand decays to zero,
repeat. The other seven reserved sizes report `available` with the same empty
reservation behind them.

Reproduce:
1. While a `v4-2048` slice is running, submit a job requesting a reserved
   `v4-128` slice in us-central2.
2. Watch `iris cluster vm status --scale-group tpu_v4-reserved_128-us-central2-b`.

Expected: advertised availability reflects the remaining shared reservation, so
a caller can tell an exhausted pool from an idle one and choose another. The
group instead reports itself available while the job holds at `No workers match
constraints`.

Impact: a Snowball 67B SFT smoke sat pending 4 hours against this pool
(`/nehashulkund/snowball-chat-smoke-v5b`, 2026-08-31) before the cause was
found. The same run has not reached a training step since; three attempts across
us-central1, us-east5, and us-central2 are queued and unplaced.

The reservation accounting compounds a wider shortage rather than causing it.
The fleet currently holds 51 ready TPU slices and zero free ones, and new
allocations above 8 chips fail across zones with `There is no more capacity in
the zone` (us-central2-b, us-east5-a, us-east5-b, us-central1-a, europe-west4).
Preemptible groups at v5p-64, v5p-128, and v6e-8 sit in health backoff around
0.10. A pool that cannot be distinguished from an idle one costs a caller hours
of pending time that a legible signal would let them spend elsewhere.
issues.title: [iris] Reserved v4 sizes advertise capacity the shared reservation cannot back

issues.author: Helw150
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment continues the Grug MoE GPU MFU work onto Blackwell with a concrete target: exceed 20% MFU on a single 8-node B200 rack. The current single-node B200 baseline reproduces the #6979 row-13 H100 config at 12.5% MFU; increasing batch barely helps, while widening the model reaches 16.2% MFU before EP1/FSDP memory pressure blocks further width. The current recommendation is to build a Blackwell-native `sonic_cute` grouped-GEMM path via QuACK/CUTLASS, validate parity and MFU delta on the d2560 config, then combine the native GEMM with wider models and scale across the rack with replica/DDP.

### Helpful links
- Baseline and next-step analysis: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7012#issuecomment-4909307573
- Parent GPU MFU tuning thread: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6979
- Higher-level tracker: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6710
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Continuing the GPU MFU tuning thread (#6979) onto Blackwell. Purpose is to get Grug MoE training MFU on a single B200 rack (8 nodes) above 20%, working up from the single-node baseline and the current `sonic` recipe.

Definition of Done: ≥20% MFU on a single rack (8 nodes) of B200 for a real trainable `model.py` config.

Tracking: #6706

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
🤖 ## Single-node B200 baseline + where the MFU is going

Reproduced the #6979 row-13 config (full `model.py`, d2560 / 26L / 64 experts top-4 / MHA / sonic / EP1+FSDP / MuonH / stacked-scan) on 8×B200 (JHU Schmidt), single node. Same absolute per-GPU throughput as row 13's H100 (~282 vs ~264 TFLOP/s/GPU), but B200's larger peak makes the MFU % much lower — this small model can't feed the chip.

| Lever | Config | B200 MFU | Throughput | Note |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| baseline | d2560, b128 | 12.5% | 2,257 TFLOP/s | row-13 replica |
| batch | d2560, b512 | 13.1% | 2,355 | plateaus; b1024 OOM (205 GiB dispatch op) |
| **width** | d4096, b256 | 15.8% | 2,847 | |
| **width** | d5120, b128 | **16.2%** | 2,914 | memory-bound above this at EP1/FSDP |

**Batch is a dead lever** (12.5→13.1% for 4×) — the workload is arithmetic-intensity-starved, not batch-starved. **Width is the live lever** (→16.2%), but at EP1+FSDP we hit ~157 GB/GPU by d5120, so we can't just keep widening on one node.

### Two things block >20%
1. **The compute-bound expert GEMM isn't a Blackwell kernel.** The `sonic` backend only vendors SonicMoE's Triton gather/combine (`reduction_over_k_gather.py`); the grouped-GEMM falls back to XLA/cuBLAS — no CLC / 2CTA-MMA / TMEM. Full [SonicMoE](https://tridao.me/blog/2026/sonicmoe-blackwell/) runs its grouped-GEMM on **QuACK** (CuTeDSL/CUTLASS) and reports +54%/+35% fwd/bwd vs DeepGEMM on Blackwell. `nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.2` + `quack 0.5.0` are already in the venv, and `gemm_gated` takes `cu_seqlens_m`/`A_idx` (grouped MoE is first-class) — so a `moe_implementation="sonic_cute"` shim via `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call` (same bridge as `gpu_fa4_cute`) is the highest-leverage next step.
2. **Memory caps width on one node.** Getting to the single-rack (8-node) DoD wants EP/replica sharding across nodes (Larry's #6979 found replica/DDP is the right multinode axis for a model that fits one node) so a wider, higher-intensity model fits.

### Next
- [ ] `sonic_cute` Blackwell grouped-GEMM shim (QuACK via `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call`), numerics parity vs `sonic`, MFU delta on the d2560 config.
- [ ] Width × native-GEMM together, then scale to the rack via replica/DDP.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
🤖 ## Update: SonicMoE (QuACK) kernel wired into the MoE path — moves whole-model MFU on 8×B200

Got Tri's QuACK SM100 grouped GEMM (the SonicMoE kernel) doing the MoE expert-MLP GEMMs inside Grug, via a vendored `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call` shim (same bridge as `gpu_fa4_cute` attention — no torch, no tvm-ffi), and measured the whole-model MFU on 8×B200.

**Whole-model 8×B200 MFU (row-13 config: 26L / 64 experts top-4 / EP1+FSDP / b128 / seq4k), `sonic` (XLA `ragged_dot`) vs `sonic_cute` (QuACK):**

| hidden | `sonic` (XLA) | **`sonic_cute` (QuACK)** | gain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| d2560 | 12.5% | 14.9% | +2.4 |
| d5120 | 16.2% | **17.8%** | +1.6 |

Loss decreases normally; forward + all gradients match the XLA `scatter` backend at bf16 tolerance (rel ~1%). The QuACK gated GEMM alone hits ~1,175 TFLOP/s (~52% of peak) on 1×B200.

**What's on QuACK vs not (≈2/3 of MoE FLOPs on the kernel):**
- QuACK: gate/up fused-SwiGLU forward, down forward, and the `dh`/`dx` backward matmuls.
- XLA still: the two weight-grad GEMMs (`dw13`/`dw2`) — a different varlen-k grouping I haven't shimmed — and the SwiGLU backward is elementwise.

**Shim gotchas** (for anyone reusing it): `TensorSpec(static=False)` (varlen gated kernel needs M/N/2N/E dynamic; static → opaque `Unexpected index` abort), n-major B `mode=(2,1,0)`, gate/up columns are **interleaved** not `[gate|up]`, and under `shard_map` pass `group_sizes`/`cu` as explicit `custom_vjp` args with `float0` cotangents (closing over them leaks; `nondiff_argnums` rejects tracers). You can compile/debug the launcher on the login node (no GPU) via `cute.compile`.

**Branch:** [`sonic-cute-moe-b200`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/sonic-cute-moe-b200) (off `dial_h100_dev`) — `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/{quack_moe_cute,sonic_cute}.py` + dispatch registration.

**Next lever to push past 20%:** shim the weight-grad GEMMs (`dw13`/`dw2`, varlen-k) onto QuACK so the whole MoE backward is on the kernel; d6144 (wider = higher arithmetic intensity) is the other knob.

@mcwitt — this overlaps directly with your FP8 expert-GMM / ragged-dot dgrad-wgrad work (#6699, #6930); the varlen-k weight-grad shim is the piece that'd complete MoE-on-QuACK, curious if you want to take that or point me at the right kernel.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body: 🤖 Independently reproduced this on 8×B200: with the same d5120 / `sonic_cute` configuration we measured **~17.9% MFU**, matching the 17.8% reported here.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Update: varlen-k wgrad shim landed (bit-exact — but not the lever) + step-time anatomy

Took the varlen-k weight-grad shim offered above — branch [`mcwitt/sonic-cute-wgrad`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/mcwitt/sonic-cute-wgrad) (off `sonic-cute-moe-b200`): a third QuACK launcher computing `dw[e] = acts_eᵀ @ grads_e` via `cu_seqlens_k`, zero-copy transposed operand views (A m-major / B n-major, expert as trailing L mode on D), env-gated `SONIC_CUTE_WGRAD=xla` fallback. Parity is bit-exact vs the XLA `ragged_dot` vjp across even / heavily-ragged / empty-expert groupings (empty experts exactly zero), and e2e gradients are unchanged.

MFU on 8×B200, row-13 config (b128, seq4k), steady-state median; each pair = both arms run sequentially on the same node to control node variance:

| hidden | sonic_cute (XLA wgrad) | + QuACK wgrad | delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| d2560 | 14.89 % | 14.97 % | +0.08 pp |
| d5120 | 17.82 % | 17.88 % | +0.06 pp |

(Controls reproduce the 14.9 / 17.8 in the table above; an independent checkout + venv also reproduced the 12.5 % `sonic` baseline at 12.499 %.)

So MoE-on-QuACK is now complete and parity-clean, but the wgrad GEMMs weren't a bottleneck. A tile autotune sweep told the same story from another angle: `tile=(256,256), cluster=(2,1,1)` beats the current `(256,128)` default at **all six** QuACK call sites, ×1.08–1.28 in isolation (gated fwd at d5120: 53 %→65 % of peak), yet moves e2e ≤ +0.04 pp. The step is not GEMM-bound.

**Where the step actually goes** — profiled at d2560 (command buffers disabled for kernel→op attribution; shares of GPU kernel time):

| bucket | share |
|---|---:|
| attention (FA4; bwd incl. rematerialized fwd) | 30.3 % |
| gradient-checkpoint recompute (`remat_mode="recompute_all"`) | ~25 % |
| MoE GEMMs (all QuACK sites) | 24.0 % |
| optimizer (MuonH; Newton–Schulz ablation = 0.60 pp total) | 4.4 % |
| NCCL (EP1 + FSDP, single node) | ~10 % |

The standout: we re-run the whole forward inside backward while peaking at 54 of 192 GiB. `remat_mode="save_moe"` does **not** recover it for `sonic_cute` (+65 GiB, ±0 pp): `_expert_mlp` is a `custom_vjp`, and `jax.checkpoint` re-executes custom_vjp forwards regardless of name-based save policies, so the saved dispatch tensors don't prevent the QuACK GEMM re-runs. The next code change is splitting the per-block checkpoint so only attention remats (estimated +2–3 pp).

Also priced two NVIDIA-stack options (the new ragged-dot fusion, which the [NGC JAX 26.05 release notes](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/frameworks/jax-release-notes/rel-26-05.html) describe as made performant; and the latency-hiding scheduler — the latter was e2e-null, likely already default): on upstream jax 0.10.1, `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_fusion` turns `jax.lax.ragged_dot` into a cuDNN fusion (`__cudnn$fusion`) that then fails autotuning on SM100 — "No supported configs found" — and without the flag, `ragged_dot` at these shapes lowers to a dense-materialized `[262144, 163840]` cuBLAS matmul (22.6 TF/s effective, ~65× under QuACK). Note that despite the "sonic (XLA ragged_dot)" shorthand in the table earlier in this thread, the `sonic` backend's grouped GEMMs lower via jax-triton rather than the `ragged_dot` HLO op — so this flag is a no-op for it either way. Currently testing the NGC JAX 26.05 container, where this path is claimed performant — in-container microbench vs QuACK plus e2e arms to follow.

Full record (commands, job-level detail, hypothesis queue): [research logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7012-b200-mfu/.agents/logbooks/7012-b200-moe-mfu.md).

Next: (1) NGC 26.05 container ragged-dot verdict; (2) attention-only remat; (3) PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation); (4) MXFP8 on the QuACK seam — ceiling now quantified at ~1.1× e2e for MoE-only, so it slots after remat.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Update: native `ragged_dot` has no fast path on any available stack — but TransformerEngine's grouped GEMM is QuACK-class

Follow-up on the ragged-dot question from the last update, now tested across three stacks at the row-13 MoE shapes (`[262144, 2560] × [64, 2560, 1280]`, bf16, 1×B200; QuACK reference ≈ 1,470–1,560 TF/s):

| stack | `jax.lax.ragged_dot` behavior | effective TF/s |
|---|---|---:|
| upstream jaxlib 0.10.1 | dense-materializes `[262144, 163840]` → cuBLAS | 22.6 |
| upstream jaxlib 0.10.1 + fusion flag | cuDNN fusion fires → autotuning: "No supported configs found" | crash |
| upstream jaxlib **0.10.2** | identical crash with the flag; identical dense path without | 23.0 / crash |
| NGC JAX 26.05 container | same dense path; fusion flag **absent from their runtime**; `use_ragged_dot_grouped_gemm` parses but is the ROCm/hipBLASLt lowering (upstream default-true, no-op on CUDA) | 25.9 |

Diagnosis: per current XLA source (`backends/gpu/autotuner/cudnn.cc`), ragged-dot fusions are delegated to cuDNN unconditionally — the empty config list means **cuDNN enumerates zero execution plans for this graph on SM100** (confirmed with cuDNN frontend logging). So this is a cuDNN capability gap, not an XLA arch gate, and a jax version bump won't fix it. (Two practical footnotes: the dense fallback materializes an ~86 GB intermediate, so it also OOMs the autotuner below `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION≈0.95`; and the "sonic (XLA ragged_dot)" path is unaffected by all of this since it lowers via jax-triton.)

The positive result: **TransformerEngine 2.15** (ships in the NGC image; pip-installable) has `te.jax.dense.grouped_dense`, and at the same shapes it hits **1,449 TF/s — parity with our tuned QuACK kernels**, ~63× over native XLA. TE also carries fp8/quantize APIs in the same module and is the delivery vehicle for NCCL_EP (TE PR #3036), so it lines up as the maintained path for the MXFP8 phase and rack-scale expert parallelism, without vendored kernels.

Given the step-time anatomy from the last update (MoE GEMMs ≈24 % of step, already QuACK-fast), swapping GEMM providers buys ~nothing e2e today — so next up remains the remat surgery (attention-only checkpointing, est. +2–3 pp), with TE slotted for the MXFP8/EP phases.

Details: [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7012-b200-mfu/.agents/logbooks/7012-b200-moe-mfu.md) entries B200MFU-010/-011.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Update: remat surgery lands — d2560 best is now **15.67 %** (up from 15.0 at the last update; +0.51 pp of that is the remat split itself)

Two batches of results since the last update, all same-node 8×B200 d2560 row-13 pairs:

**LHS / auto-PGLE: null at single node.** Three-arm ladder: control 15.02 % → `--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true` 15.03 % → + auto-PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=true`, 3 profiling runs) 15.08 %. Consistent with the step anatomy (NCCL ~10 %, intra-node NVLink, already well overlapped). Parked for the rack phase, where inter-node collectives give the scheduler something real to hide.

**Remat surgery: the ~25 % recompute tax is well defended, but +0.5 pp was extractable.** The obvious checkpoint splits both OOM, with instructive forensics (compile-only AOT probes; whole-block remat's temp arena is 36.9 GiB for reference):

| split | temp arena | why |
|---|---:|---|
| `attn_only` (checkpoint attention, MoE live) | 283.6 GiB | the sonic_cute custom_vjp pins its residuals (sorted dispatch input, the gate/up GEMM pre-activation `gu`, the expert hidden `h`) **plus the all-gathered expert weights**, and the layer scan stacks all 26 layers of them |
| `moe_only` (inverse) | 247.7 GiB | live attention pins norm/rope intermediates **in fp32** (the mixed-precision policy's upcasts) |

Name-based save policies can't reach custom_vjp residuals, so no `jax.checkpoint` policy fixes this — but we own the sonic_cute vjp. The working recipe:

1. **Slim the custom_vjp residuals**: backward re-gathers `x_dispatch` from `(x, token_dispatch)` hint args, recomputes `h = swiglu(gu)` elementwise, and stores `w13`/`w2` **FSDP-sharded** (dynamic-slice in forward, `all_gather(tiled=True)` in backward inside the shard_map — the same gather whole-block remat already pays). Full-backward parity vs the scatter reference: rel ≤ 0.011 on dx/dw13/dw2/d_combine.
2. **`remat_mode=all_but_moe`**: checkpoint attention *and* all norms (kills the fp32 saves), leaving only router → dispatch → expert GEMMs → combine live, so backward never re-runs the expert forward.

That brings the temp arena to **135 GiB** (vs 283.6/247.7 for the naive splits; whole-block remat is 36.9), and e2e: 15.157 % (recompute_all control) → **15.670 %** (+0.51 pp; step 3.276 → 3.169 s), with loss trajectories identical to within bf16 noise.

Two housekeeping notes: (a) a stale-import bug meant `lib/`-level changes never actually loaded in some earlier e2e jobs — the 256×256 QuACK tile default, which we'd measured as e2e-neutral, actually contributes **+0.14 pp** (15.02 → 15.16 control), now default-on. (b) runtime peak HBM under `all_but_moe` is 152 GiB of 192, so it's a d2560 tool; d5120 (peak 157 GiB even under whole-block remat) keeps `recompute_all` for now.

Running ledger, d2560: 12.5 (scatter) → 14.9 (sonic_cute) → 15.0 (+wgrad) → 15.16 (+tiles) → **15.67 (+remat split)**. Next up: MXFP8 via TE `grouped_dense`, plus a cheaper parallel remat increment: our attention backend (`gpu_fa4_cute`, the FlashAttention-4 port) re-runs its forward in backward for the same custom_vjp reason — its softmax log-sum-exp (`lse`) is a hidden residual. Exposing `lse` as a primal output makes (o, lse) name-saveable, skipping the attention-forward re-run (~6.7 % of kernel time per the step anatomy above; est. +~1 pp at ~+9 GiB).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Update: a clean negative result on SM specialization at single node, plus a source-read of the TransformerEngine NCCL_EP PRs that softens one of the rack-phase blockers.

**SM specialization (comm/compute SM partitioning): net loss at single-node EP1+FSDP.** Partitioning SMs between comm and compute kernels is the standard overlap recipe in public MoE EP stacks (DeepEP dedicates an SM budget to its comm kernels; TE's NCCL_EP exposes it as `max_num_sms`), so we tested the single-node analogue on our FSDP all-gathers before the rack phase. Two knobs: pinning NCCL's CTA budget (`NCCL_MIN_CTAS=NCCL_MAX_CTAS`; one CTA — CUDA thread block — occupies one SM per NCCL channel), and a new `SONIC_CUTE_SM_CARVEOUT` that sizes the QuACK persistent tile schedulers to the SM remainder (so GEMM waves stay exact given the carve-out). The control's NCCL init log shows the tuner gives our 8-GPU NVLink communicator 32 collective channels — up to 32 CTAs ≈ 22 % of B200's 148 SMs when a collective runs.

Five arms on the current best d2560 config (the 15.61 % control is the same configuration as the standing 15.67 % record, re-run for this ladder — the gap is run-to-run variance, not a regression):

| arm | steady-median MFU | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|
| control (NCCL auto = 32ch) | 15.61 % | — |
| pin 16 CTAs | 15.41 % | −0.20 pp |
| pin 8 CTAs | 14.61 % | −1.00 pp |
| carve-out 16 SMs (GEMM grid → 132, NCCL auto) | 15.54 % | −0.07 pp |
| carve-out 16 + pin 16 (two-sided) | 15.43 % | −0.18 pp |

Monotone in the pin: NCCL's CTA count buys NVLink bandwidth, and throttling the all-gathers costs more than the freed SMs gain — at the 16-SM point even when the GEMM grid is resized to match (the 8-CTA pin wasn't paired with a resize; its loss is already large without one). NCCL's autotuner is simply right at this scale. The knob stays in the tree (default off) as rack-phase tooling: at EP the contended collective is dispatch/combine, which is the regime the published ~20 %-on-the-MoE-block numbers for SM partitioning are actually about — there the carve should be tuned, not assumed.

**TE NCCL_EP source-read** ([TE PR #3034](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/pull/3034) C API + backend, [#3036](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/pull/3036) JAX FFI bindings, plus the [WIP JAX MoE-block branch](https://github.com/jberchtold-nvidia/TransformerEngine/blob/jberchtold/teddy-te-ep-integration-2026-07-08-support-quantization/transformer_engine/jax/moe.py)). Findings relevant to our rack plan:

- **The "8192-token" limit is not kernel-structural.** It's the `max_tokens_per_rank` staging-buffer sizing default at `ep_bootstrap` (recv capacity = `ep_size × max_tokens_per_rank × 2`, the ×2 being worst-case top-k fan-out slack); raising it costs HBM for staging, not a redesign. Any true ceiling would live in the closed `libnccl_ep` fork, which neither PR exposes — but the TE-side surface is a plain config knob.
- **Their SM specialization is one-sided.** Comm kernels self-cap via `max_num_sms` (default auto — no hardcoded CTA count anywhere in the TE source); the grouped GEMM runs opportunistically on whatever is free, never grid-sized to the remainder. Whether the one-sided cap is enough in the EP dispatch/combine regime is a rack-phase measurement, not something our single-node result settles.
- **No quantized dispatch yet.** The wire is bf16-only (`ep_bootstrap` rejects other dtypes); even NVIDIA's quantization branch scatters bf16 and casts to fp8/MXFP8 *after* dispatch, immediately before the grouped GEMM. For our MXFP8 phase that pins the quantize point at the `grouped_quantize → grouped_gemm` seam and takes fp8-on-the-wire off the near-term table.
- **Integration constraints to plan around:** process-per-GPU is mandatory (`ep_bootstrap` asserts `jax.local_device_count() == 1`), NCCL comm-splitting must be disabled, CUDA-graph/command-buffer capture is kept off around the EP FFI ops, and dispatch/combine run in global mesh view with only the expert FFN inside a `shard_map(check_rep=False)`. There's also a stealable detail: the padded recv tail is never zeroed — `group_sizes` lets the grouped GEMM skip empty experts, with an explicit weight-grad mask for 0-token experts.

Running d2560 ledger unchanged: best remains **15.67 %** (remat split). Next: MXFP8 via TE `grouped_dense` and the FA4 `lse`-as-primal-output remat increment. Details: [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7012-b200-mfu/.agents/logbooks/7012-b200-moe-mfu.md) entry B200MFU-016.

Methodology = the row-13 standalone benchmark exactly (d2560, b128 × seq4096, 20 steps / 8 warmup, steady-median MFU vs 2.25e15 FLOP/s/GPU, `remat_mode=recompute_all`), all arms sequential on the same node. The row-13 driver gained `--expert-parallelism`, which passes `expert_axis_size` through to `compact_grug_mesh`.

| arm | steady-median MFU | step time |
|---|---|---|
| `sonic_cute`, EP1 (control) | 15.14% | 3.28 s |
| `ring` EP2 / EP4 / EP8 | 13.32% / 13.45% / 12.88% | 3.73 / 3.69 / 3.85 s |
| `ragged_all_to_all` EP2 / EP4 / EP8 | 0.97% / 1.82% / 3.19% | 51.0 / 27.3 / 15.6 s |

Findings:

1. **`ring` is the only viable EP backend on B200 today**: ~13% MFU flat across EP2–EP8, i.e. a 1.7–2.3 pp tax vs the EP1 control.
2. Part of that tax is structural: `sonic_cute` (QuACK) is a local-only backend, so any `expert_axis_size > 1` falls back to `haliax.nn.ragged_dot` for the local grouped GEMMs. Microbench at EP-local w13 shapes: Pallas-Triton 397–859 TF/s vs tuned QuACK 1,470–1,560 (the XLA impl fails autotuning outright at the two large shapes). Wiring a QuACK-class grouped GEMM under the EP backends is the obvious recovery.
3. **`ragged_all_to_all` is unusable on GPU and it's not our code**: a profiled EP2 arm shows `stream_executor::gpu::RaggedAllToAllKernelImpl` at **90.0% of device time** — 104 calls/step (26 layers × dispatch+combine × fwd+bwd) at ~297 ms/call, flanked by `MultiGpuBarrierKernelImpl`. XLA currently lowers `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` on GPU to its own peer-copy kernel + multi-GPU barriers rather than NCCL; at our leg sizes (≲800 MB) that is ~30–60× off NVLink capability and fully explains the step-time ∝ 1/EP scaling. Recommend not spending tuning effort here; it needs an upstream XLA fix or a different dispatch vehicle.
4. Next probe: TransformerEngine NCCL_EP dispatch/combine at the same shapes, against the 297 ms/call figure (constraints noted in the logbook: process-per-GPU, bf16 dispatch wire).

Details and per-arm data: `.agents/logbooks/7012-b200-moe-mfu.md` entries B200MFU-017/-018 (commit 82f970c9d, branch `research/mcwitt/7012-b200-mfu`).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Update: SM-specialization coda (falsified in the EP regime too), and first multi-node findings.

**Comm/compute SM partitioning is now falsified on our stack in both regimes.** The earlier EP1+FSDP ladder left one open question: the published ~20 %-on-the-MoE-block numbers for SM partitioning (DeepEP's dedicated comm-SM budget, TE NCCL_EP's `max_num_sms`) are about EP dispatch/combine contending with expert GEMMs, which EP1 doesn't have. Single-node ring EP8 does — NVLink all-gather/psum-scatter dispatch/combine concurrent with the expert GEMMs — so we re-ran the CTA-pin ladder there (d2560 row-13, ring EP8, ~12.9 % baseline per the EP backend ladder above):

| arm | steady-median MFU | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|
| control (NCCL auto) | 12.97 % | — |
| pin 16 CTAs | 11.75 % | −1.22 pp |
| pin 8 CTAs | 9.78 % | −3.19 pp |

Same monotone shape as EP1, with 3–6× the damage (6× at the milder 16-CTA pin, ~3× at the aggressive one) — comm is a bigger share at EP, so capping its CTAs (which for NCCL collectives is a bandwidth cap) costs proportionally more. Conclusion: on a stack where the compiler already schedules collectives asynchronously and NCCL autotunes CTA counts, a fixed small comm-SM budget is strictly harmful. The ~20 % wins in the public designs presuppose the *other* half: comm engines built as few-SM bandwidth-optimal copy kernels fed by chunked pipelines (DeepEP-style device-initiated transports, or NCCL_EP's chunked GMEM handoff). The actionable residue for us is the decomposition, not the SM budget — i.e., the TE NCCL_EP lane, where `max_num_sms` is meaningful because the pipeline exists. (Caveat from the API probe in the logbook: TE 2.15's wheel doesn't ship the NCCL_EP JAX surface yet; testing it means building TE from the WIP integration branch.)

**Multi-node bring-up (2×8 B200).** The training driver now launches and trains across nodes — bring-up validated end-to-end with a small model over TCP transport — after three portable fixes: a Slurm prolog/`--cpus-per-task` env conflict (`unset SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK SLURM_TRES_PER_TASK`), JAX's Slurm autodetect assuming process-per-GPU (pass `local_device_ids` explicitly for process-per-host), and the login shell's 8 MB memlock limit propagating into tasks and breaking InfiniBand memory registration (`srun --propagate=NONE`). Past those, two blockers outside our stack:

1. **Inter-node RDMA is broken at the fabric level**: in a minimal 16-rank NCCL probe, a 256 MB all-reduce returns silently *wrong* results (~60 s, one rank reads zero) and a 256 MB all-gather fails with `IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR` — while every link reports ACTIVE at 400 Gb/s. GID/HCA overrides don't help; TCP transport (`NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1`) is correct. Operator escalation is being prepared — note the failure mode on the default path is silent corruption, not a crash.
2. **An XLA first-collective rendezvous deadlock** on the ring-EP path under process-per-host multi-node (only 1 of 8 local device threads reaches the first all-reduce; persists at 20-minute timeouts). Parked pending the fabric fix; minimal repro to follow if it survives.

Ledger unchanged: d2560 best remains **15.67 %**. Next: MXFP8 via TE `grouped_dense` and the FA4 `lse` remat increment. Details: [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7012-b200-mfu/.agents/logbooks/7012-b200-moe-mfu.md) entries B200MFU-020/-021.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correction + one new EP datapoint.

**Correction to the EP-backend comment above (finding 3):** the claim "XLA currently lowers `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` on GPU to its own peer-copy kernel + multi-GPU barriers rather than NCCL; … it needs an upstream XLA fix" is too strong. A source read at our exact XLA pin (jaxlib 0.10.1 → openxla/xla `9b635916ecc`) shows:

- The 297 ms/call `RaggedAllToAllKernelImpl` we profiled is the **default single-host path** — a one-shot peer-copy kernel over NCCL symmetric memory, ragged on device (it reads `send_sizes` and copies only real rows). It is *not* a dense lowering: the dense decomposer exists in-tree but is gated off by default in every released jaxlib since the op landed.
- The **same thunk carries an NCCL send/recv path with true ragged sizes on the wire**, selected by `--xla_gpu_unsupported_use_ragged_all_to_all_one_shot_kernel=false` — no rebuild, one flag. Its cost is a host sync + an index all-to-all per call. [openxla/xla#33386](https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/33386) independently measures both halves on 8×B200: ~2% of NVLink bandwidth on the default one-shot path vs ~100% wire utilization on the NCCL path (which multi-host always takes).

So "unusable on GPU" holds **at defaults only**; a one-flag a2a-vs-ring ladder is queued before writing the backend off (logbook `H-a2a-nccl`, entry B200MFU-023 has the full path-by-path breakdown and flag archaeology).

**New datapoint — `ring_cute` (QuACK grouped GEMMs under ring's dispatch):** the ring backend's expert-MLP seam now accepts the `sonic_cute` QuACK kernels, closing part of the Triton-GEMM gap called out in finding 2. Same-node EP8 pair, row-13 standalone methodology: ring **13.50% / 3.68 s** → ring_cute **13.87% / 3.58 s** (+0.38 pp), matching the arithmetic (~⅔ of MoE GEMM FLOPs moving ~800 → ~1,500 TF/s). Interpretation: the GEMM engine was the *minority* of the EP tax — the remaining ~1.4 pp vs the 15.30% EP1 control is dispatch machinery (all-gather, capacity top-k, scatter-add, ~25% capacity padding). `ring_cute` is on the [`mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep/experiments/grug/moe/standalone) benchmark branch (README updated with the corrected a2a note). Logbook: B200MFU-022.

🤖 Update: the a2a flag experiment promised in the correction above is done — **confirmed, and it changes the EP picture** — plus the EP ladder reproduced on GB200.

**H-a2a-nccl confirmed.** On a 4×GB200 node (d2560 row-13, EP4, standalone methodology; MFU below in the script's B200-peak convention — ×0.9 for GB200's 2.5 PFLOP/s peak):

| `ragged_all_to_all` EP4 arm | MFU | step |
|---|---|---|
| XLA defaults (one-shot peer-copy kernel) | 1.88% | 52.8 s |
| `--xla_gpu_unsupported_use_ragged_all_to_all_one_shot_kernel=false` (NCCL send/recv) | **14.41 / 14.48%** (two nodes) | 6.9 s |
| defaults + `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_zero_copy=true` | 1.88% | 52.8 s |

One flag, 7.7× step-time collapse, from unusable to within 0.5pp of `ring`. The "needs an upstream XLA fix" verdict from the EP-ladder comment is fully retracted: it was a default-flag artifact. (Zero-copy is a measured no-op here — it saves a ~0.3 ms D2D copy per ~300 ms call.)

**QuACK GEMMs under a2a (`ragged_all_to_all_cute`).** Since the a2a arm still ran its local grouped GEMMs on Pallas-Triton, we factored `ring_cute`'s QuACK expert-MLP seam into a shared `expert_mlp_fn` adapter and registered an a2a variant. Same-node pair, both arms with the NCCL-path flag: 14.48% → **15.82%** (+1.34pp, mirroring ring→ring_cute's +1.41pp on this hardware; losses match to bf16 noise). Single-node EP4 ranking is now:

`ring_cute` **16.32%** > `ragged_all_to_all_cute` **15.82%** > `ring` **14.90%** ≈ a2a+flag **14.48%** (EP1 `sonic_cute` control: 17.01%)

`ring_cute` keeps the single-node recommendation — the a2a NCCL path pays a host sync + index all-to-all per call (104/step) that ring doesn't. But a2a_cute is now the leading **multi-node** EP vehicle short of a TE NCCL_EP source build: multi-host a2a always takes the NCCL path (no flag needed), it never all-gathers unrouted tokens across nodes, and openxla/xla#33386 measured ~100% cross-node wire utilization on exactly that path.

**Also reproduced on GB200** (4-GPU nodes, one benchmark job per node): EP1 `sonic_cute` at GB200-peak convention is 15.31% — matching the 8×B200 15.30% control almost exactly (+11% per-GPU absolute, the power/clock bump); the ring ladder is flat in EP degree (14.9% at EP2/EP4); the a2a-at-defaults pathology reproduces quantitatively (2× per-GPU load → 2× the 8-GPU step time). Capacity: the standalone script pins `capacity_factor=1.0` (exact per-shard average — drops on any routing imbalance), so all EP numbers here are cf=1.0; a sweep under `ring_cute` EP4 gives 1.0→16.32%, 1.25→15.61%, 1.5→14.90% (≈−0.7pp per +0.25 of headroom; 20-step losses indistinguishable). `--capacity-factor` is now a flag. One clean negative: d5120×EP4 on 4 GPUs OOMs at compile — width×EP needs ≥8-way sharding.

Everything (backends, flag documentation, GB200 table, capacity flag) is on the benchmark branch: [`mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/mcwitt/moe-standalone-ep/experiments/grug/moe/standalone). Logbook: B200MFU-024/-025/-026. Next: profile the a2a-NCCL arm to split host-sync vs wire cost (that plus the one-shot-kernel numbers becomes the upstream XLA report), and SonicMoE's Triton gather/combine under ring/a2a for the remaining dispatch tax.
