comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Allocator flag correction: `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR` is a no-op in JAX — the right knob is `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`**

The anti-fragmentation allocator we believed we'd been running was never active. `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR=cuda_malloc_async` is a **TensorFlow** env var; JAX's PJRT GPU client never reads it. JAX reads `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR` (valid values `default` / `bfc` / `platform` / `cuda_async` / `vmm`, default `bfc` — `jaxlib/xla_client.py:177`). XLA VLOG confirmed `se_gpu_pjrt_client.cc: Using BFC allocator` on every run regardless of the flag.

**Consequences**
- Every 64-GPU run silently used BFC, which fragments its arena over ~8 steps until an ~81 GiB allocation can no longer find a contiguous span → deterministic step-8 OOM.
- The earlier 32-GPU "`mallocasync` fixed the OOM" result was **illusory** — the flag did nothing; b512 simply fit under BFC.

**Fix:** `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` (real CUDA async mempool; coalesces free blocks).

**Result** — 64× GB200 (single rack), d5120 L48 e64 top4, replica=2 DDP, batch 1024, MuonH:
- **23.32% MFU / 362k tok/s**, 30 steps, no OOM.
- vs 32-GPU b512 baseline: 21.76% MFU / 169k tok/s → **~2.14× throughput, MFU flat-to-up**.

**Corrections to earlier theories in this thread:** the 64-GPU OOMs were *not* caused by the Muon Newton-Schulz reshard, by DDP, or by the replica mesh — all were BFC fragmentation from the dead flag. DDP scales cleanly within the rack once the correct allocator is set.

TODO: swap `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR` → `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` in the launcher default so we stop shipping the no-op flag.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Scoping update on the inter-node RDMA blocker (B200MFU-020): **cluster-specific, not general** — with one wording correction to the earlier update.

**Differential probe (B200MFU-028).** The same minimal collectives that fail on the 8×B200 cluster (256 MB all-reduce + all-gather, exact-value checks) ran as a 2-node gang on the GB200 fleet, two arms on the same node pair. With `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0` forcing cross-node traffic onto the IB NICs — the transport that fails there — every cross-node channel connected `via NET/IB/…/GDRDMA` (IB RDMA *with GPUDirect*, 122 channels over 4 HCAs) and both collectives returned exact results (reduce 2.3 s, all-gather 0.19 s). The default arm rides `P2P/MNNVL` (NVL72 cross-node NVLink) and is equally exact. The identical JAX→XLA→NCCL path does inter-node RDMA-with-GPUDirect correctly on healthy infrastructure: the corruption travels with that cluster's environment, and no general stack fix is needed.

**Correction:** "broken at the fabric level" was over-precise. Cluster-specific is now established; *which layer* of that cluster — switch/SM fabric vs node-level GPUDirect config (ACS/IOMMU/peermem) — is not: the retry-exceeded errors and SM client-reregistration events point at the fabric, while the silent-zeros failure mode is more characteristic of node-level GDR placement (IB payloads are CRC-protected — a sick fabric stalls and retries, it doesn't corrupt silently). The discriminators (host-memory `ib_write_bw`, a `NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=LOC` arm) go with the operator escalation either way.

Bycatch for the rack phase: on GB200 NVL72 the default cross-node transport is MNNVL — IB is only exercised beyond the NVL72 domain (or under `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0`) — so the forced-IB arm doubles as a clean pre-flight for the cross-rack ladder queued in B200MFU-027. Details: [logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/mcwitt/7012-b200-mfu/.agents/logbooks/7012-b200-moe-mfu.md) entry B200MFU-028.

| recompute_all | 14.3% |
| all_but_moe | 14.8% |
| **none** | **15.0%** |

At d2560, no checkpointing at all now fits (≈18 GB/GPU params+momentum at 32-way leaves room for full activations) and is the best number. d5120 can't fit `none` but gets **16.9%** from `all_but_moe` (ring_cute EP8, up from 16.2%). Two footnotes: the slim residuals *alone* under recompute_all cost −0.3pp (backward re-gathers with no memory dividend), so they're a package with all_but_moe/none; and loss trajectories bit-match the controls.

**Step anatomy** (xplane traces of steady-state steps, device-busy shares, recompute_all-era): at 32-way the step is **collective-dominated, not GEMM-dominated**. ring_cute EP4/d2560: collectives ≈ 48% of device-busy time (all_gather 17 + reshard 15 + reduce_scatter 13 + psum 3) — the top eight individual ops are all MoE-dispatch legs — vs ≈ 32% compute (grouped-GEMM custom calls + dot_general). d5120 is 50% collectives / 41% compute. The a2a backend at EP16 spends ≈ 25% of busy in `ragged-all-to-all` kernels and ≈ 21% in dispatch machinery (scatter-add/gather/sort), but its FSDP all_gather nearly vanishes (0.7% — EP16 leaves only a 2-way data axis), which is the mechanism behind its EP-flatness. Implication: MXFP8's ceiling shrinks at this scale (GEMMs are ~⅓ of busy time); overlap/volume reduction on the dispatch + FSDP collectives is the bigger lever.

**Odds and ends:** EP2 lands at 14.1% (EP4 stays the d2560 optimum). Capacity factor at 32-way costs ≈ −0.55pp per +0.25 (1.0→14.3, 1.25→13.8, 1.5→13.2). Auto-PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE` + latency-hiding scheduler) **crashes multi-host** on this stack — the per-host recompile desynchronizes the processes and the job dies at the JAX shutdown barrier — so the PGLE overlap experiment needs the manual dump-profile → shared-FDO → replay flow; parked for now.

Current 32-GPU bests: **d2560 15.0%** (ring_cute EP4, remat none), **d5120 16.9%** (ring_cute EP8, all_but_moe).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Multi-rack scaling of the muon MoE (GB200) — clean to 4 racks; 8+ racks blocked by an FA4/CuTe device-0 metadata remat**

Follow-up to the allocator finding above. With `cuda_async` + the intra-rack muon changes, the d5120 L48 e64 top4 recipe scales near-linearly across racks — until a hard wall at 8 racks.

**Scaling curve** (per-device batch fixed at 16, `replica=N` = one DDP replica per rack, FSDP within rack, muon reshard intra-rack):

| racks | GPUs | replica | batch | MFU | tok/s | vs 1-rack |
|------:|-----:|--------:|------:|----:|------:|----------:|
| 1 | 64  | 1 | 1,024 | 21.22% | 330k | 1.00× |
| 2 | 128 | 2 | 2,048 | 20.64% | 641k | 1.94× |
| 4 | 256 | 4 | 4,096 | 19.14% | 1.19M | 3.61× (~90% eff) |
| 8 | 512 | 8 | 8,192 | — | — | **wedges** |

The gentle MFU decline (0.6% then 1.5% per doubling) is just the DP all-reduce widening over IB — expected. 8+ racks (512/640 GPU) wedge: the run reaches ~step 11 then all ranks go silent (collective deadlock / `kAllToAll … expected N threads` rendezvous timeout / `CoordinationServiceAgent::SetError` abort).

**Root cause (definitively traced via HLO dump):** the FA4 CuTe attention is bridged to JAX through `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call` → `jax.pure_callback`. Its per-token `[B,S]` int32 metadata (`lower_bounds`/`valid`, declared `TensorSpec(static=True)` in `_cutlass_attention_forward_specs`) is pinned to **`{maximal device=0}`**. Under a `replica` mesh axis, SPMD must reshard that device-0 tensor to `[num_devices, 1]` every attention — an *involuntary full rematerialization* (`spmd_partitioner.cc`). That serializes ~128 MB through device 0 per layer; the resulting cross-rank timing skew is tolerable ≤4 racks but deadlocks the all-to-all at ≥8-way replica.

Key property: **it's replica-axis-dependent** — absent at `replica=1` (0 warnings), present at `replica≥2`, fatal at `replica=8`.

**What does *not* fix it** (all verified): resharding `batch.tokens`/`loss_weight`, resharding `segment_ids`, pinning the FA4 `arange`/`zeros`/`ones` constants replicated, and adding explicit `shard_map` `in_specs`. The `pure_callback` pins its metadata to device 0 regardless of how we shard or build the inputs — a reshard can't cross the callback boundary.

**Fix is upstream** in `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` (`cutlass.jax`): the `static=True` metadata tensors must become sharding-aware (respect the mesh), or the kernel needs a shardable `custom_call` instead of a `pure_callback`. Not fixable in this repo.

**Landed and working** (these are the real wins, keep them): `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, `SCALE_MUON_INTRA_RACK` (muon 4D reshard stays on NVLink), `SCALE_MUON_PAD_NONEXPERT` (distribute the L=48 non-expert NS via padding), plus a reusable `SCALE_MEM_PROFILE` HLO-introspection path that names device-0 remat sources.

**Bottom line:** single-rack ✅ and multi-rack DDP ✅ up to 4 racks / 1.19M tok/s at ~19% MFU. 8+ racks awaits the upstream CuTe pure_callback sharding fix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Progress: the 8-rack (512 GPU) `kAllToAll` wedge is root-caused and fixed; the d5120 MoE now scales cleanly to 8 racks.**

**Root cause — the token embedding gather, not attention/MoE/scan.** The embedding table sharded its hidden dim over `("replica_dcn", "data")` = all 512 GPUs, so assembling `[B, S, hidden]` from it is an all-to-all whose token axis spans racks. At hidden 5120 that all-to-all's NCCL first-call rendezvous stalls a local rank past the 20s timeout at 8 racks. Isolated with a minimal dense-only model (no attention, no MoE, no scan): **hidden 512 → 30 clean steps, hidden 5120 → wedge**, nothing else changed. HLO confirmed the FFN is plain FSDP (all-gathers, no all-to-all) — only the embedding *gather* produces an all-to-all.

**Fix.** Fully replicate the embedding table and do the lookup as a replica-local `shard_map` gather — each shard indexes its own tokens in its own copy, zero collectives. Numerically exact vs the old gather.

**Validated on the real model** (d5120, L48, e64 top-4, muonh) at 512 GPU / 8 racks — 30 clean steps, and the scaling curve holds:

| racks | GPUs | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 128 | 0.72M | 23.3% |
| 4 | 256 | 1.39M | 22.4% |
| 8 | 512 | 2.79M | 22.4% |

~2x throughput per doubling, MFU flat.

**Supporting fixes on the branch:**
- muon now routes the 4D scanned-expert stacks `[L,E,in,out]` through Newton-Schulz (they were silently falling through to Adam under `use_array_stacked_blocks`);
- lm_head sharded intra-rack (weight all-gather stays within a rack);
- the `cuda_async` allocator (`XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR`) and `SCALE_MUON_*` knobs are now forwarded to the nested train tasks;
- FA4 per-layer segment bounds precomputed outside the scan (removes the `{maximal device=0}` involuntary-remat of the `[B,S]` metadata);
- scale launch wired to the heuristic model config + LR, plus a `SCALE_DATA` SlimPajama<->datakit toggle.

Branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/grug/embedding-gather-shard-map
Validation run (8-rack): https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-512gpu-r8-embgather-validate

**Open item (separate workstream):** long runs stall once the data-loader prefetch buffer drains (~step 40) — the host pipeline can't sustain the ~2.8M tok/s feed rate for 512 GPUs on *either* dataset (the stall step tracks loader speed: datakit 38, slim 43). Compute is fine (loss drops normally when fed); it's a data-loader-throughput issue, not the wedge.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

Ragged EP now trains the exact four-node proxy with zero routing drops and reaches 19.63% mean MFU, up from 11.28%. Two independent problems caused the original result: XLA's latency-hiding schedule corrupted the first backward at larger expert banks, and the one-shot ragged transfer launched only one 128-thread block per peer. Disabling latency hiding and splitting each peer slice into 32 updates makes the transport finite and raises its grid from 16 to 512 blocks. Reusing the existing QuACK/CuTe SM100 grouped GEMMs removes most of the remaining local expert-compute gap.

The final command-buffer arm completed cleanly but regressed the proxy to 19.34% MFU. Exact-shape weight-gradient tile sweeps bound the remaining packaged kernel gain below the target. The selected configuration therefore remains just under 20%; a full-rack validation is the remaining production gate, not another obvious NCCL or XLA flag.

### Helpful links

- [Implementation PR #8081](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8081)
- [Incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/101)
- [Original XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fra2a-s25-exact-ep16-e48-profile-20260810)
- [Split-32 XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fra2a-s29-exact-ep16-e48-split32-profile-20260810)
- [CuTe XProf](https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fra2a-s34-exact-ep16-e48-split32-cute-profile-20260810)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Experiment contract

The exact proxy used d6144/L48, 48 routed experts of width 6272, latent width 3072, top-4 routing, capacity 1.33, EP16, and 1,048,576 tokens per step across four GB200 nodes. Each node ran four one-device JAX processes. Scored jobs occupied one rack and NVLink domain. PGLE, gradient watch, eval, periodic metric steps, profiling, and checkpoints were disabled for timing runs. Results use steps 5-24.

The proxy matches the one-rack EP64 hero's per-GPU work: both route 65,536 tokens and hold three experts per GPU. EP64 raises global batch and device count together, so it does not enlarge local expert GEMMs or imply a larger-run uplift. A full-rack validation is still required before changing the hero run.

## Results

| Arm | Step time | Tokens/s | MFU | Result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| One update/peer, latency hiding on, overlap 4 | 33.7040 s | 31,112 | 11.3220% | Finite exact baseline |
| One update/peer, latency hiding off, overlap 1 | 33.8187 s | 31,006 | 11.2834% | Safe flags neutral at exact shape |
| 32 updates/peer, Pallas expert compute | 21.1090 s | 49,675 | 18.0770% | 60.21% throughput gain |
| Split-32, 4 MiB NCCL buffer | 21.1213 s | 49,647 | 18.0669% | Neutral |
| Split-32, QuACK/CuTe expert compute | 19.4429 s | 53,940 | 19.6291% | Best stable configuration |
| Split-32, CuTe, command buffers on | 19.7338 s | 53,137 | 19.3369% | 1.49% throughput regression |

Every completed exact arm had finite loss and zero dropped assignments, dropped-token fraction, or router overflow.

## Findings

- XLA latency hiding corrupts the first backward pass at larger expert banks. Disabling `--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler` restores finite training. The ragged runtime also uses collective overlap limit 1; this improved the small EP8/E96 proxy but was neutral on exact EP16/E48.
- The original ragged kernel used `grid=(16,1,1)` and consumed 13.82 seconds per step. Split-32 selects XLA's existing multi-update path, uses `grid=(16,1,32)`, and reduces the transfer to 0.78 seconds per step without changing capacity or tensor layout.
- After split-32, the gap to fixed all-to-all was expert compute. Ragged `moe_up_down` took 8.965 seconds per step versus 4.502 seconds for fixed; ragged communication was 0.886 seconds faster. The CuTe flavor keeps ragged dispatch/combine and runs the activation-path grouped GEMMs through QuACK/CuTe, reducing clean step time by another 7.89%.
- CuTe XProf measures 2.084 seconds per step in the two retained Pallas weight-gradient contractions. Exact one-GB200 sweeps covered 64/128/256 output tiles, K16/K32/K64, two/four pipeline stages, and four/eight warps. The only win was 7.54% on `dw13`; `dw2` retained its original tile. Combining the measured ceiling predicts 19.74% MFU, so it does not justify a four-node arm by itself.
- The trace already contains `ncclSymkDevKernel_AllGather_STMC`, so NCCL automatically selected its NVLS multicast path for the largest all-gathers. Forcing NVLS or SHARP cannot accelerate the custom ragged peer-write kernel. Increasing `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` from 1 MiB to 4 MiB was neutral.
- The XLA `ragged_dot_general` alternative OOMed before step zero on a single 159.32 GiB allocation. The generic symmetric put/signal backend failed with `ncclPutSignal: srcWinHost is not in a valid symmetric window`; the pinned GXL backend is unimplemented.
- Process-per-GPU needs the hero host-memory reservation. A 256 GiB four-node reservation OOM-killed a worker; 850 GiB per node completed. Auto-PGLE is not usable in this topology because four CUPTI sessions on one node collide. The separate stale retry-coordinator bug was fixed in [#8079](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8079).

## Decision

Use one process per GPU, 850 GiB of host memory per node, latency hiding disabled, collective overlap limit 1, 32 logical updates per peer, and the QuACK/CuTe ragged expert backend. Keep PGLE and periodic diagnostic work off for timing. Preserve one update per peer as the general library default and select 32 explicitly in this hero configuration until other shapes are profiled.

Keep `FUSION,CUSTOM_CALL` command buffers disabled. They completed without the historical B200 teardown failure but increased mean step time by 1.50%. Even stacking the independently measured `dw13` tile gain perfectly with that arm predicts about 19.45% MFU, so no combined four-node treatment is justified.

The conventional NCCL, transfer-splitting, packaged grouped-matmul, and bounded Pallas tile arms are exhausted for this proxy. A full one-rack EP64 run should validate the selected configuration but is not expected to improve per-GPU MFU merely through scale.

## Artifacts

- [Experiment logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weaver/hero-run-why-can-t-we-ragged-all/.agents/logbooks/ragged-ep64.md)
- [Split-32 W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ra2a-s28-exact-ep16-e48-split32-perf-20260810)
- [CuTe W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ra2a-s33-exact-ep16-e48-split32-cute-perf-20260810)
- [Command-buffer W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ra2a-s37-exact-ep16-e48-split32-cute-command-buffers-20260810)
- Weight-gradient benchmark: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/benchmarks/ragged-weight-grad-gb200/2026.08.10.38/results.json`
- [PR #8013](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8013)
- [FSDP sweep #8054](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8054)

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Milestone: disabling one-shot removes the illegal address, but the NCCL send/recv fallback exhausts HBM before step 0.

[RA2A-002](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ra2a-002-nccl-sendrecv-20260808) compiled the identical 191.82 GiB post-rematerialization executable, initialized the 64-rank clique, and did not reproduce the device-32 failure. Six seconds later every rank logged `ncclCuMemAlloc` out of memory, and `jit_train_step` raised `JaxRuntimeError: NCCL operation ncclGroupEnd() failed`.

This confirms that the default one-shot path and the fallback have separate blockers. NVIDIA documents a dedicated FIFO for every send/recv source-destination pair and recommends lowering `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` under memory pressure; its default is 4 MiB. At EP64, that is roughly 252 MiB of peer FIFOs per rank before other NCCL allocations.

I stopped the retry loop. RA2A-003 keeps one-shot disabled and changes only `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1048576`, reducing the documented peer-FIFO total to roughly 63 MiB per rank. Exact result and launch contract: [task logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/58ce5d056b/.agents/logbooks/ragged-ep64.md). NVIDIA references: [environment variable](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html#nccl-buffsize), [send/recv FIFO behavior](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2265/release-notes/rel_2-7-5.html#known-issues).

7. Sweep `--xla_gpu_nccl_p2p_max_nchannels` serially, starting at 1.
8. Test per-stream communicator disabling and communicator splitting as memory controls.
9. Test Blackwell partial CUDA graphs, `FUSION,CUSTOM_CALL`, once with an immediate crash stop.
10. Test NCCL user buffers only with an explicitly bounded external arena.
11. Test SOL/O1 only if latency hiding remains useful.
12. Test NVLS/SHARP only if a profile shows non-ragged AR/AG/RS dominating the residual step.

The ranking follows NVIDIA's current [JAX Toolbox GPU guidance](https://docs.nvidia.com/jax-toolbox/performance-profiling/gpu-performance) and Marin EP evidence from [#7279](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5064115832). NVLS/SHARP is not a direct ragged arm: the reachable ragged lowering is NCCL send/recv, whereas NVLS targets reduction collectives. AG/RS combine thresholds are likewise FSDP controls. I am also excluding `CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=1`; NVIDIA documents it as slower on Blackwell.

A result above 20% median MFU over steps 5–24 is a candidate win. Changes below the ±1.57% single-reading resolution established in #8054 require replication.

🤖 The next arms are reprioritized from the exact JAX 0.11 lowering rather than a broad NCCL sweep.

At the pinned OpenXLA revision, the dense ragged decomposer is off, one-shot is on, its NCCL barrier is on, and ragged memory defaults to private. Our current baseline overrides one-shot to false. That fallback first copies all ragged metadata to the host, transposes output offsets with a dense index all-to-all, then emits grouped send and receive operations for every local-expert/peer pair. E192/EP16 therefore launches 192 send/receive pairs per ragged call. The repeated three-minute signature is unusable throughput, but the Python thread dump alone does not prove a hard deadlock.

The serialized queue after S06 is now:

1. Add `--xla_gpu_unsupported_enable_ragged_all_to_all_multi_host_decomposer=true` while retaining one-shot false. This pass rewrites cross-host dispatch into an inter-host all-gather plus intra-host ragged all-to-all, directly reducing cross-host P2P fanout without changing FSDP.
2. Add `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=RAGGEDALLTOALL` instead, isolating async wrapping of the ragged operation rather than the already-negative latency-hiding scheduler.
3. Restore one-shot at EP16 under process-per-GPU with an immediate CUDA-failure stop. This tests whether the full-rack device-32 illegal address is specific to EP64.
4. Enable the dense ragged decomposer only as a correctness diagnostic if the native paths still make no progress.

Once an arm reaches steps, repeat it at d2048 on the same four-node NVLink domain before judging the 20% MFU target. Then tune the 1 MiB FIFO upward, `NCCL_PROTO=Simple`, and P2P channel count. NVLS/SHARP moves up only if the multi-host decomposition wins, because that rewrite introduces ordinary all-gather traffic for it to accelerate.

OpenXLA sources: [defaults](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/131bf41acb46/xla/debug_options_flags.cc#L463-L500), [multi-host pass insertion](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/131bf41acb46/xla/service/gpu/gpu_compiler.cc#L1000-L1035), [fallback runtime](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/131bf41acb46/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Upstream source changes the experiment priority: a post-JAX-0.11 device kernel now outranks generic NCCL tuning.

jaxlib 0.11.0 pins OpenXLA `131bf41acb46` from July 16. [OpenXLA #46116](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/46116), merged July 24, adds an opt-in device-initiated RA2A kernel using NCCL 2.29 LSA/GIN. It runs the collective in one CUDA launch and was specifically designed to remove per-call host coordination. That directly targets both current failure modes: the fused LSA-path illegal address and the host-synchronized send/receive fallback stall.

The arm requires both flags:

```
--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true
--xla_gpu_experimental_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers=true
```

The first flag alone silently falls through under private memory. This requirement was already identified in [#7891](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7891#issuecomment-5174781337) and confirmed by an OpenXLA contributor in the [follow-up](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7891#issuecomment-5175507921).

SHARP/NVLS and FSDP combine thresholds remain low-value here: they do not directly accelerate ragged peer copies or NCCL send/receive. NVIDIA also says `CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=1` is slower on Blackwell, and local memcpy P2P is inapplicable with one device per process.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Ranked arm queue after the PGLE-off reachability result:

1. Finish S10e's pinned-JAX one-shot baseline and score steps 5-24. This is the control for every transport arm.
2. On the same d768 screen, install JAX `0.11.1.dev20260808` and enable both `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true` and `--xla_gpu_experimental_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers=true`. This is the highest-value treatment because it replaces the host-coordinated/send-receive fallback with the post-0.11 device-initiated RA2A implementation; either flag alone is not a valid treatment.
3. Run the exact four-node d6144/L48 proxy under pinned one-shot, then repeat only the winning nightly treatment. This preserves the hero's 65,536 tokens/GPU, 16 sequences/GPU, three experts/GPU, and routed expert load, so it is the first screen that can meaningfully test the >20% MFU target.
4. If launch overhead is visible, enable `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=FUSION,CUSTOM_CALL`. NVIDIA recommends this exact subset on B200, but it is gated behind a clean baseline because the hero currently disables command buffers for #5675.
5. Sweep `--xla_gpu_nccl_p2p_max_nchannels=4`, then 8 only if 4 helps. NVIDIA identifies this as the fine-grained P2P channel knob; the default 0 delegates channel count to NCCL.
6. Test `NCCL_PROTO=Simple`, then `NCCL_PROTO=LL128` against NCCL auto-selection. Protocol is one of the few documented NCCL knobs that applies directly to this traffic pattern.
7. Test `--xla_gpu_enable_nccl_user_buffers=true` with an explicitly sized `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_COLLECTIVE_MEM_SIZE_MB` pool after measuring HBM margin. NVIDIA documents user buffers as zero-copy capable for send/recv; preallocation avoids the default grow-on-demand fragmentation.
8. Revisit scheduler controls only after the above: latency hiding off versus the current on control, then overlap limit 1 versus 4. S03/S08 were contaminated by auto-PGLE and cannot close these hypotheses.
9. Increase `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` from 1 MiB to 2 MiB and then 4 MiB only if the process-per-GPU baseline has enough HBM. The 1 MiB value was required to avoid the earlier allocator failure, so this is a lower-priority memory/performance tradeoff.

I am excluding SHARP/NVLS and the AG/RS/AR combine thresholds from the primary queue: NVIDIA documents those as reduction/FSDP optimizations, not ragged peer copies. I am also excluding local memcpy P2P because it only applies to devices managed by one process, `CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=1` because NVIDIA says it is slower on Blackwell, and `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP` because its documented hang workaround targets the discarded one-process/multiple-device topology.

Sources: [NVIDIA JAX Toolbox GPU performance guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/jax-toolbox/performance-profiling/gpu-performance), [NCCL 2.30.7 environment variables](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html), and [OpenXLA device-initiated RA2A PR #46116](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/46116).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Milestone: the stable-schedule reruns isolate a deterministic ragged correctness failure.

S10f used the 60-token-per-active-parameter ladder schedule; S10g used 750. Both ran process-per-GPU on four GB200 nodes in one NVLink domain. S10g landed on `DH1-129-US-EAST-08A` with PGLE off, a 1 MiB NCCL buffer, overlap limit 4, latency hiding enabled, and command buffers disabled.

Both runs completed a finite first step and then every rank raised `Non-finite loss (nan) at step 2`. S10g recorded 41.3079 s, 25,384.4 tokens/s, 6.4944% MFU, loss 11.8062, and 0.0289% dropped assignments for step 0. Its resolved peak rates were much lower than the short probe (MuonH 0.00697, Adam 0.00161), and the actual step-0 optimizer rates were both zero during warmup. That rules out the abbreviated schedule and high learning rate as the immediate cause.

The first update can still propagate a non-finite gradient through a zero scalar under IEEE arithmetic. The ragged tests currently compare forward values only; they do not compare gradients or reproduce the QB router-bias transition between the first two batches. The working hypothesis is therefore a ragged backward/offset edge case exposed by the changed routing pattern, not an NCCL stall.

I stopped S10g before its automatic retry. Next I will use the smallest useful process-per-GPU slice to compare ragged gradients against a stable EP backend, then resume the nightly device-kernel arm once the correctness boundary is understood. There is still no steps 5-24 timing window to score.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Milestone: the post-0.11 device kernel is incompatible with the required process-per-GPU topology.

S11 kept the failing EP8/E96 geometry and the same two hosts in `DH1-126-US-EAST-08A`, then moved all four JAX packages to `0.11.1.dev20260808` and enabled the device-kernel/symmetric-buffer pair. All eight one-device processes aborted at the first ragged collective, before a W&B training step, with:

```
RaggedAllToAllThunk: Peer access must be enabled.
```

This is a hard implementation precondition. [OpenXLA checks peer access](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/main/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc#L1070-L1081) after selecting the device-communication/symmetric-memory path and before locating the symmetric input and output buffers. A worker that sees one GPU cannot establish XLA local peer access to the other three GPUs on its host.

The coordinator was stopped before retry, so the arm released its eight GPUs. This result rules out the new LSA/GIN device kernel for our long-term process-per-GPU setup; it does not evaluate the nightly generic ragged path. The next serialized arm keeps nightly `0.11.1.dev20260808` and EP8/E96 fixed while removing only the device-kernel and symmetric-buffer flags.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Source milestone after S14: the failing implementation is more specifically XLA’s zero-copy symmetric-output one-shot path.

JAX 0.11 pins OpenXLA [`131bf41acb46`](https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/131bf41acb4650e4391a640c3f1859c1c86ad74b). That revision includes [`c1fcf2507528`](https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/c1fcf2507528eec72374aeb2eddd85d028939cc2), which made zero-copy symmetric output mandatory for multi-host one-shot ragged all-to-all and removed the prior double-copy scratch path. The CUDA kernel writes sender slices directly into peer output buffers after an NCCL barrier. The Aug 8 nightly still fails, so no subsequent fix in that window closes this case.

The dense decomposer is a correctness oracle, not likely the EP64 winner: it pads each peer slice to the full input length, uses ordinary all-to-all, then reconstructs the ragged output with masks. Ring and decomposer also agree at step 0 (`grad/norm/total` 0.240191 vs. 0.240176), further clearing model math and transpose algebra.

Revised serialized order:

1. S15 four-node EP16/E192 dense-decomposer no-watch baseline; currently correctly waiting for four nodes in one domain.
2. Clean private NCCL send/receive fallback: one-shot off, process-per-GPU, PGLE off, 1 MiB FIFO.
3. Synchronous one-shot with `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=RAGGEDALLTOALL`; add VLOG-5 bounds checking only if needed to distinguish async buffer lifetime from invalid offsets.
4. Tune only a finite path: P2P channels 4 then 8, `NCCL_PROTO=Simple` then LL128, 2 MiB FIFO if HBM permits, latency hiding/overlap, then partial command buffers.
5. If decomposer and fallback cannot meet the target, implement the suggested pooled fixed all-to-all: one fixed sender-to-receiver bucket, local expert sort plus ragged matmul. That removes per-(sender, expert) fragmentation while avoiding the faulty primitive.

SHARP/NVLS stays excluded from the direct ragged queue because it optimizes reduction collectives, not these peer copies.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Update: VLOG bounds checking races the metadata producers

- Change: repeated the failing two-node EP8/E96 one-shot run with only `TF_CPP_VMODULE=ragged_all_to_all_thunk=5` added.
- Result: all eight ranks failed before step 0 at `ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc:297` with `RaggedAllToAll: Negative sizes detected!`; the coordinator was stopped before its retry consumed GPUs.
- Interpretation: this does not show that Marin generated negative counts. JAX accepts integer metadata, and OpenXLA's canonicalizer converts all four arrays to S64 before the GPU thunk. The VLOG-5 checker then copies them with `StreamExecutor::SynchronousMemcpyD2H` without first ordering that copy behind the metadata-producing work on the execution stream. It can read uninitialized/stale values before the one-shot kernel is launched. This is a separate XLA diagnostics bug and makes the raw VLOG-5 result inconclusive about the production NaN.
- Confidence: high on the S64 canonicalization and checker ordering from pinned source; medium that the negative values are entirely a checker race until a launch-blocking run confirms it.
- Next: run the identical EP8/E96 case with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`. If gradients become finite, stream ordering is the production fault. Otherwise combine launch blocking with VLOG-5 to get a valid bounds check. The exact four-node E48 baseline remains queued with zero GPU allocation behind production.

Pinned source: [canonicalizer](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/131bf41acb4650e4391a640c3f1859c1c86ad74b/xla/backends/gpu/transforms/ragged_all_to_all_canonicalizer.cc), [one-shot checker call](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/131bf41acb4650e4391a640c3f1859c1c86ad74b/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc#L1075-L1098), [checker copies](https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/131bf41acb4650e4391a640c3f1859c1c86ad74b/xla/backends/gpu/runtime/ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc#L251-L303)

🤖 Update: synchronized bounds checks pass before the same NaN

- Change: added VLOG-5 bounds checking to the launch-blocking EP8/E96 run. The admitted workload carried both `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` and `TF_CPP_VMODULE=ragged_all_to_all_thunk=5`.
- Result: every one-shot collective passed the metadata and buffer checks: no negative offsets/sizes, input read violation, symmetric-output write violation, or receive-capacity violation appeared on any rank. comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 XProf milestone: the four-node bottleneck is the custom ragged transfer kernel, not NCCL collective selection.

The exact process-per-GPU profile completed on the same rack-129 nodes and safe flags as the paired treatment. One full traced step attributes 43.92% of exclusive device time to communication. `RaggedAllToAllWithSymmetricMemoryKernelImpl<8>` alone takes 13.6599 seconds, or 41.3% of the 33.1261-second device timeline; its two NCCL barriers total 0.9519 seconds.

The complete three-step kernel table contains 864 ragged transfers averaging 47.986 ms. Every transfer launches `grid=(16,1,1), block=(128,1,1)` on a 152-SM GB200. XProf reports a 304-block minimum occupancy grid and suggests a 1,024-thread block. The HLO buffers are 1.61 or 2.14 GB each, so each of 16 blocks loops over a large destination slice; effective source-byte throughput is only about 39 GB/s per GPU.

This matches the pinned OpenXLA source: the one-shot path hard-codes 128 threads and derives its grid only from destination count and updates per destination. This workload has one update per destination, producing exactly 16 blocks. Current OpenXLA `main` retains that geometry, and there is no tuning flag for blocks per large update.

NCCL NVLS/SHARP, protocol, or channel knobs cannot repair the dominant 41.3% because this kernel performs direct peer writes; NCCL only supplies its barriers and smaller collectives. Even deleting all measured communication would lift the 11.32% baseline to only about 20.2% MFU, so a conventional NCCL arm cannot plausibly clear the target.

Profile: https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/xprof/open?uri=s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Fra2a-s25-exact-ep16-e48-profile-20260810

Next I will screen the generic symmetric put/signal backend on two nodes. It bypasses this one-shot kernel and is distinct from the private NCCL fallback that already stalled. The serialized queue is:

1. Screen Transformer Engine JAX BF16 grouped GEMM on the exact `dw13` and `dw2` shapes.
2. Screen cuDNN Frontend grouped Wgrad on the same shapes if Transformer Engine cannot express the backward layout or misses the target.
3. Run a four-GPU, process-per-GPU Mixture-of-Kittens oracle at the exact hero-layer geometry.
4. Integrate only a backend that clears the 17.3% kernel gate, then repeat the exact four-node, same-rack S33 timing contract.

comments.body:
**Upstream issue filed: [openxla/xla#47146](https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/47146)** — the post-0.11 device-initiated ragged-all-to-all kernel (#46116) is unusable on any multi-process deployment: a `peer_access_enabled` RET_CHECK added after the kernel landed requires the entire clique to live in one process, which process-per-GPU (and even process-per-node multi-host) can never satisfy. The issue includes a 25-line plain-JAX repro that fires on a stock nightly with 4 processes on one node.

Status of the arm here: with the gate patched out locally, the kernel engages at 4 nodes × 4 GPUs (`lsa_size=16`, LSA lane) but training produces nondeterministic all-rank NaNs (onsets at steps 5, 2, 2 across three attempts on identical inputs), while the isolated collective is bitwise-clean over 500 random ragged cases even multi-node/multi-process — including chained back-to-back calls. Suspected mechanism (flagged in the issue): the LSA branch's entry barrier is `memory_order_relaxed` where the GIN branch uses acquire. Device-kernel line is parked pending upstream response; the one-shot path with split-32 transport remains the working configuration (current frontier on it: S48's active-row cuDNN backend above, 22.31% MFU at cf 1.00).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
**Campaign update (continuing the serialized queue from S48): capacity verdict, steady-state drop measurement, and EP64 status.**

**Capacity ladder closed.** S49 (`ra2a-mw-s49-exact-ep16-e48-cf098-split32-active-row-cudnn-perf-20260812`) reduced only the capacity factor from S48's 1.00 to 0.98 on the same active-row cuDNN backend: steps 5–24 averaged 17.049 s, 22.41% MFU, mean drop 2.036% (worst 2.064%) — under the 2.5% harness ceiling, but the gain over S48 (+0.07 MFU points) is inside run variance (duration sd 0.15 s). We are treating sub-1.0 capacity as irrelevant to production training and closing the ladder at cf 1.00 for harness purposes.

**Steady-state drops are the real capacity constraint, and the LR≈0 harness cannot see them.** The S-series arms pin LR≈0, which freezes the router at random init and makes load nearly uniform — S48's 0.49% drop at cf 1.00 is pure statistical fluctuation. Two measurements of the trained regime:

- *Analytical:* replaying the logged per-expert routing histograms from #8062's d2048 EP64/E192 run (trained 47k steps) through the ragged backend's pooled-receiver capacity gives cf 1.00 → 1.0–1.7% steady-state drops, cf 1.1 → ≤0.05%, cf 1.2+ → ≈0. (No conflict with #8062's 6.6–7.1% at cf 1.3: those runs used `fixed_all_to_all`, whose capacity is per-(sender, expert) cell; the ragged transport pools capacity per receiving device and drops far less at the same factor.)
- *Empirical:* 300-step real-LR runs (3000-step schedule) at the exact EP16/E48 frontier config. cf 1.00 (`ra2a-mw-r01-ep16-e48-cf1-split32-realLR-droptraj-20260812`): 16–24% drops through the router-collapse transient (steps ~10–30), decaying to 2.57% mean over steps 250–300 and still declining — marginal at best. cf 1.20 (`ra2a-mw-r02-ep16-e48-cf12-split32-realLR-droptraj-20260812`): same transient shape but gone by step 60, then 0.019% mean over steps 250–300, with final loss slightly better than cf 1.00 (3.3698 vs 3.3739).

Production capacity should therefore sit at cf 1.1–1.2; cf 1.00 is a harness setting only. The ~60-step collapse transient exists at every factor; if it matters for the hero, capacity warmup (start 1.33, anneal to ~1.2) is a launch-knob-level mitigation.

**EP64 validation: the wall is still there, on both transports.** The exact hero shape (EP64/E192, batch 1024, cf 1.0, active-row cuDNN, split-32) fails at step 0:

- One-shot path: `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` on many ranks simultaneously, 3/3 deterministic (`ra2a-mw-v01/v02/v03-...-20260812`), reproducing MNEP-017's signature on the current backend generation. A compile-cache-warm rerun still crashes, so it is first execution, not autotune.
- Send/recv fallback (`ra2a-mw-v04-ep64-e192-cf1-cudnn-oneshot-off-20260812`): compiles (8m26s) then deadlocks silently in the first collective until the 6h job timeout.
- In flight: `ra2a-mw-v05-ep64-e192-cf1-split1-cudnn-20260812` retests the one-shot path with splits-per-peer 1 — EP64 × split-32 is 2048 updates per collective, 4× the EP16 tuning point, so an update-count blowup is the cheap alternative hypothesis to rule out before concluding the one-shot kernel is rank-count-broken at 64.

Upstream: [openxla/xla#47146](https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/47146) (device-kernel peer-access gate) has no maintainer response yet. Next probe after v05: the post-#46996 multi-host decomposer (>2-host support merged upstream Aug 11; the first nightly carrying it is still unpublished — we verified dev20260811 predates it), including the fast-interconnect slice-size override as a possible EP64 workaround (4-rank one-shots per tray plus dense inter-tray exchange).

W&B: runs under `marin-community/marin_moe`, ids as named above.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **EP64 one-shot crash root-caused to a 32-peer bound in XLA's barrier kernel. With a one-constant rebuild, the hero shape (E384, top-8, expert width 3072) completes at EP64 on one rack at 20.20% MFU, meeting the >20% campaign target.**

**Root cause.** Both `MultiGpuBarrierKernel` and `MultiGpuBarrierWithNcclKernel` declare `kMaxPeers = 32` (`xla/stream_executor/gpu/multi_gpu_barrier_kernel.h`). `LaunchMultiGpuBarrier` checks `num_devices <= kMaxPeers`; the NCCL-window variant used by the one-shot ragged all-to-all has no such check, so a 64-rank clique writes past the 32-slot signal region in symmetric memory — the deterministic step-0 `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` from v01–v03 (the MNEP-017 signature). The bound is on rank count, which retires the update-count hypothesis from the last update. The device-side barrier loop is already guarded by `threadIdx.x < num_ranks`, so raising the constant is a safe recompile: we built `jax-cuda13-pjrt` at the dev20260811 pins (jax `8d1be7d`, xla `60f8069`) with `kMaxPeers` 32→128, otherwise stock. Wheel: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/research/mcwitt-ra2a/pjrt-kmax128-dev0811-20260814/`.

**A second, independent blocker masked the first.** Our wheel-install script used `--no-deps`, leaving the venv's nvidia-* runtime packages at baseline versions; on that runtime `ncclCommQueryProperties` reports zero LSA teams and the one-shot silently declines on every configuration. An A/B with bit-identical stock PJRT bits (v39) isolated it: through our installer the ragged op failed with `INVALID_ARGUMENT` (NCCL send/recv fallback disabled); through `--jax-nightly-version`, which resolves `jax-cuda13-plugin[with-cuda]` with dependencies, the same bits ran at 22.46% MFU. The launcher now installs the stock nightly set with dependencies and overlays the patched PJRT wheel. This generation also needs `--xla_gpu_ragged_all_to_all_mode=symmetric`; the default moved to private memory.

**Validation** (LR≈0 harness, steps 5–24 means):

- `ra2a-mw-v40-ep16-e48-cf1-withdeps-20260814` — EP16/E48 regression check: 22.48% MFU vs 22.46% stock. The patch is behaviorally neutral below the old bound.
- `ra2a-mw-g17-ep64-e384-k8-i3072-cf1-withdeps-20260814` — EP64, E384, top-8, intermediate 3072, batch 1024, cf 1.00, split-32, mem fraction 0.68: 25/25 steps, 18.79 s/step, 20.20% MFU (min 20.07%), drop fraction 0.396%. First completed EP64 run on the ragged one-shot path. The fixed-transport version of this shape (#8062) reached 18.6% MFU with ~25% drops.

**EP48 probe parked.** 12 nodes/E192 fails at step 0 with CUDA OOM inside `ncclAlltoAll` (`ncclCuMemAlloc`), at both the default memory fraction and 0.68 (v42, v43). EP64 fits the larger E384 model at 0.68, so we suspect the one-shot declines at 48 ranks (LSA size ≠ clique size) and the decomposed NCCL path's buffers do not fit. Unconfirmed.

**Upstream.** An openxla/xla issue for the missing bounds check and the kMaxPeers overflow is drafted with the validation results above; link to follow once filed. openxla/xla#47146 (device-kernel peer-access gate) now has maintainer engagement suggesting a slice-size cause; our `lsa_size=16 num_ranks=16` measurement from the instrumented d09 run contradicts that, and a reply is drafted.

W&B: runs under `marin-community/marin_moe`, ids as named above.

Before filing, we validated the standalone repro on the stock dev20260811 nightly (64 devices: `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`, 3/3 expected signature; 16 devices: clean pass), confirmed no duplicate report exists, and confirmed current XLA main still has `kMaxPeers = 32` with no bounds check in `LaunchMultiGpuBarrierWithNccl`.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
A Zephyr reduce shard fails when one scatter sidecar read hits a transient object-store connection error. `_read_sidecar_slice` fetches `metadata.msgpack` with [`fs.cat_file`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L289), and [`_read_sidecar_slices_parallel`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L301-L313) calls `fut.result()` with no retry. One failed sidecar out of thousands aborts the shard. The coordinator requeues the shard, and the retry redoes the whole sidecar scan.

```text
File "/app/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py", line 408, in from_sidecars
    for slice_ in _read_sidecar_slices_parallel(scatter_paths, target_shard):
File "/app/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py", line 311, in _read_sidecar_slices_parallel
    ordered[idx] = fut.result()
File "/app/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py", line 289, in _read_sidecar_slice
    meta = _sidecar_decoder().decode(fs.cat_file(fs_path))
...
botocore.exceptions.EndpointConnectionError: Could not connect to the endpoint URL: "http://marin-us-east-02a.cwlota.com/tmp/ttl%3D1d/zephyr/20260818-015021-c4811609/stage0-Map-Scatter/shard-0265/scatter/metadata.msgpack"
```

Reproduce:
1. Run a Zephyr shuffle with thousands of mapper sidecars and scatter output on CoreWeave object storage.
2. Make one `GET .../scatter/metadata.msgpack` raise `EndpointConnectionError`.
3. The reduce shard fails and the coordinator requeues the full sidecar scan.

Expected: a transient sidecar read retries with bounded attempts and backoff, and an unrecoverable read names the sidecar path.

`EndpointConnectionError` subclasses `botocore.exceptions.ConnectionError` and not `HTTPClientError`, so `s3fs.core.S3_RETRYABLE_ERRORS` does not contain it and s3fs leaves `_error_wrapper` at the first occurrence. The remaining retries come from botocore, `max_attempts=5, mode="standard"` in [`s3_compat.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/s3_compat.py#L101). That gives four delays of `rand(0,1) * 2**attempt`, so the cover is 15 s at most. Botocore also refuses a retry after its per-client quota of 500 units drains at 5 units for each retry, and 32 concurrent readers can drain it in one endpoint outage. We did not confirm the quota path for this failure.

#8265 (PR #8269) adds a retry for the Parquet footer read in `_unify_frame_schemas`. #8309 covers the chunk batch stream. Neither covers the sidecar `cat_file` read.

comments.author: Skystellan
comments.body:
I traced the failure to `fs.cat_file(meta_path)` in `_Sidecar.read()`. Retrying there avoids repeating successful sidecar reads when `read_all()` runs them concurrently.

I plan to use the existing `retry_with_backoff` and `is_transient_s3_error` helpers for transient reads only, leaving msgpack decoding non-retryable. The tests will cover recovery after a transient failure and a permanent failure that is attempted once. Please let me know if this is already being worked on.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Just kicking off: measure whether adaptive environment/problem sampling improves RL training efficiency under a fixed compute budget, versus uniform random sampling.

## Description

We run SkyRL GRPO post-training on a small Qwen policy (0.6B class) over a pool of verifiable, non-agentic environments (math datasets spanning difficulty, plus simple programmatic tasks). Each arm uses the same model, data pool, and budget; only the policy for choosing which environment/problem to roll out next differs.

Arms:

1. Naive sampling: uniform random over the pool (baseline).
2. Modified Thompson sampling: bias toward environments currently yielding reward signal (e.g. per-env reward variance / pass-rate entropy), with decay so the belief tracks policy drift.
3. Pre-graded difficulty (problems graded 0–N easiest→hardest):
   - Naive curriculum: 1/N of budget per level.
   - Adaptive curriculum: train on a level until it stops paying (saturated or not learning), then move.
   - Biased sampling: grades seed an initial belief distribution for the Thompson sampler.

Budget: fixed output-token count per run, falling back to GPU wall-time (64 H100s x fixed hours) if token accounting is impractical. Runs use INTERACTIVE priority on cw-rno2a. The experiment is wired through Marin artifact steps (`marin.rl.skyrl`) so arms are cached and rerunnable; sampler support lands on a MarinSkyRL branch if the pinned trainer lacks the hooks.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reward-signal-aware sampling concentrates rollouts where the learning signal is, so adaptive arms should reach a given eval score with fewer output tokens than uniform sampling. Quantify the value of each mechanism at fixed budget.

## Status

Kickoff. Wiring the experiment directory and a small smoke run.

Planned milestones, posted as comments:

1. Initial smoke run working end to end.
2. Curriculum/sampling infrastructure wired.
3. Results per sampling arm.
4. Final report on arm efficacy and follow-up recommendations.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Milestone 2: infrastructure wired for curricula & sampling.**

The curriculum sampler is implemented on MarinSkyRL branch [`curriculum-sampling`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/curriculum-sampling) (@2a9034fd) and validated live: naive, thompson, and grade-adaptive smoke arms all ran green end-to-end (train → HF export → eval) on cw-rno2a.

Design: a `data.sampling` config subtree selects a stateful weighted sampler over the pool's graded bins (`extra_info.data_source` / `grade`). Kinds: `naive` (stock shuffle), `thompson` (Beta posterior on the decay-weighted fraction of *informative* GRPO groups — groups whose rollout rewards are not all equal), `grade-uniform` (equal budget per grade), `grade-adaptive` (train one grade until its informative fraction stays below a threshold for a window, then advance), `grade-prior` (Thompson seeded with grade-derived optimism). The sampler is checkpoint-resumable (torchdata Stateful) and rejects duplicate rows per batch to preserve the GRPO group invariant.

Smoke evidence the machinery works (4-step runs, Qwen3-0.6B, non-thinking):
- thompson: weights collapsed to ~1% on the two bins with zero informative groups (MATH-L5, AIME) and concentrated on informative middle bins.
- grade-adaptive: 80% mass on grade 0 (gsm8k, informative_frac 0.47 — not yet exhausted, level correctly held at 0) with 20% exploration.
- Non-thinking mode fixed the truncation problem: 85% → 20% truncated, 4% → 70% parseable answers, ~500 avg output tokens.

Fixes along the way: unstepped-episode metrics crash, over-length prompts filtered at pool build (8 rows dropped), per-token reward scalarization for the sampler, batch-unique draws.

Next: full-scale arms (64 GPUs, 120 steps × 512 prompts × 8 samples each) starting with the naive baseline.

Final report with recommendations follows.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Final report: efficacy and recommendations.**

**Conclusions.**
1. *Curriculum value here is token efficiency, not a better endpoint.* At a fixed generated-token budget (146M), grade-adaptive reached mid-run-baseline quality at ~53% of naive's token spend (val-math500 0.156 vs 0.080), with thompson close behind (0.140). At a fixed step/GPU-hour budget — where generation capacity is already paid for — naive was the best MATH500 arm (0.460) and thompson the best gsm8k arm (0.516); no curriculum dominated naive.
2. *Thompson sampling is the best no-prep default.* No offline grading required, decay handles policy drift, competitive under both budget definitions, and it visibly reallocated: bins with zero informative groups (MATH L5, AIME — all-fail for a 0.6B policy) dropped to the 1% floor.
3. *Grade-prior and grade-uniform added little* — the grade-derived prior washes out once real reward evidence accumulates, and fixed 1/N allocation wastes budget on uninformative extremes.

**Recommendations.**
- Re-run naive / thompson / grade-adaptive at 3 seeds for error bars before production conclusions (~$3 × current spend; each arm is 64 GPUs × 1.75 h).
- Extend grade-adaptive to 300+ steps so it traverses all grades; its curve was still rising at half the token budget.
- Make thompson difficulty-directional (distinguish all-pass from all-fail groups) — that should recover grade-adaptive's token efficiency without pre-grading.
- Batch-level uninformative-group resampling (DAPO-style) is complementary to bin-level sampling and likely stacks.

**Artifacts.** Sampler: MarinSkyRL `curriculum-sampling` @ 2a9034fd (checkpoint-resumable `data.sampling` subtree; worth PRing to main after multi-seed validation). Experiment: `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/` (PR to follow). Runs and curves: W&B project `marin-community/marin-curriculum-rl`; exported checkpoints under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/power/checkpoints/curriculum-rl/<arm>/2026.08.29/exports/global_step_120`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 starting.** Scope, per review of round-1 results:

1. **DAPO dynamic sampling** — the pinned trainer already ships `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling` (filter/replace with cross-batch accumulation); wiring it as arm variants (naive+dapo, thompson+dapo). One fix needed first: the curriculum-stat update must run before the filter, or every bin looks 100% informative to the sampler.
2. **Prior-sensitive pool** — round 1's grade-prior collapsed to thompson because 120 steps × 512 prompts of reward evidence swamps any prior over just 6 bins. Adding procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (arithmetic chains, etc.) whose difficulty knobs give *genuine a-priori grades* and widen the bin count, so priors have room to matter. The reasoning-gym scorers only award 1.0 for a bare exact answer (full CoT responses get length-fuzz partial credit), so the env gets Minerva-style `Answer:`-line extraction first.
3. **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson on per-bin pass rate, weight ∝ sampled p(1−p), which peaks at 50% solve rate and down-weights both all-pass and all-fail bins directionally (round-1 thompson treated them identically). `grade-prior` v2 seeds this posterior with grade-decreasing prior pass rates, so the prior is used directionally instead of as undirected optimism.
4. **Dropped:** grade-uniform (no signal over its simpler relatives in round 1).

Round-2 arms: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-prior(directional), grade-adaptive, naive+dapo, thompson+dapo — same fixed budgets and eval protocol as round 1.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 infrastructure wired; smoke green.** All four follow-ups are implemented and validated end-to-end on cw-rno2a (`/power/curriculum-rl-r2-smoke2`):

- **DAPO** — `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling.type=filter` wired as arm variants `naive-dapo` / `thompson-dapo`. The curriculum sampler now updates on **raw pre-filter batches** (MarinSkyRL `9a7286b4`); previously it would have run post-filter and read every bin as 100% informative. Smoke shows the filter engaging: 33–50/64 prompts informative per raw batch, one resample batch per step.
- **Prior-sensitive datasets** — pool v3 adds seven procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (chain_sum ×3, spell_backward ×2, base_conversion ×2; 1,200 rows each) whose difficulty knobs give genuine a-priori grades, interleaved with the re-graded math bins on a shared 0–10 scale. The `reasoning_gym` env scores only the final `Answer:` line (`d36ceaaa`) — full CoT responses previously got ~0.05 fuzz credit even when correct. Smoke pass rates confirm the machinery and expose grade-placement surprises to analyze at full scale (chain_sum-med ~0.9 at grade 3; spell-backward ~0.15–0.33 vs math-l12 ~0.03 — spelling is easier for the base model than its grade assumed).
- **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson draw on each bin's decayed pass rate, weighted by p·(1−p), peaking at 50% solve rate so it distinguishes too-easy from too-hard (the informative-group signal alone cannot). `grade-prior` is redefined as its grade-seeded variant: prior pass-rate mean falls linearly from 0.85 (easiest grade) to 0.05 (hardest) with pseudo-count `grade_prior_strength` (`0b44138c`).
- **Grade-uniform dropped** from the arm catalog.

Launching round-2 full arms next: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-adaptive, grade-prior, naive-dapo, thompson-dapo — 120 steps × 64 H100s each on the expanded pool.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 # Round 2 final report: DAPO, procedural bins, and directional samplers

All seven arms completed: 120 GRPO steps each on 64 H100s (cw-rno2a, Qwen3-0.6B, batch 512×8 samples, non-thinking, ~1024-token generations). Every arm shares the same expanded pool and differs only in prompt sampling and (for the DAPO variants) group filtering. Terminal evals are Evalchemy MATH500 and GSM8K-0shot against the exported step-120 checkpoint; in-run validation is scored by the training environments on held-out slices.

## Results

| arm | generated tokens | in-run val (all) | MATH500 | GSM8K-0shot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 203M | 0.513 | 0.362 | 0.390 |
| thompson | 149M | 0.480 | 0.350 | 0.409 |
| learnability | 220M | 0.537 | 0.418 | 0.444 |
| grade-adaptive | 130M | 0.534 | 0.346 | 0.439 |
| grade-prior (directional) | 211M | 0.487 | 0.408 | 0.418 |
| naive-dapo | 190M | 0.555 | 0.414 | 0.401 |
| **thompson-dapo** | 205M | **0.571** | **0.434** | **0.456** |

Token totals include work redone after preemption-driven restarts (real spend). Round-2 numbers are not comparable to round 1: the pool now spends a large share of budget on procedural bins, which lowers math transfer for every arm equally (round-1 naive hit 0.460 MATH500 on the math-only pool).

![score vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/all-tokens.png)
![score vs steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/all-steps.png)

MATH500 and GSM8K validation trajectories against token spend:

![val-math500 vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/val-math500-tokens.png)
![val-gsm8k vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/val-gsm8k-tokens.png)

## Grading mechanism and distributions

Grades place all 13 bins on one 0–10 scale from two sources. Math bins take grades from **source metadata**: GSM8K at 1, MATH levels 1–2/3/4/5 at 2/4/6/8, AIME at 10. Procedural reasoning-gym bins take **a-priori grades from generator knobs**, assigned before any model saw a sample: chain_sum at grades 0/3/7 (2 terms 1–2 digits → 5–6 terms 4 digits signed), spell_backward at 5/9 (3–5 vs 8–10 letters), base_conversion at 5/9 (bases 2–10 values ≤500 vs bases 11–16). Train pool: 18,619 rows (gsm8k 2000, math-l12 1911, math-l3 1590, math-l4 1690, math-l5 2296, aime 932, 7 procedural bins × 1200); validation adds 128-row held-out generator draws per procedural family.

How well did the grades predict reality? Realized pass rates from the learnability arm:

| bin (grade) | pass rate @ step 10 | @ step 120 |
|---|---|---|
| rg-sum-easy (0) | 0.97 | 1.00 |
| gsm8k (1) | 0.49 | 0.84 |
| math-l12 (2) | 0.53 | 0.84 |
| rg-sum-med (3) | 0.97 | 0.99 |
| math-l3 (4) | 0.41 | 0.70 |
| rg-spell-short (5) | 0.82 | 1.00 |
| rg-base-small (5) | 0.58 | 0.90 |
| math-l4 (6) | 0.28 | 0.57 |
| rg-sum-hard (7) | 0.74 | 0.90 |
| math-l5 (8) | 0.07 | 0.27 |
| rg-base-large (9) | 0.26 | 0.96 |
| rg-spell-long (9) | 0.79 | 0.97 |
| aime (10) | 0.00 | 0.06 |

Two clear findings. **Within a family, metadata grades rank difficulty essentially perfectly** (math: 0.53 → 0.41 → 0.28 → 0.07 → 0.004 down the levels). **Across families, knob-derived grades misjudged absolute difficulty badly**: arithmetic chains are near-trivial for Qwen3-0.6B at any knob setting we chose, and spelling/base-conversion saturate within ~10 steps once the model learns the answer format — procedural tasks measure format acquisition more than reasoning. The pre-registered grades were wrong in exactly the way a real practitioner's would be, which made this a fair test of whether samplers recover from miscalibrated priors.

## Sampling mechanisms

- **naive** — the stock uniform shuffle without replacement. Control.
- **thompson** — Beta Thompson sampling on each bin's decayed *informative-group fraction* (a GRPO group is informative when its rewards are not all equal), decay 0.95, 5% probability floor. Round 1's design.
- **learnability** (new) — Thompson draw on each bin's decayed per-sample *pass rate*, weighted by p·(1−p), which peaks at 50% solve rate. Motivated by round 1's core diagnosis: informative-fraction cannot distinguish a too-easy bin from a too-hard one (both produce uniform groups), so it has no direction.
- **grade-prior** (redesigned) — learnability with grade-seeded Beta priors: prior mean pass rate falls linearly from 0.85 at the easiest grade to 0.05 at the hardest, with 8 pseudo-counts. Round 1's undirected-optimism version collapsed to thompson within ~20 steps; this version encodes the grade as a belief about *pass rate*, which the p·(1−p) weighting turns into "start in the middle band."
- **grade-adaptive** — a level pointer walking the grade ladder, advancing when the current level stops producing informative signal; 20% exploration mass off-level.
- **DAPO filter** (`naive-dapo`, `thompson-dapo`) — drop zero-advantage groups after generation and keep drawing batches until a full informative batch accumulates (the standard DAPO dynamic-sampling recipe). The curriculum sampler updates on raw pre-filter batches so filtering does not bias its statistics.

Weight trajectories show the directional machinery working as designed. Learnability zeroes the saturated procedural bins almost immediately, holds AIME near the floor, and walks its mass up the math ladder as the model improves (math-l3/l4 dominate late). Grade-prior starts mid-band per its prior, then evidence overrides the miscalibrated procedural placements within ~15 steps:

![learnability weights](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/curriculum-learnability-weight.png)
![grade-prior weights](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/curriculum-grade-prior-weight.png)

## Analysis

1. **DAPO is the single biggest win.** thompson-dapo leads every metric, and both DAPO arms beat their non-DAPO counterparts at *equal token spend*, not just equal steps — filtering converts budget that would fund zero-gradient groups into informative ones. The score-vs-tokens chart shows the DAPO curves rising fastest through the whole budget range.
2. **Direction matters more than curriculum-ness.** Learnability (0.418/0.444) beats thompson (0.350/0.409) decisively — same Thompson machinery, better signal. Plain thompson was the weakest arm, confirming round 1's suspicion that informative-fraction is a compass without a needle.
3. **Grades survive contact with reality only where they were right.** Grade-prior recovered from its miscalibrated procedural priors but paid an early-budget tax for them, landing between thompson and learnability. With honest grades (the math family) the ordering is genuinely useful; with guessed grades the evidence-driven samplers simply relearn the truth and the prior contributes little. Grading effort is only worth what the grader knows.
4. **Grade-adaptive remains the token-efficiency champion** (0.534 val-all on 130M tokens, ~64% of naive's spend), echoing round 1. Its focused single-level sampling generates shorter, more solvable rollouts.
5. **Procedural tasks are cheap curriculum filler but weak transfer vehicles.** They gave the samplers real difficulty structure to exploit and clean val curves (e.g. base-conversion 0.26→0.96), but every arm's MATH500 dropped versus round 1's math-only pool. At 0.6B, budget spent on spelling does not buy math.

## Conclusions and future work

At fixed budget, the value ranking is: DAPO filtering > directional (pass-rate) sampling > adaptive level curricula > grade priors > informative-fraction sampling. The obvious composition — **learnability + DAPO** — was not run this round and is the first follow-up: the mechanisms are orthogonal (what to sample vs what to keep) and their gains plausibly stack.

Future work, in priority order:
- **learnability-dapo arm** at the same budget point.
- **Measured grades over guessed grades**: a ~1-hour pre-pass scoring k samples per bin with the base model would have produced a nearly perfect prior for free; grade-prior with measured priors is the honest test of "grades as belief."
- **Token-budget-equalized stopping** (stop every arm at, say, 150M generated tokens) to remove the step/token conflation entirely.
- **A model one size up** (4–8B, thinking mode) where AIME-band bins are learnable and the grade ladder has more headroom.
- Infra hardening from this round is tracked separately: #8774 (gang restart after head preemption, in progress), #8781/#8782 (TAS priority preemption, merged), plus the eval endpoint queue-time fix and TTL-routed Ray session logs in #8769.

Experiment code and pins are in #8769 (`experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/`, MarinSkyRL `curriculum-sampling` @ `4a1f99fc`). Charts regenerate with `report_charts.py`; per-bin stats with `report_pool_stats.py`; terminal scores with `report_evals.py`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Milestone 3: Snowball 67B-A2B trains on the ladder; full arms launched.

The snowball-smoke (4 steps, 4 FSDP2 policy nodes + 1 expert-parallel engine node, 2k window) completed after one fix — the first attempt was OOM-killed at a 128GB host-memory request while ~134GB of shards staged through host buffers; Snowball tasks now request 512GB, matching the eval serving profile. Training signal is real: pass@4 rose 0.34 → ~0.42 and mean reward −0.54 → −0.42 over the 4 steps, with mean generations of 884 tokens against the 1024 cap.

Sampler upgrade before the full runs (MarinSkyRL `44817814`): directional arms now weight bins by group informativeness, 1 − p^n − (1−p)^n — the probability a GRPO group survives DAPO filtering — instead of p(1−p), which under-samples low-pass-rate bins ~3× relative to their actual refill cost. New `learnability-dapo` and `grade-prior-dapo` arms compose the round-2 winners; the pool adds val-amc (grade 9) and val-theoremqa (grade 13) so the grade-weighted end metric (weights ∝ 1+grade, never shown to the sampler) sees the ladder top.

Now running at `2026.08.31`:
- **Qwen3-0.6B, 6 arms** on cw-rno2a (120 steps each): naive, naive-dapo, learnability-dapo, grade-prior-dapo, grade-adaptive, grade-prior.
- **Snowball naive** on cw-us-east-02a at the snowball-full preset (60 steps, 128×8 responses, 3072-token window / 2048 response budget, 4+4 nodes) as a throughput probe; learnability-dapo and grade-prior-dapo follow once step timing confirms the budget.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round-3 finding: adaptive sampling is fragile to reward-contract mismatch; grade priors buy robustness.

The snowball-learnability-dapo arm showed val-gsm8k pass@1 = 0.000 at step 10 while snowball-naive scored 0.891 from the same base model — with learnability simultaneously beating naive on harder bins (MATH-500 0.66 vs 0.63). Retained trajectories pin the cause: Snowball answers gsm8k correctly but in its SFT style (`\boxed{300}`), while the gsm8k environment's rule grader only accepts the answer after `"####"`, so every rollout scores 0. The bin's zero pass rate measures format compliance, not ability.

The three samplers then diverge exactly along their designs:

- **naive** samples gsm8k uniformly (~54 rollouts/step); rare rollouts that happen to emit `####` get positive advantage and RL teaches the format within 10 steps → val 0.891.
- **learnability + group-informative weighting** observes pass = 0 at step 1, assigns the bin near-floor weight (0.009 vs ~0.09 for active bins), starves it, and never learns the format → val 0.000.
- **grade-prior + group-informative** keeps sampling on its grade-3 prior (9 informative groups by step 9, pass EMA 0.16 → 0.33) and recovers → val 0.828 at step 10.

Letting the arms run to 60 steps as-is: the dynamics are the experiment. For the report, the snowball headline metric will be shown with and without val-gsm8k, since the bin conflates format with difficulty for this model. Follow-up recommendation: normalize every pool bin to one answer contract (`\boxed{}` + math-verify) so grades measure difficulty only, and add cold-start optimism or a re-exploration floor to pure-feedback samplers so an observed-zero bin is revisited often enough to distinguish "too hard" from "mis-specified".

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round-3 final report: graded-ladder curricula on Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball 67B-A2B.

All nine arms completed: six Qwen arms (120 steps, 64 H100s each, ~230–247M generated tokens) and three Snowball arms (60 steps, 64 H100s each, ~64–75M tokens) on the grade 0–13 math ladder, scored by the fixed end metric (validation pass@1 weighted by 1+grade, never visible to samplers).

| arm | grade-weighted | without gsm8k | frontier grade | tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| qwen learnability-dapo | **0.312** | 0.266 | 9 | 247M |
| snowball grade-prior-dapo | **0.310** | 0.256 | **13** | 71M |
| qwen grade-prior-dapo | 0.301 | 0.255 | 9 | 245M |
| qwen naive-dapo | 0.294 | 0.248 | 5 | 229M |
| snowball naive | 0.289 | 0.232 | 5 | 64M |
| qwen grade-prior | 0.283 | 0.238 | 5 | 240M |
| qwen naive | 0.267 | 0.219 | 5 | 231M |
| qwen grade-adaptive | 0.257 | 0.211 | 5 | 144M |
| snowball learnability-dapo | 0.166 | 0.181 | 5 | 75M |

![grade-weighted score vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/grade-weighted-tokens.png)

**Qwen: curriculum sampling wins cleanly.** Both group-informative curriculum arms beat plain DAPO, which beats everything else: learnability-dapo ends +17% relative over naive (0.312 vs 0.267) and +6% over naive-dapo. Only the two curriculum-DAPO arms pushed the frontier to grade 9 (AMC pass@1 ≥ 0.25); every other arm stalled at grade 5 (MATH). Grade-adaptive (ladder-walking) finished last and also spent the fewest tokens — it parks on easy bins with short responses.

![frontier grade vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/frontier-grade-tokens.png)

**Snowball: grade priors won; pure feedback-driven sampling failed twice.** grade-prior-dapo reached 0.310 with frontier grade 13 (TheoremQA ≥ 0.25) in 71M tokens and was still improving at step 60. The learnability arm hit both failure modes:

1. *Format-contract starvation* (details in the [mid-run comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8765#issuecomment-5471696465)): gsm8k pass@1 stayed 0.000 for the entire run because an observed zero pass rate zeroes the group-informative weight; naive learned the `####` contract by step 10 (0.94 final) and grade-prior recovered through its prior (0.95 final).
2. *Late-run collapse*: stable through step 50 (MATH-500 0.64–0.70, TheoremQA 0.25–0.28), then one destabilizing update at step 60 — raw grad-norm 19,332, KL-max 9.3, entropy 0.085 — dropped every bin (MATH-500 → 0.52), and the terminal export captured the damaged checkpoint. Snowball-naive also slid from its 0.324 mid-run peak to 0.289; only grade-prior-dapo ended at its peak. Single-seed caveat applies, but concentrated sampling appears to raise late-run variance.

![val-gsm8k vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/val-gsm8k-tokens.png)

**The sampling objective checks out empirically.** Pooling per-bin pass-rate transitions across all curriculum arms, learning velocity peaks near pass rate 0.4–0.5 (~0.008/step) and falls to ~0 at both extremes — matching the flat-topped group-informative curve 1−pⁿ−(1−p)ⁿ more closely than p(1−p):

![learning velocity vs pass rate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/velocity-vs-pass-rate.png)

**Infrastructure notes.** Snowball steps ran at ~8.8 min after raising `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu` 1→4 (the FSDP update was all-gather-bound: 32 sequential re-gathers of 134GB shards for ~2B active params of compute; the fix cut policy_train 1660s→437s). Remaining round-3 ops incidents were all transient: one driver OOM at the default 1GB coordinator memory, one eval endpoint-registration timeout, one export stuck on an Iris pod race after its container completed.

**Recommendations for a round 4.**
- Normalize every bin to one answer contract (`\boxed{}` + math-verify) so grades measure difficulty, not instruction-style compliance.
- Give pure-feedback samplers cold-start optimism and a re-exploration floor that periodically re-probes zero-pass bins; without it they cannot distinguish "too hard" from "mis-specified".
- Default to grade priors when moving a curriculum to a new model: they were never worse than naive on any bin, on either model.
- Add a stability guard (KL trust region or late LR decay) for long runs under concentrated sampling; the step-60 blowup was visible in grad-norm before the eval caught it.

Full chart set and summary.json: [assets/curriculum-rl-r3](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/assets/curriculum-rl-r3).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 4 launched: `/power/curriculum-r4-full` on cw-us-east-02a — Snowball, `naive` vs `grade-prior-dapo`, 120 steps at pool version `2026.09.01.1`.

Changes from round 3:

- **Optimizer**: MuonH at lr 1e-5, weight_decay 0, grad clip 1.0 — the same recipe Snowball pretrained/SFT'd with. Round 3 used AdamW at 2e-6.
- **Batch shape**: 64 prompts × 8 samples × 120 steps (same rollout total as round 3's 60 bigger steps, 2× fresher policy), micro-batch 8 — halves the all-gather count that dominated round-3 step time.
- **Prompt contracts**: system prompt plus strengthened per-bin format instructions baked into the pool. Served-model A/B (temp 1.0, rule-graded, 100 problems/variant): gsm8k 0.00 → 0.55 and math500 0.05 → 0.15 before any RL; failures under the old prompts were correct math ending in `\boxed{}` instead of the graded answer line.
- **Curriculum**: the grade-prior-dapo arm adds `reversion_mass=2.0` — per-step pseudo-evidence that pulls starved bins back toward re-probeable weight, addressing the round-3 starvation self-lock (MarinSkyRL `129ed37a`).

Smoke (4 steps, MuonH + micro=8): step time 222s vs 534s in round 3, raw grad norm 0.38–0.47 under the 1.0 clip. At 222s/step the full arms should take ~7.5h each.

Next: monitor both arms to completion, verify think-token structure and truncation rates from retained trajectories, then the round-4 report.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 4 complete. Both Snowball arms ran 120 steps at `2026.09.01.1` (MuonH lr 1e-5, system prompt + strengthened format contracts, `reversion_mass=2.0` on the curriculum arm). The grade-prior-dapo arm finished in one attempt; naive hit two micro-batch-8 CUDA OOMs (steps 92 and 119) and resumed cleanly from checkpoint both times.

Final evals (round-3 in parentheses):

| arm | grade-weighted | frontier grade | metered tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 0.285 (0.289) | 5 (5) | 89M |
| grade-prior-dapo | **0.292** (0.310) | **13** (13) | 81M |

Headlines:

- The prompt contract moved the format unlock out of RL: both arms hit val-gsm8k ≥ 0.89 at the first eval (step 10), and the naive-vs-curriculum composite gap shrank from +0.021 to +0.007. Most of round 3's curriculum margin was exposure to a format-deceptive bin; a two-paragraph prompt buys the same thing.
- The frontier edge is what survives: grade-prior-dapo again sustained the grade-13 bin (theoremqa 0.268, crossing ~75M tokens) while naive never did — the same 13-vs-5 split as round 3 under a different optimizer, batch shape, and prompt.
- MuonH at 5× the round-3 lr was stable end to end (grad norms 0.17–0.47 under the 1.0 clip, no late-run collapse), and micro-batch 8 halved step time (222s vs 534s).
- `reversion_mass` behaved as designed: all 19 bin weights stayed within a ~3× band; no floor-lock.
- Regression: peak val-math500 fell 0.656 → 0.562 in both arms (candidates: 512 vs 1024 rollouts/step, lr drift, or the anti-`\boxed{}` contract; unresolved at one seed).
- Retained-trajectory analysis: 40–48% of rollouts still hit the 2048-token cap at end of training; frontier bins truncate near-totally (AIME 98%, Omni 99%). Successful rollouts are short, ~100% think-token structured by step 100, and `\boxed{}` was ground out of successes entirely. Generation budget, not sampling, is now the binding constraint — top round-5 lever.

Paper (round-4 section added) and all figures: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/assets/curriculum-rl-paper/paper.md

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 5 launched** (`/power/curriculum-r5-full`, version `2026.09.02.1`): naive + grade-prior-dapo, 120 steps × 64 prompts × 8 samples, with the round-4 recipe (MuonH 1e-5, clip 1.0, reversion_mass 2.0) and two changes:

- **Generation budget 2048 → 8192** (window 9216, same 1024-token prompt budget). Round 4's binding constraint: 40–48% of rollouts truncated at the cap, AIME/Omni/TheoremQA near-totally. `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu` 8 → 2 to hold activation memory at the longer sequences.

  |---|---|---|---|
  | current 111t | 0.79/0.38 | 0.60/0.16 | 0.42/0.04 |
