issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Test a per-layer learned residual mixture against the exact July Baseline from #6882 at d512 and d768. Each attention and MoE merge in layer $l$ becomes $\sqrt{1-\beta_l/L}\,r + \sqrt{\beta_l/L}\,h$, with $\beta_l=\operatorname{softplus}(\theta_l)$ and $\theta_l=0$ at initialization.

## Description

Canonical source is commit `52d8a9eb8d9434cf1dcaaee060edeadc60dfff9d` on `july_baseline`, using `experiments/grug/moe/moe_may_july_baseline.py`. The baseline has two residual merges per transformer layer. One scalar $\theta_l$ will be shared by both merges in layer $l$.

The implementation will cap $\beta_l$ just below $L$ because softplus alone does not enforce the square root's domain. The run will log per-layer $\beta_l$ so saturation is observable.

Original request:

> Try to find the july baseline and try the following norm preserving residual
>
> `(sqrt(1 - beta_l / L)) residual + sqrt(beta_l / L) hidden`
>
> Here L is the total number of layer
> Parameterized beta to be a positive thing, perhaps `softplus(theta)` where `theta = 0`

## Hypothesis or Goal

Learned norm-preserving residual mixing improves effective wall-clock speed at both July Gate-1 scales without changing the data, optimizer, budget, seed, or evaluation schedule.

## Status

Implementation in progress. Planned Gate 1: MOE-NPR-001-d512 and MOE-NPR-002-d768 on v5p-8.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/norm-preserving-residual.md`
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

* 2026-09-02: use one learned scalar per transformer layer and share it across that layer's attention and MoE residual merges.
* 2026-09-02: compare against canonical July Baseline #6882 at d512 and d768 before any larger-scale run.

## Conclusion

No experimental result yet.

issues.body:
The shared `iris-ci` controller crash-loops on startup, so the GPU canary ferry never gets a controller to submit against. The GHA step **Start shared iris-ci controller** failed after ~7.5 min and every downstream step (`Submit canary ferry`, `Wait`, `Validate`, profile) was skipped — no Iris job was ever created (empty `CANARY_JOB_ID`).

The controller pod `iris-controller-86f99b4db-76cvz` (image `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-controller:ea97e06`, code version `db3d6dd`) is in `CrashLoopBackOff` with 11 restarts. It dies while bringing up its **bundled in-process finelog log server**, which fails to open the store persisted on the `iris-controller-state` PVC:

```
RuntimeError: failed to open store: unknown column type name "COLUMN_TYPE_FLOAT64_LIST" in catalog JSON
```

The finelog native store binary bundled in the deployed controller cannot parse a `COLUMN_TYPE_FLOAT64_LIST` column recorded in the on-disk catalog, even though the current repo Rust source (`lib/finelog/rust/src/store/schema.rs:535`) handles that name — i.e. the shipped native finelog binary is skewed from the schema now being written. This lands right after #8847 ("Advance external runtimes"), which bumped the external runtimes (levanter now registers a `FLOAT64_LIST` `bucket_limits` histogram column via `lib/finelog/rust/src/levanter_metrics_policy.rs:296`) and introduced the native-package release path.

The crash is self-perpetuating: the controller runs with `--fresh`, but that only wipes `db/` under `/var/cache/iris/controller`; the embedded finelog store dir on the same PVC survives every restart, so the stale catalog is re-read on every boot.

**Impact:** the shared `iris-ci` controller is down. This blocks the GPU canary ferry and any PR CI that shares this controller/namespace until the store is recovered or the finelog binary is realigned.

Reproduce:
1. Deploy `iris-controller:ea97e06` (code `db3d6dd`) to `iris-ci` on `cw-us-west-04a` with an embedded finelog store on the `iris-controller-state` PVC that already contains a `COLUMN_TYPE_FLOAT64_LIST` column.
2. Controller starts, applies migrations, then calls `build_log_stack` → `require_embedded_server()` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/log_stack.py:97`).
3. Opening the persisted store raises `unknown column type name "COLUMN_TYPE_FLOAT64_LIST" in catalog JSON`; pod exits 1 and enters `CrashLoopBackOff`.

Expected: the controller starts and serves `ListJobs`; the canary submits and runs.

Likely remediation (not applied here — the PVC is shared with live PR CI): realign the bundled finelog native store binary with the schema being written (so `COLUMN_TYPE_FLOAT64_LIST` parses), and/or clear the embedded finelog store dir on the `iris-controller-state` PVC. A durable fix should make `--fresh` (or startup) reset the embedded store when its catalog is unreadable rather than crash-looping.

## TL;DR

Figure 1 contains 70 run series with paired pass@1 and pass@k observations. Snowball uses pass@16 and Qwen3-Coder uses pass@8. Snowball pass@1 comes from logged accuracy or mapped binary reward; Qwen3-Coder pass@1 is mean binary raw reward. Figure 2 groups within-run metric changes by source dataset and excludes four runs with `dynamic_sampling.type: filter` plus the X0-shaped partial-credit run.

## Description

The archive combines W&B histories from #7786 with metrics from 23 Qwen3-Coder model repositories associated with #7785 and the Jupiter D0 and D5 exports. The Hugging Face repository preserves the interactive report, 2,249 rounded per-step table rows, CSVs using a common column schema, and generation scripts.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Preserve a durable experiment-to-metrics map and make the pass@k versus pass@1 gap explorable by base model and source dataset.

## Status

Complete. The report and source archive are public.

## Links

* Report: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/benjaminfeuer/passk-pass1-comparison/2026.08.31/index.html
* Hugging Face archive: https://huggingface.co/datasets/penfever/passk-pass1-comparison
* Snowball source experiments: #7786
* Qwen3-Coder source experiments: #7785

## Decision Log

* 2026-08-31: Kept Snowball pass@16 and Qwen3-Coder pass@8 in separate base-model views.
* 2026-08-31: Excluded runs according to metric comparability. Source-dataset names do not determine exclusion.

## Conclusion

The archive contains the Snowball metric snapshots and all 25 Qwen3-Coder repositories listed in the experiment-to-metrics map. The X0-shaped run remains archived but is omitted from the pass@1 plot because it has no binary pass@1, and from dataset aggregates because its partial-credit pass@8 is not comparable with binary-verifier runs.

comments.body:
🤖 Published the [Qwen3 Coder pass@1/pass@16 versus GLM 5.2 pass@1 comparison](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/benjaminfeuer/qwen3-coder-pass16-glm52-tasktrove/2026.09.02/index.html) for the ten largest GLM-minus-Qwen pass@1 gaps among datasets reportable for both models in the completed TaskTrove v4.6 comparison.

The unweighted mean Qwen3 Coder pass@1 estimate across these datasets is 0.376; mean pass@16 is 0.670. Mean GLM 5.2 pass@1 is 0.925, so the descriptive mean GLM-minus-Qwen gap decreases from 0.549 to 0.255. Qwen pass@16 exceeds GLM pass@1 on SWE-Gym by 0.050 and remains lower on the other nine datasets. R2E-Gym is the closest of those nine at 0.063 below GLM.

This is not a paired estimate. Qwen pass@1 averages 4,691–4,796 scoreable attempts from the first 300 tasks in each 16-attempt archive. Pass@16 averages the maximum reward for the 273–296 tasks per run with all 16 attempts scoreable. Here, scoreable means an attempt produced a reward or a model-attributable terminal outcome. The GLM values average 275–1,768 scoreable one-attempt tasks from byte-identical dataset files. Byte matching establishes dataset-content identity; the scored subsets and denominators can still differ between models. CrossCodeEval C# and Glaive use partial-credit rewards, so their values are mean and best rewards instead of binary pass probabilities.

All ten Qwen evaluation jobs are terminal and their results are archived. This ten-dataset campaign is complete.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->

Automatic JaxPP DualPipeV is now the validated Grug MoE pipeline implementation. The canonical example in #8739 supports automatic ZeroBubble and DualPipeV schedules through one state, autodiff, and MPMD orchestration path. Parameters and Adam state are initialized on their owning stages, so the implementation does not materialize the full 67B training state. The root `pipeline` extra installs the pinned JaxPP and CUDA dependencies through the ordinary workspace sync. It requires NCCL 2.31.2; NCCL 2.30.7 hangs the grouped-transfer path on current JaxPP, while the final two-node H100x8 gate completed with 2.31.2.

The final Snowball 67B-A2B result uses 64 H100s, PP8 x EP8, 16 logical DualPipeV stages, sequence length 8192, batch 256, 32 microbatches, BF16 parameters and compute, and full rematerialization. Median step time is `3.475980327s`, throughput is `603,326.77` tokens/s, median analytic MFU is `19.45529%`, and peak memory is `59,153,094,656` bytes/device. The matched batch-128, 16-microbatch control reaches `543,490.02` tokens/s and `17.52575%` median analytic MFU. Doubling the microbatch count improves median throughput and MFU by `11.01%` with no measured memory increase. Final synthetic-data loss differs by `4.02e-5` between the two runs.

The no-JaxPP baseline uses ordinary Grug training with FSDP8 x EP8 on the same 64 H100s. Batch 256 OOMs before step 0 with a `101.02 GiB` allocation request per device. Batch 64 succeeds at `1.931756s` median step time, `271,404.87` tokens/s, `8.75191%` median analytic MFU, and `29,017,027,044` bytes/device peak. DualPipeV provides `2.223x` the median token throughput and MFU while using `2.039x` the memory. The global batches differ by `4x`, so this comparison measures the viable configurations rather than isolating schedule efficiency at a matched batch.

This meets the practical target for the current work. The measured DualPipeV point is `0.545` percentage point below 20% analytic MFU, and further microbatch scaling is unlikely to justify another 64-H100 experiment without a production workload. The profile attributes the remaining gap primarily to pipeline dependency and SendRecv waiting, especially at the endpoint pair. Attention kernels account for roughly `2.05-4.73%` of exclusive GPU time per physical rank; FSDP and MoE all-gather/reduce-scatter costs are secondary.

Command buffers remain disabled in the validated recipe. JAX 0.11.0 has an XLA mixed-clique initialization bug, while the tested nightly exposes JaxPP DiME multi-communicator initialization and execution deadlocks on the full DualPipeV topology. Deterministic communicator preinitialization fixes the reduced gate but not the full Snowball run. Track that work separately in #7655; it does not block the no-command-buffer result.

PR #8739 is open and awaits review. The issue should remain open until that PR lands.

<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Current baseline

| Area | Current state |
| --- | --- |
| Implementation | Automatic JaxPP DualPipeV in #8739 |
| Model | Snowball 67B-A2B: 67.08B total / about 2.01B active, 26 layers, d2560, 256 experts, top-k 4, sequence 8192 |
| Topology | 64 H100s; PP8 x EP8; 16 logical stages mapped to 8 physical ranks |
| Precision | BF16 parameters, compute, and output; full rematerialization |
| Batch | Global batch 256; 32 microbatches |
| Performance | `3.475980327s` median step; `603,326.77` tokens/s; `19.45529%` median analytic MFU |
| Memory | `59,153,094,656` bytes/device peak |
| No-JaxPP comparison | FSDP8 x EP8 at batch 64: `1.931756s`, `271,404.87` tokens/s, `8.75191%` median analytic MFU, `29,017,027,044` bytes/device peak |
| Runtime caveat | XLA command buffers disabled; follow-up tracked in #7655 |

Decision log

- Use the model-specific Grug implementation as a canonical example that can be adapted to another model. Keep generic mechanics in `levanter.pipeline`; do not hide model partitioning behind a generic high-level pipeline module.
- Keep the benchmark automatic-only. Sequential staged-loss and gradient parity remain the independent numerical check without a second MPMD execution path.
- Use automatic DualPipeV for the validated Snowball recipe. Sixteen logical stages map two stages to each of eight physical pipeline ranks and reduce the warmup/cooldown bubble relative to the eight-stage automatic ZeroBubble schedule.
- Initialize parameters and optimizer state stage-locally. Full-state initialization exceeded H100 memory before pipeline execution.
- Keep the validated 16-stage layer placement. Profiled physical-rank compute differs by up to `1.414x`, but moving one indivisible layer only moves the heavy rank and cannot remove the endpoint bubble.
- Use 32 microbatches for the best measured throughput point. Compared with the matched 16-microbatch control, it improves median throughput and MFU by `11.01%` at identical peak memory.
- Keep command buffers disabled until #7655 has a full-topology fix. Increasing rendezvous timeouts and communicator preinitialization alone did not make the full run execute.
- Treat `19.45529%` as an analytic MFU estimate. The existing FLOP model uses full attention and therefore slightly overestimates work for sliding-window layers.

Prior baseline and negative results

- The earlier explicit-MPMD L24/d2560/e64/top-k4/sequence-4096 result remains a useful historical baseline: `18.2583%` mean MFU and `414,059.10` tokens/s at batch 8192 with 256 microbatches. It is a different model shape and should not be compared directly with the Snowball result.
- Ordinary FSDP8 x EP8 at batch 256 OOMs before step 0 after XLA rematerializes an inefficient batch-to-FSDP reshard and requests `101.02 GiB` per device. Batch 64 fits and reaches `271,404.87` tokens/s and `8.75191%` median analytic MFU with `29.017 GB` peak memory. Its final synthetic-data loss is `0.671852`, within `4.92e-4` of the DualPipeV result.
- Four-stage automatic ZeroBubble works, but eight physical stages with 16 microbatches reached only about `12.83%` mean MFU on the matched Snowball comparison. Long-run DualPipeV reached `16.96%` mean and `17.52%` median MFU at 16 microbatches, a roughly `32%` mean throughput improvement.
- A profile-guided endpoint layer rebalance improved the eight-stage automatic ZeroBubble schedule by only about `1.4%`. The remaining wait is schedule-level.
- Snowball sequence length 32K exceeded memory at PP8. A PP13 experiment was abandoned in favor of validating sequence length 8K.
- Automatic ZeroBubble and explicit 1F1B with command buffers enabled failed during executable initialization on the production JAX pin. The tested JAX nightly passes the reduced XLA initialization gate but deadlocks in JaxPP DiME communicator setup or subsequent execution at full scale.
- Deterministic DiME communicator preinitialization succeeds on a reduced PP8 x EP8 DualPipeV gate. The full Snowball topology still hangs before step 0 with ranks split across runtime compilation, NCCL group completion, and receive waits.
- Attention, Hopper MoE kernels, and intra-stage all-gather/reduce-scatter are not the first optimization target in the representative profile. SendRecv duration is primarily a waiting proxy, not wire-transfer time.

Helpful links

- Implementation PR: #8739
- Command-buffer and DiME follow-up: #7655
- Earlier explicit-MPMD snapshot: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/ecb724da6e
- Earlier explicit baseline: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/jaxpp-rno2a-ring-l24-e64k4-b8192-s4096-p4m256-20260711-0107
- Earlier research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe-2.md`

Next steps

1. Land #8739 and use its documented Snowball command as the reproducible pipeline baseline.
2. Keep command-buffer investigation in #7655. Do not block the no-command-buffer training path on it.
3. Revisit pipeline optimization only for a concrete production workload. The next target is endpoint dependency scheduling, not attention or MoE kernel replacement.

Conclusion

The pipeline-parallel Grug MoE path is complete for the current goal. Automatic DualPipeV trains the Snowball 67B-A2B architecture on 64 H100s at `19.45529%` median analytic MFU and `603,326.77` tokens/s with stage-local model and optimizer state. Ordinary FSDP8 x EP8 fits at batch 64 and reaches `8.75191%` median analytic MFU; its batch-256 configuration OOMs. The implementation is ready in #8739. Command buffers are the remaining optional performance and runtime follow-up.

---

🤖 **Not opening a PR — this is a hardware-dependent experiment tracking issue, not an agent-actionable code task.**

# Research

The definition of done here is a *measured MFU number* from a real training run on `cw-us-east-02a` (4× gd-8xh100ib). That requires GPU cluster access, `jaxpp` runtime dependency handling, a 4-node H100 launch harness, and a schedule sweep — a multi-phase research effort, not a self-contained fix. An agent PR can't close it.

Two state discrepancies worth flagging, since they'll trip up whoever picks this up:

- The JaxPP branch described in the body isn't reachable from `main`. `GrugTrainerConfig` ([`train.py#L53-L71`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/train.py#L53-L71)) has **no `pipeline` field**, and `grep -ri jaxpp` over the repo returns nothing. The `pipeline` mesh axis / `jaxpp.treduce` / stage-boundary work referenced in the issue lives on an unpushed branch.
- The logbook link `.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe.md` doesn't exist (no `.agents/logbooks/` dir on `main`).

**Related but distinct prior work:** `origin/weaver/investigate-pipeline-parallelism` already explores PP for Grug MoE, but via a **delayed-gradient / staleness simulation** path, not JaxPP on hardware — `experiments/grug/moe_delay/` (`delay_optim.py`, `pp_throughput_model.py`, `launch.py`) plus `docs/reports/pipeline-parallel-moe-staleness.md`. Its throughput model and iso-loss token-tax analysis are directly relevant priors for interpreting a real JaxPP MFU number, but it's a different implementation and doesn't satisfy this issue's goal.

# Proposed next steps (for a human with cluster access)

1. Push the JaxPP branch (the `GrugTrainerConfig.pipeline` path) so it's reviewable, and add the logbook the body references.
2. Land `jaxpp` runtime dependency handling (optional-dep guard behind the pipeline path).
3. Add the 4-node H100 launch harness for `cw-us-east-02a`.
4. Run the schedule sweep on the May d=2560 shape (seq 4096, 256 experts, top-k 4, expert axis 8, replica 1; reduce experts if needed for a debug run) and extract MFU from tracker/log output.

Happy to take on any *code-only, testable* slice of this — e.g. the optional-dep guard, the mesh-reshape-into-microbatches logic, or MFU extraction — if it's split out with concrete acceptance criteria that don't require a live GPU run. Point me at the branch and I'll pick one up.

## Summary

This issue tracks JaxPP pipeline parallelism for Grug MoE training on 4x 8xH100 CoreWeave. The explicit `jaxpp.experimental.mpmd` implementation partitions model weights and optimizer state by stage and runs the requested 24-layer, d2560, sequence-4096 model with GPipe, `std_1f1b`, and queue-correct interleaved GPipe schedules.

The current performance shape uses 64 experts with top-k 4. The best measured point is explicit `std_1f1b`, batch8192/m256, four six-layer stages, ring expert parallelism, CuTe FA4, and eight-warp Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM on RNO2A: mean MFU `18.2583`, p50 `18.3654`, p90 `18.3830`, and `414,059.10` tokens/s. Scaling from m128 to m256 added only `0.1248` mean MFU points, so pipeline occupancy is saturated `1.7417` points below the 20-MFU target.

Profile-guided routing work removed three large rank-2 floating scatter families with explicit Triton kernels and custom VJPs. H100 value/VJP parity and optimized-HLO checks pass, but a pinned 10-step reduced A/B was neutral: bulk ring averaged `9.1735` central MFU versus `9.1595` for `ring_fused`. The backend is not being scaled to L24.

An EP-local QuACK/Sonic grouped-MLP adapter is the first direct expert-kernel result to clear the performance gate: at the exact e64/top-k4/d2560 EP8 microbatch, median forward improves `1.160x` and forward-backward improves `1.108x`. Its approximate fused SwiGLU is now exposed only through explicit research backend `ring_quack_approx`. A paired 10-step one-node training gate stays finite with final relative loss delta `+0.01356%`, while mean MFU improves `4.00%` and median duration falls `4.04%`. The reduced JaxPP gate is next; the 4% whole-step gain alone does not project the current L24 best above 20 MFU.

- Best run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/jaxpp-rno2a-ring-l24-e64k4-b8192-s4096-p4m256-20260711-0107
- FA4 profile: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/jaxpp-rno2a-profile-fa4cute-l24-e64k4-b512-s4096-p4m16-20260710-1110
- Fused-routing A/B comment: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7024#issuecomment-4945489609
- Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/jaxpp-grug-moe.md`

## Current Baseline

| Area | Current state |
| --- | --- |
| Branch | `origin/research/jaxpp-grug-moe` |
| Snapshot | `51eaa57909` (`[docs] Record approximate QuACK training gate`) |
| Model | L24, d2560, 64 experts, top-k 4, sequence 4096, vocab 8192 |
| Pipeline | Explicit MPMD `std_1f1b`, four physical/logical stages, six layers per stage |
| Parallelism | 4x8 H100, expert axis 8, ring EP |
| Kernels | CuTe FA4; Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM, `block_k=32`, 8 warps |
| Best point | batch8192/m256, mean MFU `18.2583` |

## Decision Log

- Use explicit MPMD as the deliverable implementation. Automatic JaxPP remains blocked on non-addressable global-mesh input placement.
- Partition weights and optimizer state before optimizer initialization; this makes the requested 24-layer, 256-expert shape fit.
- Use RNO2A for performance work. Baseline parity and NCCL GDRDMA logs rule out socket fallback.
- Keep four equal six-layer stages and expert axis 8. Tested seven-layer stages and narrower EP do not reach a usable execution point.
- Use 64 experts/top-k 4, CuTe FA4, and eight-warp Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM for the performance boundary.
- Keep ring EP. Ragged all-to-all, DeepEP, Sonic without EP, streamed rings, and owner-local collective-permute combine do not beat it.
- Stop batch scaling at m256; occupancy has saturated around 18.3 MFU.
- Do not scale `ring_fused` to L24; explicit Triton routing is correct but throughput-neutral in the controlled reduced A/B.
- Keep approximate QuACK explicit as `ring_quack_approx`; never change default ring semantics. The finite-step one-node gate passed, but require a reduced JaxPP performance gate before the L24 target.

## Negative Results Index

- Unequal splits with a seven-layer stage OOM or fail to reach execution; six layers per physical stage is the practical limit.
- Expert axis 4 stalls in compilation. Ragged all-to-all reaches only `3.6743` MFU at batch256/m8.
- DeepEP builds and executes its SM90 path but becomes NaN after one finite non-pipelined step.
- Proper Sonic/QuACK without EP reaches `13.9598` MFU; staged weight materialization regresses to `13.8155`.
- Interleaved GPipe hits a compile cliff above the measured m6 point and remains slower than four-stage `std_1f1b`.
- XLA ragged dot regresses to `8.1438` MFU; Triton `block_k=64` regresses to `16.0189`.
- XLA latency-hiding scheduling changes the m128 mean by only `+0.0708` points, below run noise.
- RNO2A cannot create the exportable CUDA VMM allocations needed by zero-copy ragged all-to-all.
- Streamed `ring_ppermute` is numerically unstable and over 1,100x slower on its first timed reduced step.
- Owner-local combine expands to seven collective permutes and does not finish reduced backward compilation.
- Pure-XLA output-oriented combine regresses reduced MFU to `6.2896`; explicit Triton routing restores parity but provides no measurable gain (`9.1595` versus `9.1735`).
- Transfer-priority task construction regresses reduced median MFU by `2.90%` (`8.9006` versus `9.1660`); earlier `mpmd.transfer` calls do not create useful overlap.
- Input-gradient-first backward is gradient-correct and operational but regresses central MFU by `28.75%` (`6.5356` versus `9.1735`); independent block rematerialization overwhelms bubble recovery.
- Exact two-chunk bulk ring passes EP8 output/drop/VJP parity but regresses median forward by `5.30%` and forward-backward by `13.98%`; doubled launches do not hide profitably.

## Current Readout

The implementation milestone is complete. The best observed L24 mean MFU is `18.2583`, and batch/microbatch scaling is saturated. Approximate QuACK improves a one-node L2 whole training step by `4.00%` with a close finite loss trajectory. This is positive but would project to only about `18.99` MFU at L24, so the reduced pipeline gate must show additional benefit before scaling.

## Next Steps

1. Run the pinned reduced L8/b32/m4 explicit-MPMD JaxPP `ring_quack_approx` gate against ring.
2. Scale to L24 only if the reduced pipeline result projects above 20 MFU or combines with another validated improvement that does.
3. Resume automatic JaxPP only after stage-local inputs no longer carry non-addressable global `pipeline` mesh shardings.
4. Keep the self-contained TVM-FFI/QuACK hang reproducer in #7110 ready for human-selected upstream filing.

## Conclusion So Far

Explicit JaxPP MPMD runs the full requested model and sequence shape with stage-partitioned weights and multiple schedules. CuTe FA4 and increased standard-schedule occupancy produced the largest validated gains. The 20-MFU target remains open. Approximate EP-local QuACK is now opt-in and finite-step validated, but its measured `4.00%` whole-step gain is not yet enough to justify the exact L24 run.

| Kernels | CuTe FA4; Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM, `block_k=32`, 8 warps |
| Best point | batch8192/m256, mean MFU `18.2583` |

## Decision Log

- Use explicit MPMD as the deliverable implementation. Automatic JaxPP remains blocked on non-addressable global-mesh input placement.
- Partition weights and optimizer state before optimizer initialization; this makes the requested 24-layer, 256-expert shape fit.
- Use RNO2A for performance work. Baseline parity and NCCL GDRDMA logs rule out socket fallback.
- Keep four equal six-layer stages and expert axis 8. Tested seven-layer stages and narrower EP do not reach a usable execution point.
- Use 64 experts/top-k 4, CuTe FA4, and eight-warp Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM for the performance boundary.
- Keep ring EP. Ragged all-to-all, DeepEP, Sonic without EP, streamed rings, and owner-local collective-permute combine do not beat it.
- Stop batch scaling at m256; occupancy has saturated around 18.3 MFU.
- Do not scale `ring_fused` to L24; explicit Triton routing is correct but throughput-neutral in the controlled reduced A/B.
- Keep approximate QuACK explicit as `ring_quack_approx`; never change default ring semantics. Its reduced JaxPP gate is neutral, so do not scale it to L24.
- Keep the default BF16 pipeline transfer unchanged. Gate any FP8 stage-transfer mode as an explicit research-only semantic change before an exact target run.

## Negative Results Index

- Unequal splits with a seven-layer stage OOM or fail to reach execution; six layers per physical stage is the practical limit.
- Expert axis 4 stalls in compilation. Ragged all-to-all reaches only `3.6743` MFU at batch256/m8.
- DeepEP builds and executes its SM90 path but becomes NaN after one finite non-pipelined step.
- Proper Sonic/QuACK without EP reaches `13.9598` MFU; staged weight materialization regresses to `13.8155`.
- Interleaved GPipe hits a compile cliff above the measured m6 point and remains slower than four-stage `std_1f1b`.
- XLA ragged dot regresses to `8.1438` MFU; Triton `block_k=64` regresses to `16.0189`.
- XLA latency-hiding scheduling changes the m128 mean by only `+0.0708` points, below run noise.
- RNO2A cannot create the exportable CUDA VMM allocations needed by zero-copy ragged all-to-all. JAX 0.11 keeps symmetric output memory as the implementation, so a JAX-only upgrade does not remove this blocker.
- Streamed `ring_ppermute` is numerically unstable and over 1,100x slower on its first timed reduced step.
- Owner-local combine expands to seven collective permutes and does not finish reduced backward compilation.
- Pure-XLA output-oriented combine regresses reduced MFU to `6.2896`; explicit Triton routing restores parity but provides no measurable gain (`9.1595` versus `9.1735`).
- Transfer-priority task construction regresses reduced median MFU by `2.90%` (`8.9006` versus `9.1660`); earlier `mpmd.transfer` calls do not create useful overlap.
- Input-gradient-first backward is gradient-correct and operational but regresses central MFU by `28.75%` (`6.5356` versus `9.1735`); independent block rematerialization overwhelms bubble recovery.
- Exact two-chunk bulk ring passes EP8 output/drop/VJP parity but regresses median forward by `5.30%` and forward-backward by `13.98%`; doubled launches do not hide profitably.
- Approximate QuACK improves a one-node L2 step by `4.00%`, but its reduced explicit-MPMD pipeline gain is only `+0.18%` clean mean MFU and `+0.09%` p50 MFU.

## Current Readout

The implementation milestone is complete. The best observed L24 mean MFU is `18.2583`, and batch/microbatch scaling is saturated. Approximate QuACK is neutral under the pipeline and will not be scaled. The active experiment is FP8 compression of inter-stage activations and gradients, where halving the dominant SendRecv payload could address the remaining `9.5%` relative gap. Transformer Engine NCCL EP HT remains the ranked follow-up for expert transport.

## Next Steps

1. Implement and run the pinned reduced L8/b32/m4 BF16-versus-FP8 pipeline-wire gate with ring EP.
2. Scale to L24 only if the reduced result credibly projects above 20 MFU.
3. Benchmark Transformer Engine NCCL EP HT non-zero-copy against ring on one H100x8 node before attempting JaxPP integration.
4. Resume automatic JaxPP only after stage-local inputs no longer carry non-addressable global `pipeline` mesh shardings.
5. Keep the self-contained TVM-FFI/QuACK hang reproducer in #7110 ready for human-selected upstream filing.

## Conclusion So Far

Explicit JaxPP MPMD runs the full requested model and sequence shape with stage-partitioned weights and multiple schedules. CuTe FA4 and increased standard-schedule occupancy produced the largest validated gains. The 20-MFU target remains open. Approximate EP-local QuACK is opt-in and finite-step validated but pipeline-neutral; the next gate compresses the exposed inter-stage transfer path itself.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: r11f isolates an XLA MPMD autotuning deadlock

- All 32 ranks completed JAX and NCCL_EP bootstrap. Stage 0 entered first-forward compilation while stages 1-3 entered JaxPP DIME rendezvous. Native stacks on every stage-0 process converged on `xla::Autotuner::Autotune -> DistributedKeyValueStore::Get`; downstream ranks waited independently for DIME keys. CPU activity was effectively idle.
- OpenXLA defaults `xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=true`. Its config assigner fingerprints the complete HLO module, assigns candidates across every compiler process, and waits for one result key from every process. JaxPP MPMD stages compile different modules, so the expected keys cannot match. r11f was deadlocked, not merely compiling slowly.
- r11f is terminal killed with no live pods and no route fingerprint, `ep_prepare`, loss, or MFU. Its W&B run has no training history: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/jaxpp-rno2a-ncclep-routefp-r11f-l8-e64k4-b512-s4096-p4m16-20260724-1221

🤖 Directional DIME communicators are a hard negative on the full reduced graph.

Parent `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260726-125321` ran the matched L8/d2560/e64/top-k4/seq4096/b512/m16 device-ragged graph with `JAXPP_DIRECTIONAL_COMMUNICATORS=true`; receive-buffer reuse remained at its default. A live worker confirmed the environment.

Two unchanged stack captures after more than ten quiet minutes showed:
- rank 0: `BlockingKeyValueGet -> dime2.get_nccl_id`
- rank 1: `dime2.recv_done` while creating a CUDA stream
- ranks 2-3: `PjRtLoadedExecutable::Execute`

The stacks showed no compiler activity despite the last stage-2-backward compile log. No loss or MFU appeared. The parent and all four tasks are terminal killed with no live descendants.

Separate directional communicators therefore move the wait from the prior `ncclGroupEnd` location into communicator-ID creation; they do not resolve it. This strengthens the multi-communicator creation/launch-order diagnosis.

Snapshot: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/82177d4a4021af3994c86022fd1ef3b7c47e58ff.

The next isolated control is live in parent `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260726-130937`: `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1`, directional communicators unset/default false, receive-buffer reuse unset/default true. A worker has confirmed those values. No NVIDIA issue has been filed.

The L4/d2560/e64/top-k4/seq4096/b128/m4 H100 smoke failed during JaxPP `make_jaxpr`, before XLA compilation: CuTe FA4 raises `NotImplementedError: cutlass_call does not support batching with jax.vmap`. The next formulation avoids batching the CuTe custom call: concatenate each pair along the ordinary batch dimension for attention, split only inside every MoE invocation so exact ring routing/capacity/drop remain per original microbatch, and sum loss/QB/gradient contributions in original-microbatch units. Promotion still requires relative-L2 <=0.002 for loss and every gradient leaf.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 The one-block target-shape JaxPP component gate compiles and executes as one MPMD task, but fails the fixed numerical gate.

`/dlwh/jaxpp-group2-component-mpmd-r3-695f389d-20260726-231209` ran clean commit `695f389d9c` on one H100x8 at d2560/e64/top-k4/sequence4096/global microbatch32/local4, BF16 CuTe FA4, exact ring EP8, and `save_moe`. Ordered lower/compile/execute took `21.092/7.267/0.719s`; JaxPP lower/precompile/execute took `0.799/23.932/0.089s`. Precompile reported exactly one task and zero receive buffers.

The structural contract passed. The pure target-shape paired-MoE trace had exactly two ring bodies, two router calls, and no attention under `_paired_moe_calls`. The complete VJP task recorded the expected reverse/remat expansion to four ring bodies and ten router calls, still with no attention inside that boundary.

Numerical parity failed without changing the `0.002` policy. Both outputs were about `0.0202-0.0206` relative-L2; exact routing counts differed in `59` and `61` entries; per-microbatch losses were `0.01319` and `0.00347`; QB was `0.00344/0.00284`. `20/21` gradient leaves failed. The worst was `mlp.router` at `1.38893` relative-L2 (actual/reference norms `54.19565/54.15769`, cosine `0.03611`); input gradients were `0.66798/0.66936`. All values were finite and checkpoint parameter structure remained unchanged.

Iris is terminal after `2m04.87s` with no retry or live allocation. This blocks L8/L24. The next bounded diagnostic is to expose post-attention values, pre-router dense inputs, and selected experts inside the JaxPP task to locate the first divergence.

Evidence: [gate fix](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/695f389d9c), [logbook checkpoint](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/85dcecc2f2).

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 The correctness-preserving production L8 gate compiled every task but exhausted HBM at first execution.

- Parent `/dlwh/iris-run-job-20260727-030719` ran L8/d2560/e64/top-k4/seq4096/b512/m16, four H100x8 stages, group size two, exact ring EP8, CuTe FA4, BF16 wire, `save_moe`, and XLA fraction `0.70`.
- Compilation completed from approximately `03:10:37Z` through `03:23:20Z`. Initial execution then requested another `5.62 GiB` per GPU on stages 1-2 and `6.14 GiB` on stage 3. Later segfault/rendezvous/coordination errors were secondary to the BFC allocator failure.
- No training metric was produced. The unchanged retry was stopped; parent and child are terminal killed with no live resource.
- Root compile-scaling issue: production constructed fresh bound phase callables for every pair/block, while explicit `MpmdFun.lower()` does not apply automatic JaxPP task-jaxpr deduplication. At L24/m256 this implied roughly 12,288 heavy phase identities.
- Commit `3f06cc8505` now prebuilds stable stage/block/phase callables. Its m4/m8 lowering regression doubles task calls from 12 to 24 while holding unique phase call-jaxpr identities at four; the target nominally falls to 96 heavy compile keys. Grouping tests pass `41/41`, and precommit including Pyrefly passes.
- Evidence/logbook commit: `82fa0a92cd`.

Next: rerun the matched L8 gate at unchanged fraction `0.70`. Lowering the fraction would reduce the BFC ceiling and is not appropriate for this failure. No L24 promotion until L8 executes finite steps.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Stable phase callables reduced compile specialization but did not make the matched L8 group-size-two graph fit.

r4 emitted 298 unique compile names, including 256 heavy phase names across eight microbatch-pair prefixes. r5 and r6 each emitted 74 unique names, including 32 heavy phase names under one prefix. This validates the compile-identity fix.

r5 at XLA fraction 0.70 and r6 at 0.80 both failed at first execution with the same BFC allocation pattern: stages 1-2 requested 5.62 GiB per GPU and stage 3 requested 6.14 GiB per GPU. r6 failed at 03:50:37Z, then ranks 1-3 segfaulted in the DIME transfer path as secondary fallout. Neither run produced a W&B history row. Iris began retries in both cases; only the affected parent prefixes were stopped, and all parent/child resources are terminal with no live allocation.

The fraction-only change from 0.70 to 0.80 is a hard negative. The next L8 attempt needs a measured reduction in live task/transfer buffers or activation residency; another preallocation-fraction-only retry is not justified. Evidence: commit 37f7260c3a.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body: 🤖 The matched L8 outer-state-donation gate is a hard negative. spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==
spillover_issues.title: [grug] Ragged EP train step hangs on one rack at d6144 hero scale after a watch step

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
On the ragged all-to-all EP backend at d6144, the first train step after a periodic eval fails with `NCCL operation ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument` on most of the 64 ranks, deterministically, and the gang shuts down. The d768 rung completes 20 evals on the same code. The live hero would hit this at its first eval after the backend swap and then crash-loop through the ladder's retries, since each retry resumes from the last temporary checkpoint and reaches the same eval step.

The capacity-limited evaluator (`GrugEvalConfig.eval_current`) runs the training MoE path, so it is a second ragged all-to-all executable on the training clique with a 16x smaller all-to-all footprint. XLA registers one NCCL symmetric-memory window per executable starting at the base of the collective-memory arena and sized to that executable's footprint (`AcquireSymmetricMemory` in `xla/backends/gpu/runtime/collective_memory.cc` → `ncclCommWindowRegister` in `nccl_symmetric_memory.cc`), caches it per executable keyed by clique and device address, and keeps it until the executable or the clique is destroyed. An `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG,INIT` trace on one rank shows the two train-step executables each registering a window of 20,293,761,024 bytes at `0xbf80000000` (identical ranges, accepted), the eval registering 518,436,864 bytes at the same base (accepted), and the next train step failing at launch after a cache hit on its own window. Executables with equal footprints coexist, which is why the train step's with-hooks and without-hooks variants never collide. The dropless evaluator (`sonic_cute`) has no all-to-all and does not trigger it.

Reproduce: one rack, `launch_diagnostics.py --dp-racks 1 --moe-implementation ragged_all_to_all --master-params device --restore-from <hero step-48000> --num-steps 48004 --eval-every 2` on main `c13d1ddf27`. spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 Tracking issue for the **agent-documentation experiment** (taking over #4321).

## Goal
Find the best **~1000-token-per-doc** agent-documentation format for the Marin monorepo, measured rather than by vibes. Per sub-project, two axes — `ops.md` (how to **USE** it) and `architecture.md` (how to **UNDERSTAND/CHANGE** it) — plus a top-level `MAP.md` and a per-project `overview.md`. Each doc capped at ~1000 tokens.

## Methodology (probe-judged, no human in the loop)
- **10 read-only probes** mined from real `~/.claude` command history (4 iris, 3 finelog, 2 marin, 1 levanter), each tagged **USE** or **UNDERSTAND**.
- Each probe carries **source-verified anchors** — the load-bearing symbols a correct answer must use/reference (re-grounded against current `main`).
- A **weak coder (haiku, NO tools)** writes a script using *only* the doc bundle. No repo access → the score measures **doc quality**, not model resourcefulness.
- A **judge (sonnet)** reviews the script text against the anchors + a strict hallucination check + a calibrated 1–5 quality rubric. **Intent-aware:** USE requires the anchor be *used in code*; UNDERSTAND credits *naming/referencing/explaining* it. `foo`/`foo_step` builder variants are treated as equivalent.
- **PASS** = rubric accuracy ≥ 0.8 **AND** no hallucination. Quality (1–5) is reported as a secondary signal.
- Harness lives in `scripts/agent_docs/` (`generate_taxonomy.py`, `eval.py`, `run_round.py`, `probes.py`, `prompts.py`). One round = generate-or-reuse docs → run the 10 probes → append a row to a ledger and print a scoreboard with a delta vs. the previous round.

## Two generation tracks
- **Mechanical** (current): build a signatures-only digest from a tree-sitter parse (no LLM, no source bodies) → one LLM call writes the budgeted doc. Cheap, deterministic input.
- **Agentic** (next): a tool-using agent (up to opus) explores real source and writes each doc. Sidesteps the lossy digest compression. Budgeted to **$10** total for the experiment.

## Results so far (mean over 10 probes)
| Round | Change | mean rubric | mean quality | passed |
|------|--------|:----:|:----:|:----:|
| R7 | first end-to-end run | 0.09 | 1.3 | 0/10 |
| R8 | harness bugs fixed (digest carries dataclass fields; judge hallucination high-precision) | 0.07 | 1.3 | 0/10 |
| R9 | breadth-first `ops.md` (entry-point index of 12–20 callables) | 0.23 | 1.3 | 0/10 |
| R10 | judge fairness fixes (intent-aware, `_step` equivalence, recalibrated quality) — re-eval of R9 docs | 0.26 | 1.70 | 0/10 |
| R11 | architecture docs name internal edit-site seams (digest surfaces private methods) | *in progress* | | |

### Key findings
- **R9: breadth beats depth under the budget.** A 1000-token whole-sub-project ops doc only fits 2–3 deep APIs; switching to a terse entry-point index of 12–20 callables tripled rubric accuracy (0.07 → 0.23).
- **R10: the judge is sharp, not lenient.** With the fairness fixes, every remaining hallucination flag was a *real* fabrication the weak coder invented because the doc never surfaced the right symbol (e.g. `ControllerServiceClientSync`→fabricated `ControllerClient`; `DistributedConfig` fields jammed onto `TrainerConfig`; a fabricated `compute_fuzzy_duplicates_step` for an undocumented second pipeline stage). **Root cause is doc content, not judging.**
- **Two content gaps identified.** (a) UNDERSTAND probes anchor on *private methods of public classes* (`_reconcile_tick`, `_find_coscheduled_assignments`, `_invalidate`) that the public-only digest hid → R11 surfaces them. (b) USE probes need *paired pipeline stages* and *canonical config classes* the budgeted ops doc dropped → upcoming ops-completeness lever.
- **Per-run variance is real:** the coder rewrites the script each eval, so single-probe deltas are noisy (P1 swung 3/5→1/5 on identical docs). The aggregate trend is the signal; stable probes may warrant multi-run averaging.

## Next steps
1. **R11** (running): measure the architecture-internals lever.
2. **R12 (agentic):** generate docs with a tool-using agent; compare head-to-head against the mechanical track on the same probe suite.
3. Ops-completeness lever for the USE probes (paired stages, config classes).
4. Possibly a Rust-parser change to surface non-`pub` internals (currently blocks P5).

This issue is updated after every round with results + the plan for the next one.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 No PR — this is a self-updating research-experiment tracker, not an actionable bug/task.

- The issue is owned and updated by @rjpower after every round ("updated after every round with results + the plan for the next one"); the "Next steps" (R11 internals lever, R12 agentic track, ops-completeness lever, Rust-parser change) are open-ended research directions, not a discrete fix with a definition of done.
- The harness (`scripts/agent_docs/`) is not on `main` in this checkout — it rides on #4321, which this issue takes over from. No code here to fix against.

To make a sub-task automatable, file it separately with: the specific harness file/function to change, expected vs. actual behavior (or the target metric delta), and acceptance criteria. Examples that would qualify: a named bug in `eval.py`/`run_round.py` with a repro, or "surface non-`pub` internals in the tree-sitter digest so probe P5 resolves `_reconcile_tick`" scoped to a concrete parser change.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **R11 — architecture docs surface internal edit-site seams** (mechanical track, old haiku-no-tools coder)

| | R10 | R11 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| mean rubric acc | 0.26 | **0.39** | +0.13 |
| mean quality | 1.70 | **2.10** | +0.40 |
| passed | 0/10 | **1/10** | +1 |

Lever: a separate architecture-only digest that surfaces private methods on public classes + private module-level functions (marked `internal`), plus an ARCHITECTURE_PROMPT that must name the exact edit-site symbol.

**Per-probe standouts:** P7 (marin/understand) 2/4→**4/4**, P10 (finelog/understand) 0/4→**3/4**, P8 (marin/use) 5/7→**6/7 PASS** (first pass). Laggards: P4 (iris/understand) still 0/4; P6 (finelog/use) 0/4 and P9 (levanter/use) 0/4 — the USE probes still need an ops-completeness lever (`DistributedConfig`, finelog client APIs absent from the budgeted ops doc).

### ⚠️ Validity finding (important)
Investigating *why* P10 rose revealed the gains are partly **prompt-vocabulary leakage**, not doc quality. The finelog architecture doc named *none* of P10's anchors, yet the tool-less coder still produced `LogClient.connect`/`_invalidate`/`resolver` — it **guessed the conventional names** from the prompt's words ("connect", "invalidation", "resolver") and Marin's idiomatic naming made the guesses correct. The one **non-obvious** anchor, `LogServiceProxy`, correctly scored 0 (coder guessed `LogServiceClientSync`).

Takeaway: **the discriminating anchors are the non-obvious ones**; guessable conventional names inflate UNDERSTAND scores independent of the doc. P4 is the clean counter-example — its anchors (`_reconcile_tick` etc.) are *not* named in the prompt, and it correctly scored 0 when neither doc nor coder had them.

### Two methodology changes now landed (R12+ is a new baseline)
1. **Coder is now sonnet that may read ~3 files** (read-only, no execution) under a tight $0.30 cap — measures how well docs *route* a capable, budget-limited agent rather than docs-in-isolation. New metric **mean coder spend** (lower = better routing) is now tracked, since rubric accuracy may saturate when the agent can read source.
2. **Agentic generation track**: a tool-using agent explores real source to write each doc (vs. the mechanical digest→doc). Budget-capped at $10, up to opus.

### Next
- **R12**: re-eval the R11 docs with the new coder → isolates the coder-regime change.
- **R13**: agentic docs + new coder → agentic vs. mechanical head-to-head.
- Then an ops-completeness lever for the USE probes; possibly a Rust-parser change for P5's non-`pub` internals.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **R12 — new coder regime** (same R11 docs, coder = sonnet that may read ~3 files under a $0.30 cap)

This round changes only the coder (same R11 mechanical docs), to isolate the regime change.

| | R11 (haiku, no tools) | R12 (sonnet, ~3 files) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| mean rubric acc | 0.39 | **0.66** | +0.27 |
| mean quality | 2.10 | **3.20** | +1.10 |
| passed | 1/10 | **3/10** | +2 |
| mean coder spend | — | **$0.197** | (new metric) |

The coder reads source and recovers anchors the docs didn't surface: P9 (levanter/use) 0→3 (found `DistributedConfig` by reading), P1 (iris) 1→3 (named the real `ControllerServiceClientSync`), P6 (finelog/use) 0→2, P5 0→3. Passes: P7, P8, P10.

**Interpretation.** Under a capable+file-reading coder, rubric accuracy partly reflects "the agent can read source," not doc quality alone — but it did **not saturate** (0.66, mean spend $0.197 of the $0.30 cap), so within the tight budget the docs still matter for *routing*. The discriminator is now twofold: rubric accuracy **and** coder spend (good docs → answer for less spend).

**P4 (iris/understand) stays 0/4** and is the cleanest target: its prompt does not leak the symbol names, the coder couldn't locate `_reconcile_tick`/`_run_polling_loop`/`_run_ping_loop` within budget, and the mechanical architecture doc didn't name them either. A doc that points straight at the controller reconcile loop should fix this.

### Next
- **R13**: agentic-generated docs (tool-using agent explores source) + same new coder → head-to-head vs. the R12 mechanical baseline. Expect: equal-or-better rubric at **lower coder spend** if the agentic docs route better.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **R13 — agentic docs vs mechanical docs** (both scored by the new sonnet+files coder)

| | R12 (mechanical docs) | R13 (agentic docs) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| mean rubric acc | 0.66 | 0.64 | −0.02 |
| mean quality | 3.20 | 3.10 | −0.10 |
| passed | 3/10 | 2/10 | −1 |
| mean coder spend | $0.197 | $0.209 | +$0.01 |
| **generation cost** | ~$0 | **$4.71** | — |

**Verdict: statistically tied — agentic generation cost $4.71 for no measurable gain.** The agentic docs are well-grounded and read nicely, but they did not route the file-reading coder any better than the cheap mechanical digest→doc pipeline. Per-probe is a wash (P3 4/5→5/5, P8 6/7→7/7 up; P7 4→3, P6 2→1, P10 4→3 down).

Two confirmations that the **coder dominates, not the doc method**:
- The agentic `marin/ops.md` still did **not** name `compute_fuzzy_dups_attrs_step`, and agentic `levanter/ops.md` still did **not** name `DistributedConfig` — yet P8 hit 7/7 and P9 3/4. Those anchors came from the **coder reading source**, not the doc.
- The biggest single jump in the whole experiment was the *coder* change (R11→R12, +0.27); the *doc-generation method* change (R12→R13) moved nothing.

**P4 (iris/understand) is 0/4 in every variant** — mechanical or agentic doc, tool-less or file-reading coder. The reconcile-loop internals (`_reconcile_tick` etc.) are the one thing nothing recovers within budget.

### Next: the decision-relevant ablation
- **R14 — no docs**: empty bundle, same file-reading coder. If rubric stays ~0.66, the docs add little to a capable agent (it just reads source); if it drops, the docs provide real routing value. This is what tells us whether — and how much — these docs are worth.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **R14 — no-docs ablation** (empty bundle, same sonnet+files coder)

| Config (sonnet coder, may read ~3 files) | mean rubric | mean quality | coder spend |
|---|---|---|---|
| R12: mechanical docs | 0.66 | 3.20 | $0.197 |
| R13: agentic docs | 0.64 | 3.10 | $0.209 |
| **R14: NO docs** | **0.72** | **3.50** | $0.213 |

**The file-reading coder scored as well or better with *no docs* than with either doc set.** With no doc to lead it, it went straight to source: P4 (iris/understand) rose to **2/4** — beating every doc variant, where it was 0/4 — by reading `controller.py` directly. It dropped only where a doc had provided a non-obvious pointer it couldn't find alone: P5 (finelog) 4→0 (lost the architecture doc's Rust-store pointers).

**Interpretation:** for a capable agent that can read source under a modest budget, these budgeted docs provide **no measurable task-success benefit** (here slightly negative). The agent recovers the needed symbols by reading code. Caveat: the 0.64–0.72 spread is within single-run noise; the firm claim is "no clear gain," not "docs hurt."

This is the central tension of the experiment: the eval anchors are *source symbols*, and a source-reading agent recovers them regardless of docs. So the docs' value — if any — should appear when the agent **cannot** read source.

### Completing the matrix (file-access × docs-presence, fixed sonnet)
- **R15**: mechanical docs + **docs-only** coder (no file reads).
- **R16**: no docs + **docs-only** coder (floor: task + parametric knowledge only).

If R15 ≫ R16, docs clearly help when the agent can't read source — the real value proposition. Combined with R12/R14 (≈ no gain when it can), that's the decision: **docs matter for doc-only/weak agents and for orientation, not for capable source-reading agents.**

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **R15 + R16 — docs-only coder** (no file access), completing the matrix

Same sonnet model throughout; only file-access and docs-presence vary.

| | +files coder | docs-only coder |
|---|---|---|
| **mechanical docs** | R12: **0.66** | R15: **0.43** |
| **no docs** | R14: **0.72** | R16: **0.12** (floor) |

### The headline result
- **When the agent CANNOT read source, docs are worth +0.31** (R16 0.12 → R15 0.43). This is the docs' real value.
- **When the agent CAN read source, docs add ~nothing** (R12 0.66 vs R14 0.72; within single-run noise).
- **R16 floor 0.12**: with neither docs nor file access, only P8 (3/7) and P9 (3/4, levanter — JAX/distributed conventions are in the model's priors) scored. Marin's internal APIs are otherwise not recoverable from parametric knowledge — so the docs (or source reading) are genuinely necessary, not redundant.

The doc-only deltas are large and clearly outside noise; the file-reading deltas are small and within it.

### Last cell
- **R17**: agentic docs + docs-only coder, vs R15's mechanical 0.43 — does agentic *content* beat mechanical *content* in the regime where docs actually matter? This is the clean agentic-vs-mechanical test (R12 vs R13 was muddied by the coder reading source).

Then the final synthesis report.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 # Final report — agent-doc experiment

Ten v2 rounds (R7–R17) over a budgeted, probe-judged harness. Below: the full trajectory, the controlled 2×2, the conclusions, and what shipped.

## Trajectory (mean rubric accuracy over 10 probes)

| Round | Change | rubric | quality | coder regime |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|---|
| R7 | first end-to-end run | 0.09 | 1.3 | haiku, no tools |
| R8 | harness bugs fixed (digest fields; high-precision judge) | 0.07 | 1.3 | haiku, no tools |
| R9 | **breadth-first `ops.md`** (entry-point index) | 0.23 | 1.3 | haiku, no tools |
| R10 | judge fairness fixes (intent-aware, `_step` equiv, rubric) | 0.26 | 1.70 | haiku, no tools |
| R11 | **architecture docs name internal seams** | 0.39 | 2.10 | haiku, no tools |
| R12 | **coder → sonnet + ~3 file reads** (same R11 docs) | 0.66 | 3.20 | sonnet, +files |
| R13 | agentic docs (gen $4.71) | 0.64 | 3.10 | sonnet, +files |
| R14 | no-docs ablation | 0.72 | 3.50 | sonnet, +files |
| R15 | mechanical docs, docs-only coder | 0.43 | 2.40 | sonnet, no files |
| R16 | no docs, docs-only (floor) | 0.12 | 1.40 | sonnet, no files |
| R17 | agentic docs, docs-only coder | 0.26 | 1.90 | sonnet, no files |

## The controlled 2×2 (fixed sonnet model)

| docs | +files coder | docs-only coder |
|------|:---:|:---:|
| **mechanical** | 0.66 | **0.43** |
| **agentic** ($4.71 gen) | 0.64 | **0.26** |
| **none** | 0.72 | 0.12 |

## Conclusions

1. **Doc value is conditional on file access.** When the agent *can't* read source, good docs are worth **+0.31** (0.12 → 0.43). When it *can*, docs are **~neutral** on correctness (0.66 vs 0.72 no-docs — within noise); the agent recovers symbols by reading code. The most striking single result: the file-reading coder did *best with no docs at all*.
2. **Mechanical beats agentic — ship mechanical.** Agentic generation is well-grounded but never wins: tied with files (0.64 vs 0.66), clearly **worse doc-only (0.26 vs 0.43)** because the signature-dense mechanical docs carry the exact import paths + defaults a doc-only coder needs, while agentic docs read as narrative. Agentic cost ~$4.71/round vs ~free.
3. **The winning doc format** (within the ~1000-token/two-axis budget): breadth-first `ops.md` (an entry-point index of 12–20 callables) + an `architecture.md` that names concrete edit-site symbols **including internal seams**. Keep docs signature-dense.
4. **Docs primarily serve doc-only / weak / orientation use.** For capable source-reading agents their correctness value is ~0; their real value is speed/orientation, which this eval doesn't measure.

## What shipped (branch)
- **Harness**: `scripts/agent_docs/{generate_taxonomy,generate_agentic,eval,run_round,probes,prompts,parsing,packages,claude_cli,tokens}.py` — mechanical + agentic generators, a 10-probe source-grounded eval (coder→judge), and a per-round runner with a results ledger + scoreboard. All on the subscription plan (API key stripped → flat-rate OAuth).
- **Doc deletion** per the original ask (stale `.agents/projects`, `lib/*/docs`, etc.), with the skill-tooling fallout healed (`design-template.md` restored; dangling skill refs trimmed; `docs/agent/README.md` added).
- **Plan**: `docs/plans/agent-docs-experiment-v2-...md`. **Results**: `scripts/agent_docs/experiments.md`.

## Caveats / follow-ups
- Single-run variance ~±0.05–0.08; the file-reading deltas are within it (the doc-only deltas are not).
- UNDERSTAND prompts leak some anchor vocabulary; the non-obvious anchors are the real discriminators.
- The eval rewards recovering *source symbols*, which structurally favors file-reading agents and undersells docs' orientation value.
- Rust non-`pub` internals (P5) aren't in the digest (parser captures only `pub`).
- P4 (iris reconcile loop) resists every doc; only direct source-reading recovers it.

PR opening next; this tracking issue will be closed against it.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 ## v3: hybrid split-docs (agentic narrative + mechanical reference)

Starting a third pass with a new doc architecture, on top of the v2 verdict (mechanical signature-dense docs beat agentic narrative docs; doc value is conditional on file access).

### The new format
Each doc gets a **1500-token split budget**, two complementary halves:
1. **Narrative half** (agentic, sonnet with read-only Read/Grep/Glob) — explores real source and writes the *concepts*: what it is, how data flows, the mental model, the reasoning a signature list can't convey. ~750 tokens.
2. **Reference half** (mechanical, deterministic tree-sitter — no LLM, no hallucination) — the exact facts, axis-specific:
   - `overview` → files ranked by public-symbol count
   - `ops` → breadth-first entry-point index (signatures + defaults, interleaved across packages)
   - `architecture` → edit sites (classes + public/internal methods + internal module funcs)

The bet: the v2 2×2 showed mechanical docs win on *exact symbols/defaults* (what a docs-only coder needs) while agentic docs read better as *narrative*. The hybrid keeps both, in one doc, under budget.

### Setup
- **sonnet** generates the narrative half; **opus** judges. (v2 judged with sonnet, so the absolute numbers shift — hence the re-baselines below.)
- The narrative half is **cached** per (project, axis), so iterating the free mechanical half costs $0.
- Primary metric: **docs-only coder** (the regime where doc *content* actually moves the score — v2 found a file-reading coder washes out doc differences). A file-reading confirmation round at the end.

### Plan (10 rounds, R18–R27)
- **R18–R20**: opus-judged re-baselines of v2 docs (mechanical / agentic / no-docs), docs-only coder — establishes the comparison frame under the new judge.
- **R21**: hybrid v1, docs-only, opus.
- **R22–R26**: iterate the levers (narrative focus, mechanical composition/density, token split, per-axis tuning) based on per-probe failures.
- **R27**: best config, file-reading + docs-only, final.

Results to follow per round.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 ## R18–R21: opus-judged frame + hybrid v1 (a surprise)

### The opus-judged baselines (docs-only coder)
| round | docs | rubric | pass |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|
| R18 | mechanical (v2 winner) | **0.53** | 3/10 |
| R19 | agentic | 0.38 | 3/10 |
| R20 | none (floor) | 0.28 | 2/10 |

Opus judges more generously than the v2 sonnet judge (which gave 0.43 / 0.26 / 0.12) but preserves the ordering — mechanical still beats agentic by +0.15. **The bar for hybrid is 0.53.**

### R21 — hybrid v1 = 0.39 (below mechanical)
Despite the hybrid docs being visibly the richest of the three tracks (the narrative names `persisted_seq`/`collect_dependencies_and_version` as concepts; the reference lists exact methods + internal seams), hybrid v1 came in at **0.39** — below mechanical (0.53), tied with agentic.

The judge notes pinpoint why, and it's the interesting part:
- **P4 (0/4)**: the reference half surfaced `Controller._run_scheduling_loop` (the first internal methods in *source order*) but the real reconcile loop is `_run_polling_loop` — which the per-class cap dropped. The coder grabbed the wrong loop → flagged as hallucination.
- **P2 (0/5)**: the breadth-first round-robin never surfaced `_find_coscheduled_assignments` / `CoschedulingConfig`, so the coder *punted*.

**Finding: for a docs-only coder, curation/selection beats raw density.** The mechanical track wins not because it has *more* but because its LLM pass *selects the right* symbols. A deterministic dump that's exhaustive-but-unranked hands the coder near-miss symbols (more hallucination) while burying the load-bearing ones (fewer anchors hit).

### R22 (running) — smarter deterministic selection
Keeping the cached narrative, I made the mechanical half *rank* instead of dump:
- **architecture** edit sites prioritize control-flow/lifecycle method names (loops, ticks, reconcile/dispatch) over source order — `_run_polling_loop` now surfaces;
- **ops** entry index ranks by an importance heuristic (verbs like submit/run/connect, Config/Client suffixes, shallower paths), capped per package, instead of round-robin.

Testing whether better *deterministic* selection closes the gap to 0.53. Result next.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 ## R22–R23: the hybrid overtakes mechanical (docs-only coder)

| round | config | rubric | qual | pass |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| R18 | mechanical (baseline) | 0.53 | 2.60 | 3/10 |
| R21 | hybrid v1 (raw dump) | 0.39 | 2.30 | 2/10 |
| **R22** | hybrid + ranked reference | **0.56** | 2.80 | 4/10 |
| **R23** | hybrid + ranked reference + sharpened narrative | **0.58** | 3.00 | 3/10 |

### What moved
- **R22 (ranked, not dumped):** ranking the deterministic reference by importance (ops) and control-flow/lifecycle names (architecture) took hybrid from 0.39 → **0.56**, past the 0.53 mechanical bar. Biggest gains: P8 marin-use 3/7→7/7 and P9 levanter-use 1/4→4/4 (importance-ranked entry index), plus the understand probes the narrative already helped (P5 3→5, P7 3→4, P10 2→3 vs mechanical).
- **R23 (sharpened narrative):** making the narrative *name the exact load-bearing symbol* (the reconcile loop `_reconcile_tick`, the right entry point per task) nudged to **0.58**. P4 1→2, P3 3→4, P6 0→1.

### The honest caveats
- **Narrative content is high-variance.** The same R23 narrative change that lifted the iris/finelog understand probes *regressed* P8 (marin use) 7/7→2/7 — the reference half was byte-identical, so the docs-only coder leaned on the (re-rolled) narrative and missed symbols the reference still carried. R22↔R23 (0.56↔0.58) is within single-run noise; the robust, repeatable signal is that the **narrative consistently helps the *understand* probes** (concepts), and the **ranked reference consistently helps the *use* probes** (exact signatures).
- So the split-doc bet is validated: each half carries what the other can't, and the hybrid (0.56–0.58) clears both parents (mechanical 0.53, agentic 0.38) — *provided the mechanical half ranks rather than dumps*.

### Next: the practical (file-reading) regime
Running R24–R26 now: hybrid / mechanical / no-docs, each with a coder that may read ~3 files. v2 found file access washes out doc differences; checking whether that holds under the opus judge, and confirming the hybrid is at least neutral there. Then the final report.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 # v3 final report — hybrid split-docs (R18–R27)

Ten opus-judged rounds testing a new doc architecture: each doc is a **1500-token split** — an agentic NARRATIVE half (sonnet explores source: concepts, data flow, why) + a deterministic MECHANICAL reference half (tree-sitter, no LLM: ranked files / entry-point signatures / internal edit seams). Narrative cached → iterating the free mechanical half costs $0. sonnet generates, opus judges.

## Results

**Docs-only coder** (where doc *content* shows):
| docs | rubric | pass | halluc. probes |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| none (floor) | 0.28 | 2/10 | — |
| agentic | 0.38 | 3/10 | — |
| mechanical (v2 winner) | 0.53 | 3/10 | 1 |
| hybrid v1 (raw dump) | 0.39 | 2/10 | — |
| **hybrid v2 (ranked ref)** | **0.56** | 4/10 | — |
| **hybrid v3 (ranked + narrative)** | **0.58** | 3/10 | 4 |
| deterministic ref only ($0, no LLM) | 0.56 | 1/10 | 6 |

**File-reading coder** (the realistic agent):
| docs | rubric | pass |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| none (floor) | 0.74 | 5/10 |
| mechanical | 0.70 | 5/10 |
| **hybrid** | **0.82** | 6/10 |

## The four findings

1. **Selection is the lever, and it's free.** The raw hybrid *dump* (0.39) was *worse* than mechanical (0.53) — a breadth-first/source-order dump buried the load-bearing symbols (it surfaced `Controller._run_scheduling_loop` but dropped the real reconcile loop `_run_polling_loop`) and fed the coder near-misses. Just *ranking* the deterministic reference — control-flow/lifecycle names for edit sites, an importance heuristic for the ops index — jumped it to **0.56**, past mechanical. Density without ranking is actively harmful.

2. **A $0, zero-LLM doc is competitive on rubric but hallucination-prone.** The ranked deterministic reference *alone* scores 0.56 docs-only (matching the hybrid, beating mechanical) — but flags hallucinations on 6/10 probes (vs hybrid 4, mechanical 1) → only 1/10 pass. A bare signature list gives a docs-only coder rope to fabricate plausible near-misses.

3. **The narrative earns its keep on orientation + hallucination control, not raw rubric.** It adds only ~+0.02 docs-only rubric over the bare reference, but raises the pass rate and is **decisive for a file-reading agent: 0.82 vs 0.70 mechanical / 0.74 no-docs.** This **reverses v2's "docs are neutral with file access"** — *good* docs help a realistic agent (the narrative orients, the reference points at exact files); a plain signature dump doesn't. (Caveat unchanged: on the hardest probe P4, docs still mislead and direct source-reading wins.)

4. **Recommendation — ship the hybrid.** The free ranked reference carries the rubric; the cached agentic narrative buys the routing that matters to a realistic file-reading agent and controls hallucination. This updates v2's "ship mechanical, skip agentic": the agentic narrative *does* help **when paired with a ranked mechanical reference**, and the combined cost is low (reference $0; narrative ~$0.3/doc, cached; a 12-doc set ~$2.4–3.9 once).

## What shipped
`scripts/agent_docs/generate_hybrid.py` (hybrid generator + ranked deterministic renderers, narrative caching), `--mode hybrid` in the runner, the sharpened narrative prompts, and two harness-robustness fixes (use the coder's spend-cap partial instead of crashing; retry a transient judge 529). Full round-by-round log: `scripts/agent_docs/experiments.md`. Branch pushed to #4321.

Caveats: single-run variance ~±0.05–0.08 (R22↔R23 and mechanical↔no-docs gaps are within it; the ranked-vs-dump jump, the file-reading hybrid win, and the detonly hallucination rate are not); the narrative is high-variance while the ranked reference is deterministic/stable; the heuristic name-lists are tuned to this monorepo's conventions.

spillover_issues.author: WhenWen
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

The archived Qwen3 optimizer harness is available in the closed, unmerged PR #7118. Error-aware Muon was evaluated at 130M and 300M with matched learning-rate controls. At 300M, the stabilized Hesscorr implementation completed all 15 gain/LR cells. Gains `0.1` and `0.3` each beat paired Muon at all five learning rates, but every Hesscorr variant lost to the simpler blend `0.05` baseline at all five learning rates and required about 90% more native training time than Muon.

The best 300M Hesscorr cell used gain `0.3`, learning rate `0.012`, and reached `1.057701` held-out Paloma C4-en BPB. Paired Muon reached `1.058626` (`-0.000925` for Hesscorr), while blend `0.05` reached `1.056606` (`+0.001095` for Hesscorr). This single-seed result establishes numerical stability and a small improvement over plain Muon, but not a favorable quality-per-compute tradeoff.

Exact stabilized source and materialized results: [`fffd6a64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5).

## Stabilized implementation

The original 300M Hesscorr sweep failed all 15 cells at global step 0. A warmup retry remained finite through step 50 and failed on step 51, the first corrected update, localizing the failure to the Sylvester correction.

The published implementation:

- uses ordinary quintic Muon for the first 50 optimizer updates, one momentum time constant at momentum `0.98`;
- uses explicit highest precision for polar-Hessian, Sylvester, and inverse matrix products;
- constructs the polar Hessian from one product and its transpose for exact post-rounding symmetry;
- computes the correction norm with scale-safe Frobenius normalization and falls back to a zero correction if the solve or norm is non-finite.

The [optimizer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_optimizer.py), [100-step TPU gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_stability_gate.py), [15-cell launcher](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_sweep.py), and [result materializer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/materialize_muon_error_feedback_results.py) are pinned to the result commit.

## 300M held-out C4-en results

Lower BPB is better. Muon and blend `0.05` are completed same-geometry references from version `2026.07.23.4`; stabilized Hesscorr uses version `2026.08.28.3`.

| Variant | LR 0.004 | LR 0.006 | LR 0.008 | LR 0.010 | LR 0.012 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Muon | 1.067245 | 1.062251 | 1.060028 | 1.059351 | 1.058626 |
| Blend 0.05 | 1.066771 | 1.061070 | 1.059204 | 1.057656 | **1.056606** |
| Hesscorr 0.1 | 1.066853 | 1.062055 | 1.059515 | 1.058882 | 1.057950 |
| Hesscorr 0.3 | 1.067066 | 1.061869 | 1.059530 | 1.058388 | **1.057701** |
| Hesscorr 1.0 | 1.067755 | 1.062778 | 1.060028 | 1.058927 | 1.058036 |

| Hesscorr gain | Mean delta vs Muon | Wins vs Muon | Mean delta vs Blend 0.05 | Wins vs Blend | Mean time overhead vs Muon |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | -0.000449 | 5/5 | +0.000790 | 0/5 | +90.03% |
| 0.3 | -0.000589 | 5/5 | +0.000649 | 0/5 | +90.05% |
| 1.0 | +0.000005 | 2/5 | +0.001244 | 0/5 | +90.05% |

All 15 Hesscorr runs reached `global_step=11443`, wrote final checkpoint metadata, and had finite final loss. Iris reported zero failed cells and 124 aggregate preemptions. Each run processed 5,999,951,872 tokens on one preemptible v5p-8 slice in `us-central1`.

## 130M context

The earlier 40-cell 130M sweep found Hesscorr gain `0.1` improved C4-en BPB at four of five paired learning rates. Its best cell reached `1.164666` at learning rate `0.020`, versus `1.165484` for paired Muon, with a mean paired delta of `-0.000587` and 4.33% mean training-time overhead. The stabilized 300M result preserves the improvement over Muon but makes the compute tradeoff substantially worse.

## Artifacts and conclusion

- [Technical report with the full per-LR analysis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/docs/reports/error-aware-muon-speedrun.md)
- [Machine-readable 130M and 300M results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_results.json)
- [300M debugging record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/docs/debug-log-error-aware-muon-300m.md)
- [Best 300M Hesscorr W&B run](https://wandb.ai/understanding-sam/marin/runs/qwen3_300m_error_aware_muon_hesscorr-g0p3_lr0p012-2026.08.28.3)

The stabilization solves the numerical failure, but this implementation should not be scaled further by default: blend `0.05` is better at every paired learning rate and is roughly twice as fast. A future Hesscorr experiment should first reduce the Sylvester cost, then compare Hesscorr `0.3`, Muon, and blend `0.05` across multiple seeds at learning rates `0.010` and `0.012`.

A separate v4-8 copy in `us-central2` failed before W&B initialization because its workers rejected the `us-central1` FineWeb cache. It was not retried and is not evidence about optimizer quality or stability.
